entry_json.definition: to become separated from the thing you were attached to or resting on, and drop to the ground. The object follows 'off' and the phrase never splits: fall off the shelf, not fall the shelf off.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Half the tiles fell off the roof in the storm, and the landlord took a month to replace them.
example_sentences: My phone fell off the table and the screen cracked straight down the middle.
Cyclists are far more likely to fall off in wet weather, which is why helmets should be compulsory.
collocations: fall off the back of sth

contexts.text: I fell off my bike twice in the first week and decided to take proper lessons.
contexts.note: Everyday spoken narrative, Part 2 story.

contexts.text: Without the object, 'fall off' can also mean to decrease: attendance fell off sharply after the fees rose.
contexts.note: Second sense, useful for describing a graph.

contexts.text: Numbers fell off in the second half of the year, though they never returned to the 2010 low.

confusables.difference: You fall off something you were on top of or attached to. You fall down when you were standing and end up on the ground, with no surface named.
minimal_pair: He fell off the ladder.
He fell down in the street.

entry_json.avoid: Do not split it: 'fall the bike off' is not English, and the object always comes after 'off'.
entry_json.audio_hint: The two words link: fall-off, with the stress on OFF.

entry_json.definition: a person who belongs to your family: a parent, child, sibling, or wider relative. Countable, so it needs a or the in the singular: a family member, three family members.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In my country it is normal for an older family member to live with the children rather than move into a home.
example_sentences: A close family member helped me pay for my first year of university.
Many patients rely on a family member for transport to hospital appointments.

contexts.text: The person I admire most is actually a family member, my aunt.
contexts.note: Very common opening for the Part 2 'describe a person' card.

contexts.text: Care for the elderly is still provided largely by family members rather than by the state.
contexts.note: Plural, no article, for a general statement.

contexts.text: I am writing to ask whether a family member may visit outside normal hours.

confusables.difference: A relative is usually someone outside the household: cousins, uncles, in-laws. A family member covers everyone, including the parents and children you live with.
minimal_pair: My family members were all at the wedding.
My relatives came from three different countries.

confusables.difference: Family is the whole group, family member is one person in it. You cannot say 'a family' when you mean one person.
minimal_pair: My family is large.
One family member is a doctor.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'a familiar member'. And in the singular it must have an article: 'family member helped me' is missing 'a'.

entry_json.definition: a long distance from here, or from the place being talked about. It works as an adverb after the verb, and before a noun it is hyphenated: a far-away village.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My university was far away from home, so I only went back twice a year.
example_sentences: The nearest hospital is forty kilometres away, which is far too far away in an emergency.
Working from home means it no longer matters how far away the office is.

contexts.text: Is your flat far away from the city centre? No, it is about ten minutes on foot.
contexts.note: Part 1 question about where you live.

contexts.text: Rural patients living far away from specialist centres wait significantly longer for treatment.
In questions and negatives we normally drop 'away': How far is the station? It is not far.
contexts.note: Pattern note: 'far' alone is more natural in questions and negatives.

confusables.difference: In positive statements native speakers prefer 'a long way': It is a long way from here. 'Far away' is more natural with 'too', 'not' or 'how'.
minimal_pair: It is a long way from here.
It is not far away from here.

entry_json.avoid: In a plain positive sentence 'It is far from here' sounds odd to a British ear; say 'It is a long way from here'.
entry_json.audio_hint: The r in 'far' is pronounced because 'away' begins with a vowel: fa-ra-way.

entry_json.definition: used to say that the opposite is true, or that something is nowhere near finished. After 'from' you must use the -ing form: far from solving the problem, not far from solve.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Far from solving congestion, the new ring road simply moved the traffic to a different set of streets.
example_sentences: Far from being a waste of time, learning a second language changes how you think.
The government is far from meeting its own target of halving emissions by 2030.

contexts.text: Far from reducing inequality, free university places have mainly benefited middle-class families.
contexts.note: Fronted, with a comma: a strong Task 2 counter-argument opener.

contexts.text: We are far from knowing what the long-term effects of these apps on teenagers will be.
contexts.note: Mid-sentence use after 'be'.

contexts.text: Honestly, I am far from being an expert, but I do read a lot about it.
contexts.note: A useful hedge in Part 3.

confusables.difference: 'Instead of' names the alternative you chose. 'Far from' denies the expected result and usually introduces the opposite one.
minimal_pair: Instead of solving congestion, they built houses.
Far from solving congestion, the road made it worse.

entry_json.avoid: Never follow it with an infinitive: 'far from solve the problem' is wrong; it must be 'far from solving'.

entry_json.definition: a long way from a place, or, with an adjective or noun, the opposite of it: far from perfect means not perfect at all.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The results were far from clear, so the study had to be repeated with a larger sample.
example_sentences: Our house is quite far from the nearest station, which is why we still need a car.
The system is far from ideal, but replacing it would cost more than the city can afford.

contexts.text: I live quite far from the centre, so my commute is about an hour each way.
contexts.note: Literal distance.

contexts.text: The evidence for a link between screen time and poor sleep is far from conclusive.
contexts.note: Figurative: a strong, formal way of saying 'not at all'.

contexts.text: That explanation is far from the truth, as the committee later admitted.

confusables.difference: 'Far from clear' is much stronger than 'not very clear'. It means there is no clarity at all, not just a little.
minimal_pair: The results were not very clear.
The results were far from clear.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for a small shortfall. 'Far from' claims the opposite, so it overstates if the thing is only slightly imperfect.

entry_json.definition: much more. 'Far' is an intensifier used only with comparatives, so it goes before more, less, better, worse and never before a plain adjective.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cities in the north receive far more rainfall than the coastal south, which explains the difference in farming.
example_sentences: Online courses reach far more students than a lecture hall ever could.
I enjoy reading far more than watching television, though I do both.

contexts.text: I spend far more time on my phone than I would like to admit.
The chart shows that far more households owned a car in 2020 than in 1990.
contexts.note: A cleaner alternative to 'a lot more' in Task 1.

contexts.text: Young people are far more likely to rent than to buy.

confusables.difference: 'Very' cannot go with a comparative. Use 'far more' or 'much more', never 'very more'.
minimal_pair: It is far more expensive.
It is very expensive.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'far many more people' and never 'very more'. With countable nouns say 'far more people'.

entry_json.definition: much more important. A ready-made comparison used to rank two things, normally followed by 'than' or by 'to do sth'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In my view, teaching children how to cook is far more important than teaching them a second language at primary level.
example_sentences: Practical experience is far more important than a long list of qualifications in this industry.
What is far more important is that the water supply stays clean.
collocations: far more important to do sth

chunk.pattern: X is far more important than Y

contexts.text: For me, sleep is far more important than a long gym session.
contexts.note: Part 3 opinion, comparing two options.

contexts.text: Reducing industrial emissions is far more important than asking individuals to recycle.
contexts.note: Task 2 thesis: it ranks one solution above another.

contexts.text: The cost mattered, but reliability was far more important to us.

confusables.difference: 'Far more important' compares two things. 'The most important' picks one out of all of them and needs 'the'.
minimal_pair: Health is far more important than money.
Health is the most important thing of all.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'far more importanter' or 'more far important'. The order is fixed: far + more + adjective.

entry_json.definition: many more chances to do something. A high-frequency Task 2 and Part 3 partnership, usually completed by 'to do sth', 'for sb' or 'than'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Living in a capital city gives young people far more opportunities to find work in their own field.
example_sentences: Students who speak English have far more opportunities to study abroad.
Remote working offers far more opportunities for parents with young children.
collocations: far more opportunities to do sth

chunk.pattern: give / offer / have + far more opportunities + to do sth

contexts.text: There are far more opportunities here than in the town I grew up in.
Urban migration continues because cities offer far more opportunities for skilled work.
contexts.note: Standard Task 2 reason for rural-to-urban migration.

contexts.text: The scholarship gave me far more opportunities than I had expected.

confusables.difference: In this pattern 'opportunity' is countable and plural: far more opportunities. 'Much opportunity' is uncountable and sounds odd here.
minimal_pair: far more opportunities
a great deal of opportunity

entry_json.avoid: Not 'far more opportunity of studying'. The natural follow-on is 'to study' or 'for study'.
entry_json.audio_hint: British 'opportunities' has a y-sound in the middle: op-uh-TYOO-nuh-teez.

entry_json.definition: much more than is acceptable or necessary. It goes before an adjective or adverb, or before much and many: far too expensive, far too many cars.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rents in the capital are far too high for anyone on an average salary.
example_sentences: The city has far too few green spaces for the number of people living there.
I think teenagers spend far too long staring at a screen.

contexts.text: It was far too crowded, so we left after about ten minutes.
Far too little attention has been paid to what happens to these devices once they are thrown away.
contexts.note: Works with 'little' and 'few' as well as 'much' and 'many'.

contexts.text: The instructions were far too complicated for a first-time user.

confusables.difference: 'Very' just measures. 'Far too' judges: it says the amount is beyond what is acceptable. Very expensive may still be worth buying; far too expensive is not.
minimal_pair: The flat is very expensive.
The flat is far too expensive.

entry_json.avoid: Do not put a noun straight after it. Say 'far too many cars', not 'far too cars'.

entry_json.definition: a great deal more homework than a student can reasonably do. Homework is uncountable, so it takes 'much' and never a plural s.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Children in my country are given far too much homework, and it leaves them no time for sport or family.
example_sentences: Teachers set far too much homework in the final year, which is one reason students burn out.
Parents often complain that primary pupils are given far too much homework.
collocations: be given far too much homework
far too much homework to do

chunk.pattern: give / set + sb + far too much homework

contexts.text: We had far too much homework at secondary school, honestly about three hours a night.
contexts.note: Part 1 school question.

contexts.text: Setting far too much homework can reduce motivation rather than improve results.
contexts.note: Common Task 2 topic: should homework be reduced?

contexts.text: I am writing because my son is being given far too much homework this term.
contexts.note: A complaint letter, General Training Task 1.

confusables.difference: Homework never takes a plural or 'many'. If you need to count, say 'far too many homework assignments'.
minimal_pair: far too much homework
far too many assignments

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'homeworks'. The word has no plural in English, however many exercises there are.

entry_json.definition: annoyed and bored with a situation that has gone on too long. It follows a linking verb (be, get, feel) and takes 'with' before the cause: fed up with the noise.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I got fed up with commuting three hours a day, so I looked for a job closer to home.
example_sentences: A lot of residents are fed up with the constant roadworks on the high street.
I was getting fed up with my old phone freezing every time I opened the camera.

chunk.pattern: be / get fed up with + noun / -ing

contexts.text: To be honest, I was fed up with the weather by the end of February.
contexts.note: Natural in Speaking, informal.

contexts.text: In an essay, write 'residents are increasingly frustrated with the delays' rather than 'fed up'.
contexts.note: Register warning: fed up is too informal for Task 2.

contexts.text: She finally got fed up with waiting and cancelled the order.

confusables.difference: Bored means there is nothing interesting happening. Fed up adds irritation: you have had enough of something that keeps happening.
minimal_pair: I was bored during the lecture.
I was fed up with the lecturer always arriving late.

entry_json.avoid: Spoken only. Using 'fed up' in Task 2 lowers your lexical score; use 'frustrated' or 'dissatisfied' there. Also, the preposition is 'with', not 'of' or 'about'.

entry_json.definition: to be happy, healthy or satisfied. 'Feel' is a linking verb here, so it takes the adjective good, not the adverb well in this sense.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Half an hour of exercise in the morning makes me feel good for the rest of the day.
example_sentences: It feels good to finish a piece of work you have put real effort into.
Volunteering makes people feel good about themselves, which is why so many keep doing it.
collocations: it feels good to do sth

chunk.pattern: make sb feel good / feel good about sth

contexts.text: Swimming is the one sport that always makes me feel good afterwards.
Time spent outdoors makes people feel good, and there is now solid evidence behind that impression.
I did not feel well enough to go in, so I worked from home.
contexts.note: Contrast: health uses 'feel well', mood uses 'feel good'.

confusables.difference: Feel well is about physical health only, and is mostly used in questions and negatives. Feel good covers mood, confidence and satisfaction.
minimal_pair: I do not feel well, I think I have a cold.
I feel good about the interview.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'I feel goodly'. After a linking verb like feel you need the adjective, not an adverb.

entry_json.definition: to want something, or to seem like something. When it means 'want', the next verb takes -ing: I feel like going out. It also introduces a comparison: it feels like winter.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: After a long week I never feel like cooking, which is why we order food far too often.
example_sentences: I do not feel like studying this evening, so I will start early tomorrow instead.
The exam felt like a marathon rather than a test of knowledge.

contexts.text: At the weekend I usually feel like doing nothing at all, and I think that is healthy.
contexts.note: The 'want' sense: informal, Speaking only.

contexts.text: Standing in that square, it felt like stepping back two hundred years.
contexts.note: The 'seem like' sense, good for a Part 2 description.

contexts.text: For many commuters the journey feels like a second working day.
contexts.note: The comparison sense is acceptable in writing; the 'want' sense is not.

confusables.difference: Would like is a polite request or offer and takes 'to' plus the infinitive. Feel like is a casual mood and takes -ing.
minimal_pair: I would like to go out tonight.
I feel like going out tonight.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'I feel like to go'. After 'feel like' use the -ing form or a noun.

entry_json.definition: to work out the answer to something, or come to understand a person, after some thought. It is separable: figure out the problem or figure the problem out, but with a pronoun it must split: figure it out.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took me a whole afternoon to figure out how the referencing software actually worked.
example_sentences: I could not figure out why the bill was so high until I checked the heating settings.
Once you figure the timetable out, getting around the city is straightforward.
collocations: figure out how to do sth

contexts.text: I am still trying to figure out how to use half the features on my new phone.
With a pronoun the phrase always splits: I gave her the map and she figured it out in seconds.
contexts.note: Pattern: never 'figured out it'.

contexts.text: In formal writing prefer 'determine' or 'establish': researchers have yet to establish why the effect disappears.
contexts.note: Register warning: figure out is informal.

confusables.difference: You find out a fact by asking or looking it up. You figure something out by thinking it through yourself.
minimal_pair: I found out the price by ringing the office.
I figured out the price from the table in the brochure.

entry_json.avoid: Never say 'figure out it'. A pronoun object goes in the middle: figure it out.
entry_json.audio_hint: The r links into out: FIG-ger-OWT.

entry_json.definition: to write the required information in the spaces on a form or document. It is separable: fill in the form, fill the form in, fill it in.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: You have to fill in an online application form and upload two references before the deadline.
example_sentences: Please fill in the registration form and bring it to reception on your first day.
I filled it in twice because the website timed out the first time.

contexts.text: It only takes five minutes to fill the form in if you have your passport with you.
Applicants must fill in section three before the interview.
contexts.note: Formal letter, instructions.

contexts.text: Americans usually say fill out a form; British English prefers fill in.
contexts.note: Variety note: both are correct, fill in is the British norm.

confusables.difference: Fill up means make a container full: fill up the tank. Fill in means write in the blank spaces on a form.
minimal_pair: I filled up the car before the journey.
I filled in the visa form before the journey.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'fill in it'. With a pronoun the phrase must split: fill it in.

vocab_new.lemma: find it difficult to do sth

entry_json.headword: find it difficult to do sth
entry_json.definition: to experience something as hard to do. The 'it' is a dummy subject standing in for the to-infinitive that follows, and it cannot be left out.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many students find it difficult to concentrate when they are studying in a shared flat.
example_sentences: Older workers often find it difficult to retrain for jobs in technology.
I find it difficult to speak English on the phone, even though I am fine face to face.
collocations: find it hard to do sth
find it easy to do sth

chunk.pattern: find + it + adjective + to do sth

contexts.text: I find it difficult to get up early in winter, so I do my studying at night.
Low-income families find it difficult to afford housing near the schools their children attend.
contexts.note: A clean Task 2 way of stating a problem without the word 'problem'.

contexts.text: The same frame works with other adjectives: I find it easy to remember faces but impossible to remember names.

confusables.term: it is difficult for sb to do sth
confusables.difference: Both are correct. 'Find it difficult' reports a personal experience; 'it is difficult for' states a general fact.
minimal_pair: I find it difficult to save money.
It is difficult for young people to save money.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the 'it': 'I find difficult to concentrate' is a very common error and is ungrammatical.

entry_json.definition: to learn a fact for the first time, by asking, reading or being told. It is often followed by a that-clause or a wh-clause in statement word order.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I only found out that the course had a language requirement a week before the deadline.
example_sentences: I rang the college to find out when the results would be published.
Most people find out about local events through social media rather than the newspaper.

contexts.text: How did you find out about this school? A friend of mine recommended it.
The wh-clause keeps statement order: I want to find out how much it costs, not how much does it cost.
contexts.gap_span: find out how much it costs
contexts.note: Embedded question pattern.

contexts.text: Researchers set out to find out whether the effect held in colder climates.
contexts.note: Acceptable in writing, though 'determine' is more formal.

confusables.difference: Find out is the moment of learning; know is the state afterwards. You cannot 'know' a fact for the first time.
minimal_pair: I found out yesterday that she had left.
I know that she has left.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use question word order after it: 'I want to find out where is the office' should be 'where the office is'.

entry_json.definition: to get information on a subject, usually by looking for it. 'About' introduces the topic, and the phrase never splits around it.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Before applying, I spent a week finding out about the cost of living in each city.
example_sentences: I would like to find out about the evening courses your college offers.
Most travellers find out about a destination online long before they arrive.

contexts.text: How do you usually find out about news? Mostly from my phone, on the way to work.
contexts.note: Extremely common Part 1 question frame.

contexts.text: I am writing to find out about the membership fees for the sports centre.
contexts.note: Standard opening of a General Training request letter.

contexts.text: Students should find out about visa rules before they accept a place.

confusables.difference: Hear about is passive: the news reached you. Find out about means you went looking for it.
minimal_pair: I heard about the strike on the radio.
I found out about the strike by checking their website.

entry_json.avoid: The preposition is 'about', not 'for'. 'Find out for the fees' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: to get further information about something you already know a little about. 'More' can stand alone or be followed by 'about sth'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: If you want to find out more, the college runs an open day every March.
example_sentences: I would like to find out more about the scholarships you mentioned in your letter.
Anyone wanting to find out more can attend the free session on Thursday evening.
collocations: to find out more, visit sth

contexts.text: It sounded interesting, so I stayed behind to find out more.
Could you tell me where I can find out more about the timetable?
contexts.note: Polite request in a letter or email.

contexts.text: Readers who wish to find out more are directed to the appendix.

confusables.difference: Find out more is the act of getting the information; know more is the result of having got it.
minimal_pair: I want to find out more about it.
I know more about it than I did last year.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add 'informations'. If you name the thing, use 'more about' plus a noun: find out more about the course.

entry_json.definition: to realise you are doing something, or are in a situation, that you did not plan or expect. The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject: he found himself, they found themselves.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: After two months in the job I found myself working every weekend without ever having agreed to it.
example_sentences: Many graduates find themselves doing work that has nothing to do with their degree.
I often find myself checking my phone before I have even got out of bed.
collocations: find yourself unable to do sth

contexts.text: I find myself using English more at work than in my own language these days.
contexts.note: A natural way to describe an unplanned habit.

contexts.text: Rural households increasingly find themselves paying more for basic services than city dwellers.
contexts.note: The reflexive must match the plural subject.

contexts.text: It can also take a place or adjective: after the flight was cancelled we found ourselves stuck in the airport overnight.

confusables.difference: Start doing is a deliberate beginning. Find yourself doing stresses that it happened without a decision, and you only noticed afterwards.
minimal_pair: I started working weekends to earn more.
I found myself working weekends without meaning to.

entry_json.avoid: The verb after it must be -ing, and the pronoun must agree: not 'they found himself working'.

entry_json.definition: before anything else. It introduces the first item in a sequence of points or steps, and normally sits at the start of the sentence with a comma after it.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: First of all, the government would need to make public transport cheap enough for people to give up their cars.
example_sentences: First of all, I would like to thank the committee for inviting me.
There are two reasons for this. First of all, the equipment is expensive; secondly, few staff know how to use it.
collocations: first of all, I would like to

contexts.text: Well, first of all I would say the weather, and secondly the cost of living.
contexts.note: In speech the comma is often dropped.

contexts.text: First of all, the raw material is crushed and washed.
contexts.note: Opening step of a process description.

contexts.text: If you have only one point, do not use it: 'first of all' promises a second item.
contexts.note: Discourse rule learners often break.

confusables.difference: At first contrasts the beginning with what happened later. First of all just numbers your points.
minimal_pair: At first I found it hard, but later it got easier.
First of all, I want to explain the cost.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'at the first of all' or 'firstly of all'. And do not use it unless a second point follows.

entry_json.definition: to give your attention to one thing rather than others. The preposition 'on' is fixed and never drops, and a verb after it takes -ing.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Schools should focus on teaching children how to think rather than what to remember.
example_sentences: This essay will focus on the environmental costs of cheap air travel.
I find it hard to focus on reading when my phone is on the desk.

contexts.text: In my last year I decided to focus on just two subjects, and my marks improved.
Policy has focused on building new roads rather than on reducing the need to travel.
contexts.note: Present perfect, common in a Task 2 background sentence.

contexts.text: The report focuses on three regions, all of which lost population after 2015.

confusables.difference: Almost interchangeable, but concentrate is mainly about mental effort in the moment, while focus can also describe what a report, policy or course is mostly about.
minimal_pair: I could not concentrate on the lecture.
The course focuses on medieval history.

entry_json.avoid: Never drop the preposition: 'focus the problem' is wrong. It is always focus on.

entry_json.definition: to take further action on something that has already started, such as chasing a reply or investigating a lead. It is separable: follow up the request, follow it up.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I sent the application in March and had to follow it up twice before anyone replied.
example_sentences: The clinic follows up every patient six months after treatment.
I will follow up your enquiry with the finance office and let you know.

contexts.text: Nobody got back to me, so I followed it up with a phone call.
I would be grateful if you could follow up my request before the end of the month.
contexts.note: Formal letter of complaint or enquiry.

contexts.text: As a noun it is hyphenated: patients were seen at a six-month follow-up.
contexts.note: Noun form, hyphen required.

confusables.difference: Follow without 'up' means go behind, or obey. Follow up means take the next step on something already begun.
minimal_pair: I followed the guide through the old town.
I followed up the complaint a week later.

entry_json.avoid: As a verb do not hyphenate: write 'I will follow up the request', and keep the hyphen only for the noun 'a follow-up'.

entry_json.definition: coming immediately after something in a list, a ranking or a sequence. It is a passive participle phrase, so it attaches to the item that came first.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: China was the largest producer, followed by the United States and India.
example_sentences: The most popular subject was business, followed closely by engineering.
The seeds are planted in spring, followed by three months of regular watering.
collocations: followed by a period of sth

contexts.text: Cycling was the most common way of getting to work, followed by walking.
contexts.note: The standard Task 1 device for ranking without repeating 'the second was'.

contexts.text: The mixture is heated for an hour, followed by a slow cooling period.
contexts.note: Process diagram, sequencing two stages.

contexts.text: In speech we normally say 'and then': first the tea, and then the cake.
contexts.note: Register note: 'followed by' sounds stiff in conversation.

confusables.difference: 'Following' means after, and points forwards to what comes next. 'Followed by' points from the first item to the one behind it. Swapping them reverses the order.
minimal_pair: Following the meeting, we ate.
The meeting was followed by lunch.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'followed by' when you mean 'after'. 'Followed by the meeting we ate' reverses the sequence you intended.

entry_json.definition: over a period of many months or years. With the present perfect it means the period continues; with the past simple it is finished.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have lived in the same neighbourhood for a long time, so I know almost everyone on the street.
example_sentences: Coal was the main source of energy for a long time, but its share has fallen steadily.
We waited for a long time before anyone came to the counter.

contexts.text: Have you known each other for a long time? Since primary school, actually.
The number stayed flat for a long time before rising sharply after 2010.
contexts.note: Describing a plateau on a line graph.

contexts.text: In the negative it often means 'not recently': I have not seen her for a long time.

confusables.difference: 'For' takes a length of time; 'since' takes the point it started. For a long time, but since 2015.
minimal_pair: I have worked here for a long time.
I have worked here since 2015.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'during a long time' and not 'since a long time'. The preposition is 'for'.

entry_json.definition: for a very short time, a few seconds. It is also used to frame a hypothetical: suppose for a moment that...
entry_json.own_context_sentence: For a moment I thought I had left my passport at the hotel, and my heart stopped.
example_sentences: The lights went out for a moment and then came back on.
Let us assume for a moment that the technology works exactly as promised.
collocations: for a moment I thought sth

contexts.text: Could you hold this for a moment while I find my ticket?
contexts.note: Everyday request.

contexts.text: For a moment the crowd went completely quiet, and that is the part I remember.
contexts.note: Narrative detail in a Part 2 answer.

contexts.text: Suppose for a moment that fuel prices doubled overnight.
contexts.note: Framing a hypothetical in an essay.

confusables.difference: At the moment means now. For a moment measures a short duration. They are not interchangeable.
minimal_pair: I am busy at the moment.
I was busy for a moment and then free again.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for now. 'For a moment I am living in Leeds' should be 'At the moment'.

entry_json.definition: for a period of time that is fairly long but not exact, from several minutes to several months depending on context.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I worked in a cafe for a while before I started my degree, and it taught me more than I expected.
example_sentences: Prices fell for a while, but by the end of the decade they had recovered.
Let us sit outside for a while, the room is too warm.

contexts.text: I have been thinking about moving for a while now, but rents keep going up.
contexts.note: 'for a while now' with the present perfect continuous is very natural.

contexts.text: The figure remained stable for a while before climbing again in 2018.
We lost touch for a while, then met again at a conference.

confusables.difference: For a moment is seconds. For a while is much longer and deliberately vague.
minimal_pair: The screen froze for a moment.
The website was down for a while.

entry_json.avoid: 'While' here is a noun, so it needs 'a'. Not 'for while'.

entry_json.definition: used to introduce one case that illustrates a general point. It can open a sentence with a comma after it, or sit inside one between commas.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Some jobs cannot be done from home. Surgeons, for example, have to be in the room with the patient.
example_sentences: Many everyday products contain hidden sugar. Breakfast cereal, for example, can be a third sugar by weight.
For example, Singapore reduced car ownership by making licences extremely expensive.

contexts.text: I do quite a lot of exercise. Swimming, for example, three times a week.
contexts.note: Mid-sentence, between commas, is very natural in speech.

contexts.text: For example, the Netherlands has built separate cycle networks in almost every city.
contexts.note: The example must be a full sentence when 'for example' opens one.

contexts.text: Written as an abbreviation it is e.g., used only inside brackets: renewable sources (e.g. wind, solar).
contexts.note: Do not use e.g. in the running text of an IELTS essay; write the words.

confusables.difference: 'Such as' is followed by nouns only and needs no comma after it. 'For example' can introduce a whole clause and takes a comma.
minimal_pair: Renewable sources such as wind and solar are cheaper now.
For example, wind power is now cheaper than coal.

entry_json.avoid: Do not follow it directly with a noun list and no comma: 'for example wind, solar' should be 'such as wind and solar'.

entry_json.definition: without paying anything. It goes after the verb or object: they give it away for free.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The city library lets anyone borrow e-books for free, which saved me a fortune as a student.
example_sentences: Several museums in London let visitors in for free.
The app is available for free, but the useful features cost money.

contexts.text: I got the ticket for free because I volunteered at the event.
In formal writing prefer 'free of charge': entry is free of charge for under-18s.
contexts.note: Register upgrade for Task 2.

contexts.text: Could you tell me whether the shuttle bus is for free?

confusables.difference: As an adjective 'free' comes after 'be' or before a noun: the bus is free, free entry. 'For free' is adverbial and follows an action verb: they give it away for free.
minimal_pair: Entry is free.
They let us in for free.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'it is for free' with the verb be. Say 'it is free', or 'free of charge' in formal writing.

entry_json.definition: used to introduce an example. It works exactly like 'for example' and is slightly more formal, which makes it a useful alternative when you have already written 'for example' once.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Some cities have made real progress on air quality. Oslo, for instance, has banned diesel cars from the centre on the worst days.
example_sentences: For instance, a single long-haul flight can produce more carbon than a year of driving.
Certain subjects attract far more applicants. Medicine, for instance, turns away most of the people who apply.

contexts.text: For instance, countries with high fuel taxes tend to have smaller cars.
contexts.note: Use it the second time so you do not repeat 'for example'.

contexts.text: My brother, for instance, has never owned a car and cycles everywhere.
contexts.note: Acceptable in speech, though 'for example' is more common there.

contexts.text: Several materials can be recycled indefinitely, glass for instance.
contexts.note: It can also sit at the end of the sentence.

confusables.difference: The meaning is the same. 'For instance' is a shade more formal and slightly less frequent, which is exactly why it is useful for variety.
minimal_pair: For example, wind power is cheap.
For instance, wind power is cheap.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'for an instance' and not 'for instant'. An instant is a moment of time, an instance is a case.

entry_json.definition: for the rest of somebody's life, permanently. No article: for life, not for the life.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A job for life is now rare, and most graduates expect to change career at least twice.
example_sentences: Learning to swim is a skill you keep for life.
The injury left him unable to run for life, though he still coaches.

contexts.text: We met at university and have been friends for life.
The idea of a job for life disappeared with the old manufacturing industries.
contexts.note: A ready-made Task 2 phrase about changing employment patterns.

contexts.text: Membership costs 200 pounds for life rather than an annual fee.

confusables.difference: For life is fixed and idiomatic. 'For a lifetime' emphasises the length of the period rather than permanence, and is less common.
minimal_pair: He was jailed for life.
It was enough food for a lifetime.

entry_json.avoid: No article and no plural: not 'for the life', not 'for lives'.

entry_json.definition: for a long time. It is used almost only in questions and negatives; in a positive statement English prefers 'for a long time'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I did not stay in that job for long, because the commute was simply unsustainable.
example_sentences: Have you been waiting for long? Only about five minutes.
The good weather did not last for long, and by Sunday it was raining again.
collocations: have you been here for long?

contexts.text: Did you live there for long? No, less than a year.
contexts.note: Question form, extremely natural.

contexts.text: The price rise did not hold for long: within six months it had fallen back.
contexts.note: Negative context in a written report.

contexts.text: In a positive sentence switch to 'for a long time': I have known him for a long time.
contexts.note: This is the rule learners break most often.

confusables.difference: 'For a long time' works everywhere. 'For long' is restricted to questions and negatives.
minimal_pair: I have lived here for a long time.
I have not lived here for long.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it in a plain positive statement: 'I have worked here for long' is wrong; say 'for a long time'.

entry_json.definition: as the meal you eat in the middle of the day, or for the purpose of eating it. Meal names take no article in this pattern: for lunch, for breakfast, for dinner.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I usually have something quick for lunch, normally a sandwich at my desk.
example_sentences: We stopped at a small place by the river for lunch.
What do you normally have for lunch on a working day?

contexts.text: What did you have for lunch today? Just rice and vegetables.
contexts.note: Classic Part 1 food question.

contexts.text: We are meeting for lunch on Friday to go through the plan.
The article is available in the appendix; note that with a modifier the article returns: we had a long lunch.
contexts.note: Article rule: zero article only when the meal is unmodified.

confusables.difference: At lunch means during the lunch break. For lunch names what you ate or why you went.
minimal_pair: She is at lunch until two.
She had soup for lunch.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'for the lunch' or 'for a lunch' unless there is an adjective, as in 'for a quick lunch'.

entry_json.definition: over a long period measured in years. With the present perfect the period reaches the present; with the past simple it ended.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: For many years the factory was the only large employer in the town, and its closure changed everything.
example_sentences: Coal has been mined in this valley for many years, though the last pit closed in 1994.
For many years it was assumed that the two variables were unrelated.

contexts.text: My grandmother taught at the same school for many years.
For many years the figure remained below 20 per cent before rising sharply in 2005.
contexts.note: Useful for a long flat section of a line graph.

contexts.text: Fossil fuels will remain part of the mix for many years to come.
contexts.note: The forward-looking variant.

confusables.difference: 'Since' cannot take a length of time. Use 'for many years' or 'since 1994'.
minimal_pair: I have lived here for many years.
I have lived here since 2001.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'since many years'. This is one of the most recognisable non-native errors in Writing.

entry_json.definition: for a fairly long period, left deliberately vague. It is a more formal alternative to 'for a while' and is common in academic writing.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Economists have warned for some time that housing costs would eventually limit growth in the region.
example_sentences: The link between air pollution and asthma has been known for some time.
The road was closed for some time after the accident.
collocations: have been sth for some time

chunk.pattern: have + past participle + for some time

contexts.text: Researchers have suspected for some time that the effect is smaller than first reported.
contexts.note: Present perfect: a strong opening move for a Task 2 background.

contexts.text: I have been meaning to take it up again for some time.
The shortage is likely to continue for some time to come.

confusables.difference: 'For some time' is a duration reaching into the present. 'Some time ago' is a point in the past.
minimal_pair: I have known for some time.
I found out some time ago.

entry_json.avoid: Keep 'some time' as two words here. 'Sometime' as one word means at an unspecified point, which is a different meaning.

entry_json.definition: used to add a second case which the same point also covers, often a stronger or wider one. It comes after the added item and is separated by commas.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have never enjoyed running, or any competitive sport for that matter.
example_sentences: The town has no cinema, or theatre for that matter.
Neither the students nor, for that matter, most of the staff had been told about the change.

contexts.text: I do not really watch television, or films for that matter.
contexts.note: Natural in Speaking; it extends your own answer without repeating yourself.

contexts.text: There is little evidence for this claim, or for the opposite one for that matter.
contexts.note: Acceptable in essays, though it stays slightly conversational.

contexts.text: The bus never runs on time, and nor for that matter does the train.

confusables.difference: 'As a matter of fact' corrects or adds a surprising truth. 'For that matter' extends the same point to another case.
minimal_pair: As a matter of fact, I have already read it.
I have not read it, or anything else by her for that matter.

entry_json.avoid: It cannot open a sentence on its own. It must follow the extra item it is attaching to.

entry_json.definition: in order to help a particular person or group, or so that they gain from it. The 'the' is fixed and the person follows 'of'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The scheme was set up for the benefit of families who cannot afford private tuition.
example_sentences: Green spaces are maintained for the benefit of everyone living in the area, not just those with gardens.
For the benefit of new members, I will summarise what was agreed last month.
collocations: for the benefit of future generations
for the mutual benefit of sb

chunk.pattern: for the benefit of + person / group

contexts.text: Public funding for the arts exists for the benefit of the whole population, not only those who buy tickets.
contexts.note: Strong Task 2 phrasing for a public-good argument.

contexts.text: Resources should be managed for the benefit of future generations.
For the benefit of anyone who missed the announcement, the deadline has moved to Friday.

confusables.difference: Benefit from is a verb: people benefit from the scheme. For the benefit of is a purpose phrase: the scheme exists for the benefit of people.
minimal_pair: Students benefit from small classes.
The class was reduced for the benefit of the students.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'the' or swap the preposition: not 'for benefit of' and not 'for the benefit to'.

entry_json.definition: on the first occasion something has ever happened. It often signals a milestone, and pairs naturally with the present perfect or past simple.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Last year, for the first time, more electricity came from renewables than from coal.
example_sentences: I flew for the first time when I was nineteen, and I was terrified.
For the first time since records began, the river dried up completely in August.
collocations: for the first time in years
for the first time since sth

chunk.pattern: for the first time (in / since + period)

contexts.text: I tried cooking it myself for the first time last month and it went surprisingly well.
In 2019, for the first time, the number of online purchases overtook shop sales.
contexts.note: Marking a crossover point on a graph, a high-value Task 1 move.

contexts.text: This is the first time I have visited the UK, so everything still feels new.
contexts.gap_span: the first time I have visited
contexts.note: Related pattern: 'It is the first time + present perfect'.

confusables.difference: At first contrasts an early stage with what came later. For the first time counts occasions: it was occasion number one.
minimal_pair: At first I did not like it.
I tried it for the first time in 2019.

entry_json.avoid: Keep 'the': not 'for first time'. And after 'It is the first time' use the present perfect, not the present simple.

entry_json.definition: for all the remaining part of a period or a group. The verb agrees with what follows 'of': the rest of the week is, the rest of the students are.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It rained on the first morning and then stayed dry for the rest of the trip.
example_sentences: He was ill on Monday and worked from home for the rest of the week.
A decision made at eighteen can shape what you do for the rest of your life.
collocations: for the rest of the day
for the rest of your life
for the rest of the year

chunk.pattern: for the rest of + the + period

contexts.text: If I have a coffee after four I am awake for the rest of the night.
Numbers rose in January and remained stable for the rest of the year.
A criminal record can limit your options for the rest of your life.

confusables.difference: 'The rest of' takes a following noun phrase. 'The others' stands alone and refers back to a group already mentioned.
minimal_pair: The rest of the students stayed.
Two left and the others stayed.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'of' before a noun: 'for the rest the week' is wrong. And 'rest' here is singular even when what follows is plural.

entry_json.definition: in order to help somebody, or in order to achieve something. With a person it means for their good; with a noun such as clarity or argument it means in order to get that.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many parents stay in a job they dislike for the sake of their children.
example_sentences: For the sake of clarity, the figures have been rounded to the nearest thousand.
They moved to a quieter town for the sake of their daughter, who has asthma.

chunk.pattern: for the sake of + person / abstract noun

contexts.text: For the sake of argument, let us assume that fuel prices stay where they are.
contexts.note: A neat way to set up a hypothetical in an essay.

contexts.text: I gave up smoking for the sake of my family more than for my own health.
With a possessive the shape changes: they did it for their children's sake.
contexts.note: Alternative pattern: possessive + sake.

confusables.difference: Because of gives the cause. For the sake of gives the purpose or the person you are trying to benefit.
minimal_pair: We moved because of his job.
We moved for the sake of his health.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for a plain cause. 'I was late for the sake of the traffic' is wrong; that needs 'because of'.

entry_json.definition: because of what has just been said. It links back to the previous sentence, so it cannot be the first sentence of a paragraph with nothing before it.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rents near the university have doubled in five years. For this reason, many students now commute from neighbouring towns.
example_sentences: Batteries are expensive to recycle. For this reason, most of them end up in landfill.
The evidence is limited and partly contradictory; for these reasons the policy has not been adopted.

contexts.text: Air quality in the centre is poor. For this reason, several cities have introduced charges for older vehicles.
contexts.note: A cleaner result linker than 'so' in Task 2.

contexts.text: Use the plural when you have listed more than one cause: for these reasons.
contexts.note: Agreement point learners miss.

contexts.text: In speech people simply say 'that is why': that is why I moved.
contexts.note: Spoken equivalent.

confusables.difference: Both link cause to result. 'For this reason' is slightly more formal and always starts a new sentence; 'because of this' is more common in speech.
minimal_pair: For this reason, the plan was dropped.
Because of this, the plan was dropped.

entry_json.avoid: It points backwards, so do not open an essay with it. There must be a stated cause immediately before.

entry_json.definition: to do something wrong and not be caught or punished for it. Both particles are fixed and the object always comes last: get away with it, never get it away with.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: If fines are small enough, companies simply pay them and get away with polluting the river.
example_sentences: Nobody should be able to get away with cheating in an examination.
He got away with it for years before an audit uncovered the payments.
collocations: let sb get away with sth

contexts.text: When the fine is lower than the profit, firms get away with breaking the rules.
contexts.note: Good for a Task 2 argument about punishment being too weak.

contexts.text: You can get away with a light jacket in October, but not in November.
contexts.note: Weaker sense: manage with something less than ideal.

contexts.text: It is worrying how many people get away with driving while using a phone.

confusables.difference: Get away on its own means escape or take a holiday. Get away with adds the idea of avoiding punishment for something you did.
minimal_pair: We got away for a few days in June.
He got away with taking the money.

entry_json.avoid: The verb after it must be -ing: 'get away with cheat' is wrong. And never split the particles.

entry_json.definition: to return to the place you came from. With 'to' it names the destination: get back to work, get back to the hotel. Before 'home' there is no 'to'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: By the time I get back from work it is usually dark, so I exercise at the weekend instead.
example_sentences: We got back to the hotel just before the storm started.
I will get back to you as soon as I have spoken to the office.

contexts.text: What time do you usually get back home? About seven, if the traffic is normal.
contexts.note: Note: get back home, never get back to home.

contexts.text: I would be grateful if someone could get back to me before Friday.
contexts.note: 'Get back to sb' means reply, and is fine in a semi-formal email.

contexts.text: After the break it took me a while to get back into the habit of studying every evening.
contexts.note: Related: get back into sth means restart a habit.

confusables.difference: Come back is movement towards the speaker. Get back emphasises arriving after a journey, and works from any viewpoint.
minimal_pair: Come back when you are ready.
I got back at midnight.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'get back to home'. Home takes no preposition after a verb of movement.

entry_json.definition: to improve, or to recover from an illness. 'Get' here means become, so it is followed by the comparative adjective, and 'at' introduces the skill: get better at cooking.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My listening got better once I stopped using subtitles.
example_sentences: Air quality in the city has got better since the low-emission zone was introduced.
She was off work for a week but is getting better now.

contexts.text: I am slowly getting better at speaking without translating in my head first.
contexts.note: The skill sense; 'at' plus -ing.

contexts.text: He caught flu in January and did not really get better until March.
contexts.note: The recovery sense.

contexts.text: In an essay prefer 'improve': water quality has improved considerably since 2005.
contexts.note: Register upgrade: 'get better' is a little plain for Writing.

confusables.difference: Both are grammatical, but 'get better' is the ordinary spoken form. 'Become' sounds formal and is rarely used with 'better' in conversation.
minimal_pair: I got better at it.
Conditions became better after the reforms.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'get more better'. And after 'better at' use the -ing form, not the infinitive.

entry_json.definition: to arrive at the place you live. 'Home' works as an adverb here, so there is no preposition and no article.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I rarely get home before eight, which is why I do most of my cooking at the weekend.
example_sentences: It takes me about fifty minutes to get home if I miss the express train.
Text me when you get home so I know you arrived safely.

contexts.text: How long does it take you to get home from work? Around forty minutes on a good day.
contexts.note: Very common Part 1 exchange.

contexts.text: The first thing I do when I get home is put the kettle on.
contexts.note: Present simple after 'when' for a routine.

contexts.text: Later trains would allow shift workers to get home safely after midnight.

confusables.difference: Go home is leaving for home; get home is arriving there.
minimal_pair: I went home at six.
I got home at seven.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'get to home' or 'get at home'. With home the preposition disappears.

entry_json.definition: to enter a small enclosed vehicle such as a car or taxi, to arrive somewhere, or to be admitted to a place or institution. With cars and taxis you get in; with buses, trains and planes you get on.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Our flight got in at two in the morning, so we slept most of the first day.
example_sentences: Get in, I will drive you to the station.
She applied to three universities and got in to all of them.

contexts.text: We got in a taxi because the last bus had already gone.
contexts.note: Cars and taxis take 'in', not 'on'.

contexts.text: What time does your train get in? Half past nine, if it is on time.
contexts.note: The 'arrive' sense, used with trains and flights.

contexts.text: Competition is so strong that even excellent candidates do not always get in.
contexts.note: The admission sense.

confusables.difference: Get in is for vehicles you sit down inside without standing up: cars, taxis, small boats. Get on is for anything you can walk about in: buses, trains, planes.
minimal_pair: I got in the car.
I got on the bus.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'get in the bus'. Buses take 'on', however crowded they are.

entry_json.definition: to contact somebody by phone, message or email. It takes 'with' before the person: get in touch with the office.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: If you need any further information, please get in touch with the admissions office directly.
example_sentences: I got in touch with an old classmate through a professional network.
Do get in touch if anything is unclear before the deadline.

contexts.text: Please get in touch with me on the number below if the date does not suit you.
contexts.note: The standard closing line of a General Training letter.

contexts.text: We got in touch again after about ten years, which felt strange at first.
'Touch' has no article here, and 'in' never becomes 'into'.
contexts.note: Form note.

confusables.difference: Get in touch is making contact once. Keep in touch is staying in contact over time.
minimal_pair: I got in touch with her last week.
We have kept in touch ever since.

entry_json.avoid: The preposition before the person is 'with', not 'to': not 'get in touch to the office'.

entry_json.definition: to become involved or interested in something, to be admitted to an institution, or to enter a place or vehicle. The object always follows 'into'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I got into photography during the pandemic and it has become the thing I spend most of my free time on.
example_sentences: It is very hard to get into medicine without top grades.
Do not get into an argument with someone who is only trying to provoke you.

contexts.text: How did you get into running? A colleague asked me to join a charity race.
contexts.note: The 'become interested' sense: perfect for a Part 2 hobby card.

contexts.text: Students from poorer areas are still far less likely to get into the most selective universities.
contexts.note: The admission sense.

contexts.text: Once you get into the habit of walking to work, it is hard to go back to driving.
contexts.note: Fixed collocation, followed by -ing.

confusables.difference: Get in has no object; get into names the thing entered. You get in and you get into the car.
minimal_pair: Get in, we are late.
He got into the car and drove off.

entry_json.avoid: After 'get into the habit of' you must use -ing: not 'the habit of walk'.

entry_json.definition: to become unable to find your way. 'Get' means become, and 'lost' is an adjective here, so it never takes an object.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We got lost in the old part of the city, which turned out to be the best afternoon of the holiday.
example_sentences: It is easy to get lost in a hospital that size, even with signs everywhere.
I got lost twice on my first day and arrived late to both lectures.
collocations: get lost on the way to sth

contexts.text: I got lost on the way there because my phone had no signal.
contexts.note: A reliable detail for a Part 2 travel story.

contexts.text: Clearer signage would stop visitors getting lost between the two terminals.
As a rude command, 'get lost!' means go away, and should be avoided in the exam.
contexts.note: Warning: the imperative is offensive.

confusables.difference: 'Lose' takes an object: you lose your keys. 'Get lost' has no object and describes what happens to you.
minimal_pair: I lost my keys.
I got lost.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it with an object: 'I got lost my way' is wrong. Say 'I lost my way' or 'I got lost'.

entry_json.definition: to become somebody's husband or wife. The partner follows 'to', never 'with': she got married to a doctor.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: People in my country tend to get married later than they did a generation ago.
example_sentences: My sister got married last summer in a very small ceremony.
The average age at which people get married has risen by almost six years since 1990.
collocations: the age at which people get married

contexts.text: Most of my friends got married in their early thirties.
The chart shows that fewer couples got married in 2020 than in any previous year.
The state 'be married' is different from the event 'get married': they have been married for ten years.
contexts.note: Event versus state.

confusables.difference: 'Marry' takes a direct object with no preposition: he married her. 'Get married' takes 'to'.
minimal_pair: He married her in 2019.
He got married to her in 2019.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'get married with somebody'. The preposition is 'to', and 'marry with' is wrong as well.

entry_json.definition: to leave a bus, train, plane or bicycle. It can stand alone or take the vehicle as an object: get off at the next stop, get off the train.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Get off at the third stop and the museum is directly opposite.
example_sentences: We got off two stops early and walked the rest of the way.
Passengers should let people get off before they try to get on.

contexts.text: Which stop do I get off at for the stadium?
contexts.note: The preposition can end the question in normal speech.

contexts.text: Passengers must not get off while the vehicle is moving.
It also means finish work: I get off at five on Fridays.
contexts.note: Second sense, informal.

confusables.difference: You get off buses, trains, planes and bikes. You get out of cars and taxis.
minimal_pair: I got off the train.
I got out of the taxi.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'get off from the bus'. The vehicle follows 'off' directly.

entry_json.definition: to leave a bus at a stop. Buses, trains, planes and bicycles all take 'off' because you can stand up and walk about in them.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I get off the bus one stop early so that I walk for at least ten minutes each morning.
example_sentences: She got off the bus at the wrong stop and had to wait twenty minutes for the next one.
Wait for the doors to open fully before you get off the bus.
collocations: get off the bus at sth
let passengers get off the bus

contexts.text: I usually get off the bus near the market and walk from there.
Elderly passengers need more time to get off the bus safely.
contexts.note: Useful in a letter suggesting a service improvement.

contexts.text: The same pattern covers trains and planes: get off the train, get off the plane.

confusables.difference: 'Get down from' is a direct translation many learners make, but English uses 'get off'.
minimal_pair: I got off the bus.
I climbed down from the roof.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'get down from the bus' and not 'get off from the bus'.

entry_json.definition: to board a bus, train or plane, or to make progress with something. With 'with' plus a person it means to have a friendly relationship.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I get on at the second stop, which means I almost always find a seat.
example_sentences: Everyone got on at once and the doors would not close.
How are you getting on with the report? Slowly, but I should finish by Thursday.

chunk.pattern: get on (+ vehicle) / get on with + sth

contexts.text: We got on at Victoria and the train was already full.
contexts.note: The boarding sense.

contexts.text: How are you getting on with your studies? Better than last term, thank you.
contexts.note: The progress sense, very common in British English.

contexts.text: In writing use 'progress': the project is progressing more slowly than expected.
contexts.note: Register upgrade.

confusables.difference: You get on a bus, train or plane. You get in a car or taxi.
minimal_pair: I got on the plane.
I got in the taxi.

entry_json.avoid: Do not mix the senses. 'Get on with sb' is about relationships; 'get on with sth' is about work.

entry_json.definition: to board a bus. Public vehicles you can walk about in take 'on': the bus, the train, the plane, the underground.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I get on the bus at half past seven and it takes about forty minutes to reach the office.
example_sentences: Let the passengers off before you get on the bus.
He got on the bus without a ticket and had to pay a fine.
collocations: get on the bus at sth

contexts.text: I get on the bus outside my building, so I never have to walk far in the rain.
Fewer people would get on the bus if the service were reduced to once an hour.
I got on the wrong bus and ended up on the other side of the city.

confusables.difference: 'In' is only for cars and taxis. A bus always takes 'on', even though you are inside it.
minimal_pair: I got on the bus.
I got in the car.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'get in the bus' and not 'get up the bus'.

entry_json.definition: to have a friendly, easy relationship with somebody. It is normally used with an adverb such as well or badly, and both particles are fixed.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I get on well with the people I share a flat with, which makes a real difference to daily life.
example_sentences: She gets on with almost everyone in the team, which is why she was chosen to lead it.
My brother and I did not get on at all as teenagers, but we are close now.

contexts.text: Do you get on well with your neighbours? Yes, though we do not see each other often.
contexts.note: A standard Part 1 question about neighbours or colleagues.

contexts.text: Teams whose members get on with one another tend to lose fewer staff.
In American English people say 'get along with', which means the same thing.
contexts.note: Variety note.

confusables.difference: With a person it means have a good relationship. With a thing it means continue doing it: get on with your homework.
minimal_pair: I get on with my boss.
I need to get on with my essay.

entry_json.avoid: The adverb goes before 'with': 'get on well with him', not 'get on with him well'.

entry_json.definition: to leave a place, especially a car or a building, or to go out socially. Without an object it often means escape or leave quickly.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I try to get out of the house at lunchtime, even if it is only for ten minutes.
example_sentences: The alarm went off and everyone got out within two minutes.
Since the baby was born we hardly ever get out in the evening.

contexts.text: I should get out more at the weekend instead of staying in with my laptop.
contexts.note: The social sense, always with no object.

contexts.text: Everyone managed to get out before the fire spread to the second floor.
As a shouted command it is aggressive: 'get out!' means leave immediately.
contexts.note: Tone warning.

confusables.difference: Go out is usually planned social activity. Get out stresses leaving an enclosed place, or escaping the house.
minimal_pair: We went out for dinner.
I need to get out of this room for five minutes.

entry_json.avoid: If you name the place you must add 'of': 'get out the car' is non-standard; write 'get out of the car'.

entry_json.definition: to leave a car or an enclosed space, or to avoid a duty you had agreed to. In the avoidance sense the verb after 'of' takes -ing: get out of doing the washing-up.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I could not get out of the meeting, so I rearranged the appointment instead.
example_sentences: She got out of the taxi and realised she had left her bag on the seat.
Some students try to get out of group work because they find it stressful.
collocations: get out of the habit of sth

contexts.text: We got out of the car and walked the last half mile because the road was blocked.
contexts.note: The literal sense: cars take 'out of', not 'off'.

contexts.text: I have got out of the habit of reading before bed, and my sleep is worse for it.
contexts.gap_span: got out of the habit of
contexts.note: Fixed pattern, followed by -ing.

contexts.text: Firms should not be able to get out of paying compensation by restructuring.
contexts.note: The avoidance sense.

confusables.difference: Get off is for buses, trains and bikes. Get out of is for cars, taxis and rooms.
minimal_pair: I got off the train.
I got out of the car.

entry_json.avoid: In the avoidance sense never use an infinitive: 'get out of to pay' is wrong; it must be 'get out of paying'.

entry_json.definition: to recover from an illness, a shock or a difficult experience, or to stop feeling upset about a person. The object always follows 'over' and never splits it.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took me a month to get over the flu, and even then I was tired for weeks.
example_sentences: It can take years to get over the loss of a close friend.
She never really got over the disappointment of not being selected.

contexts.text: I got over the jet lag after about three days.
Communities take a long time to get over a disaster of that scale.
contexts.note: In an essay 'recover from' is a little more formal.

contexts.text: There is a separate idiom: I cannot get over how much the city has changed, meaning I am amazed.
contexts.note: Idiomatic second sense, spoken only.

confusables.difference: Overcome is about defeating a difficulty by effort: overcome an obstacle. Get over is about recovering emotionally or physically, with time.
minimal_pair: She overcame her fear of flying.
She got over the illness in a week.

entry_json.avoid: Never split it: 'get it over' means something different, and 'get over it' is the only correct order with a pronoun.

entry_json.definition: to prepare yourself for something that is about to happen. 'Get' means become, and it takes no object unless you add one: get the children ready.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It takes me about twenty minutes to get ready in the morning, mostly because of breakfast.
example_sentences: Give me five minutes to get ready and we can leave.
The whole family was getting ready for the wedding at the same time.

contexts.text: How long does it take you to get ready in the morning? Around half an hour.
contexts.note: Classic Part 1 daily-routine question.

contexts.text: With an object it splits around the person: I get the children ready before I get ready myself.
contexts.note: Pattern: get + person + ready.

contexts.text: In writing prefer 'prepare': staff were given a week to prepare for the inspection.
contexts.note: Register upgrade.

confusables.difference: Be ready is the finished state. Get ready is the process of becoming ready.
minimal_pair: I am ready.
I am getting ready.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add 'myself' unnecessarily: 'I get ready' is correct English; 'I get myself ready' sounds odd unless you are contrasting yourself with someone else.

entry_json.definition: to prepare for a particular event. The event follows 'for' as a noun; if you want a verb, use 'get ready to do sth' instead.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I spent three months getting ready for the exam, mostly working on my writing.
example_sentences: Farmers were getting ready for the harvest when the storm hit.
The city spent two years getting ready for the tournament.

contexts.text: How are you getting ready for the test? Mainly by doing practice papers.
Coastal towns are getting ready for higher sea levels by rebuilding their defences.
contexts.note: In an essay 'preparing for' is more formal.

contexts.text: For an action use the infinitive instead: we got ready to leave as soon as the rain stopped.
contexts.note: Contrast with the to-infinitive pattern.

confusables.difference: The same meaning, but 'prepare for' is more formal and is the better choice in Task 2.
minimal_pair: I am getting ready for the exam.
Candidates should prepare for the examination carefully.

entry_json.avoid: Do not put a verb straight after 'for': not 'get ready for leave'. Use 'get ready to leave'.

entry_json.definition: to prepare so that you can do something. This is the pattern that takes a verb; use 'get ready for' when what follows is a noun.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We were getting ready to leave when the airline sent a message saying the flight was delayed.
example_sentences: Passengers should get ready to board about twenty minutes before departure.
The company is getting ready to open two more branches this year.

contexts.text: I was just getting ready to go out when it started pouring with rain.
contexts.note: Past continuous, setting the scene in a story.

contexts.text: Schools are getting ready to teach the new syllabus from September.
With a noun the preposition changes: get ready for the journey, not get ready to the journey.
contexts.note: Pattern contrast.

confusables.difference: 'To do sth' takes a verb; 'for sth' takes a noun. Choosing the wrong one is the commonest mistake with this phrase.
minimal_pair: get ready to travel
get ready for the journey

entry_json.avoid: Not 'get ready to leaving' and not 'get ready for leave'. Verb takes 'to', noun takes 'for'.

entry_json.definition: to remove or throw away something you no longer want, or to make somebody leave. The three words are fixed and the object always comes after 'of'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Before I moved I got rid of about half my books, and I have not missed a single one.
example_sentences: The council is trying to get rid of the illegal dumping along the canal.
Simply banning plastic bags will not get rid of the problem on its own.
collocations: try to get rid of sth

contexts.text: I finally got rid of my old laptop by taking it to a recycling point.
In formal writing prefer 'eliminate' or 'remove': the policy aims to eliminate single-use packaging by 2030.
contexts.note: Register upgrade for Task 2.

contexts.text: It is far harder to get rid of a bad habit than to form a good one.

confusables.difference: Throw away is literally putting something in the bin. Get rid of is broader: you can sell, give away or destroy it.
minimal_pair: I threw the packaging away.
I got rid of the car by selling it.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'get rid off' with two f's, and never drop 'of': 'get rid the rubbish' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: to arrive at the place already mentioned. 'There' is an adverb, so no preposition is used. It also means to succeed eventually: we are getting there.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is about an hour by train, but if you drive at rush hour you will never get there on time.
example_sentences: How do you get there from the station?
The project is not finished, but we are getting there.

contexts.text: It takes about twenty minutes to get there if the traffic is light.
The best way to get there is the coastal path, which takes about two hours on foot.
contexts.note: Giving directions in a letter.

contexts.text: My English is not perfect yet, but I am getting there.
contexts.note: The 'making progress' idiom, spoken only.

confusables.difference: Both are correct, but 'get there' is far more common in speech and focuses on the journey; 'arrive' is more formal.
minimal_pair: We got there at six.
The delegation arrived at six.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'get to there'. Adverbs like there, here and home take no preposition.

entry_json.definition: to come to know somebody gradually, over a period of time. 'Know' is a state; 'get to know' is the process of reaching that state.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took me a term to get to know anyone properly, because I was commuting rather than living on campus.
example_sentences: Sharing a flat is the fastest way to get to know people in a new city.
Once you get to know her, she is very direct and easy to work with.
collocations: take time to get to know sb

contexts.text: The best thing about the course was getting to know students from other countries.
Newcomers who never get to know their neighbours are far more likely to move away again.
It works with places and systems too: it took a month to get to know the city.

confusables.difference: Meet is the single first occasion. Get to know is the slow process afterwards.
minimal_pair: I met her at a conference.
I got to know her over the following year.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'know' for the first meeting: 'I knew him last week' is wrong; say 'I met him last week'.

entry_json.definition: to reach a place, or, before a verb, to have the chance to do something. Before a place name it needs 'to'; before home, there and here it does not.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It takes me about forty minutes to get to work if I leave before eight.
example_sentences: What time did you get to the airport?
I never got to see the exhibition because it closed early.

chunk.pattern: get to + place / get to + verb

contexts.text: How do you get to university every day? By tram, and it is usually reliable.
contexts.note: The most frequent Part 1 transport question.

contexts.text: Before home, there and here the 'to' disappears: get home, get there, get here.
contexts.note: The exception learners forget.

contexts.text: On that trip I got to try food I had never even heard of.
contexts.note: The 'had the opportunity' sense, informal.

confusables.difference: Get to is neutral and very common in speech. Arrive takes 'in' with towns and countries and 'at' with buildings, and is more formal.
minimal_pair: I got to the office at nine.
I arrived at the office at nine.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'get to home'. And do not confuse it with 'have got to', which means must.
entry_json.audio_hint: In fast speech 'get to' is often heard as getta.

entry_json.definition: to leave your bed after sleeping, or to stand up from a sitting position. It has no object, and it is the moment of getting out of bed, not of waking.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I get up at half past six on weekdays, though at the weekend I let myself sleep in.
example_sentences: He got up, opened the curtains and went straight back to bed.
Older employees who have to get up before five report far worse sleep quality.
collocations: have to get up at sth

contexts.text: What time do you usually get up? Around seven, but earlier if I am working.
contexts.note: The most predictable Part 1 routine question of all.

contexts.text: She got up to answer the door and did not sit down again for an hour.
contexts.note: The 'stand up' sense.

contexts.text: Teenagers forced to get up at six for school are chronically short of sleep.

confusables.difference: Wake up is opening your eyes; get up is leaving the bed. You can wake up at six and get up at seven.
minimal_pair: I woke up at six.
I got up at seven.

entry_json.avoid: It takes no object: 'get up the children' is wrong. To rouse someone else say 'wake the children up'.

entry_json.definition: to become familiar with something over time so that it stops feeling strange. Here 'to' is a preposition, so the verb after it must be -ing, not the infinitive.
