You soon get used to paying for things with your phone.
collocations: take time to get used to sth

contexts.text: I am still getting used to working from home; I miss the routine of the office.
contexts.note: Present continuous: the process is still going on.

contexts.text: Older workers may need longer to get used to using new software.

confusables.difference: 'Used to do' is a habit that stopped in the past and takes the infinitive. 'Get used to doing' is becoming familiar with something now, and takes -ing.
minimal_pair: I used to live alone.
I got used to living alone.

entry_json.avoid: The commonest error in the whole language: 'I am getting used to live here' should be 'to living here'.
entry_json.audio_hint: 'used' here is pronounced with an s sound, not a z: yoost.

entry_json.definition: to become familiar with something new so that it no longer feels strange. With a noun after 'to' the pattern is straightforward; with a verb it must be -ing.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took me about a month to get used to the climate, especially how early it gets dark.
example_sentences: I never really got used to the noise of living beside a main road.
New arrivals have to get used to a completely different working culture.
collocations: get used to a new job
hard to get used to sth

contexts.text: Have you got used to the food here? Mostly, although I still cook at home a lot.
Commuters have got used to delays, which is perhaps the most worrying part of the story.
'Be used to' is the finished state: I am used to the cold now.
contexts.note: Process versus state.

confusables.difference: 'Be used to' is the state of already being familiar. 'Get used to' is the change into that state.
minimal_pair: I am used to the cold.
I am getting used to the cold.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the 'to': 'get used the weather' is wrong. And do not confuse it with 'use', which is a plain verb.

entry_json.definition: to stop doing something you did regularly, especially a habit, or to hand something over. It is separable: give up smoking, give it up.

example_sentences: She gave up a well-paid job to retrain as a teacher.
Most people who give smoking up do so several times before it lasts.

contexts.text: My father gave up smoking twenty years ago and has never gone back to it.
contexts.note: The habit sense, followed by -ing or a noun.

contexts.text: Higher taxes alone will not persuade people to give up driving in city centres.
With a pronoun it must split: I loved that class but I had to give it up.
contexts.note: Never 'give up it'.

confusables.difference: Stop is neutral and can be temporary. Give up implies ending a long-standing habit or activity for good, often with effort.
minimal_pair: I stopped working at six.
I gave up working at weekends.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'give up it'. A pronoun object always goes between the two words.

entry_json.definition: to stop trying because something is too difficult. Used without an object it means to admit defeat, which is a different sense from 'give sth up'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I almost gave up in the second year, but a tutor persuaded me to stay on the course.
example_sentences: Do not give up after one rejection; most people apply several times.
The team was losing three nil at half time but refused to give up.

contexts.text: I nearly gave up learning the guitar, and I am glad I did not.
Students who give up early often do so because nobody explained why the subject matters.
In formal writing prefer 'abandon the attempt' or 'withdraw'.
contexts.note: Register upgrade.

confusables.difference: With no object it means stop trying. With an object it means quit a habit or activity: give up sugar.
minimal_pair: I gave up after an hour.
I gave up sugar in January.

entry_json.avoid: Do not follow the no-object sense with 'to do': 'I gave up to study' is wrong; say 'I gave up studying'.

entry_json.definition: considering the fact that. It introduces a known fact that makes the main clause reasonable, and it is followed by a full clause with a subject and verb.

example_sentences: Given that the population is ageing, demand for health care can only increase.
The result is surprising, given that the sample was so small.
collocations: given that sth is the case

contexts.text: Given that tuition fees have tripled, it is not surprising that fewer mature students apply.
contexts.note: A high-value Task 2 opener: it concedes a fact and draws a conclusion in one sentence.

contexts.text: It can also follow the main clause: fewer students apply, given that fees have tripled.
contexts.note: Position is flexible; the comma moves with it.

contexts.text: Before a noun, drop 'that': given the cost, most families choose the state system.
contexts.note: 'Given + noun' is the shorter form.

confusables.difference: Because presents new information as the cause. Given that presents something already accepted and builds on it, which sounds more analytical.
minimal_pair: Fewer apply because fees have risen.
Given that fees have risen, fewer apply.

entry_json.avoid: Do not follow 'given that' with a noun alone. Either use a full clause, or drop 'that' and write 'given the cost'.

example_sentences: Cutting methane emissions would slow global warming faster than almost any other measure.
Global warming is expected to make heatwaves both longer and more frequent.

contexts.text: Global warming is caused largely by the burning of fossil fuels.
contexts.note: The single most common Task 2 environment topic.

contexts.text: People talk about global warming a lot more than they did ten years ago.
Scientists increasingly prefer 'climate change', because warming is only one of the effects.
contexts.note: Useful synonym for avoiding repetition.

confusables.difference: Global warming names the temperature rise itself. Climate change covers all its consequences, including flooding, drought and shifting seasons, so it is the wider term.
minimal_pair: Global warming has raised sea temperatures.

entry_json.avoid: No article and no plural: not 'the global warming' and never 'global warmings'.

entry_json.definition: to happen as planned, or to begin doing something. As a reply it gives permission: go ahead, meaning please do.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The festival went ahead despite the weather, though the crowd was half the usual size.

May I ask a question? Go ahead.

contexts.text: The match went ahead even though the pitch was almost under water.
The expansion is unlikely to go ahead without central government funding.
As a one-word reply it grants permission: Can I start? Go ahead.
contexts.note: Spoken function: permission.

confusables.difference: Take place is neutral: an event happens. Go ahead implies there was doubt, and it happened anyway.
minimal_pair: The meeting takes place on Fridays.
The meeting went ahead despite the strike.

entry_json.avoid: As a verb it is two words. Only the noun and adjective take a hyphen, as in 'they were given the go-ahead'.

entry_json.definition: to continue with a plan that was uncertain or that others may have objected to. The plan follows 'with' as a noun or -ing form.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The council decided to go ahead with the pedestrian zone despite objections from local shopkeepers.
example_sentences: The hospital went ahead with the expansion after securing private funding.
We decided to go ahead with buying the flat even though prices were falling.
collocations: decide to go ahead with sth

contexts.text: Ministers confirmed that they would go ahead with the ban on new petrol cars.
contexts.note: Reporting a decision in an essay.

contexts.text: In the end we went ahead with the trip and it was the right decision.
After 'with' a verb takes -ing: they went ahead with building the bypass.
contexts.note: Pattern note.

confusables.difference: Carry on means continue something already in progress. Go ahead with means start or proceed with a plan that might not have happened.

They went ahead with the work despite the protest.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'go ahead the plan'. The preposition 'with' is compulsory when you name what is proceeding.

entry_json.definition: to leave in order to fetch somebody who can help, especially in an emergency. 'Help' here is uncountable, so it takes no article.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: One of us stayed with him while the other went to get help from the ranger station.
example_sentences: If someone collapses, call an ambulance rather than going to get help yourself.
She told the children to stay where they were while she went and got help.

contexts.text: In the past tense both verbs change: I went and got help.

contexts.text: In writing prefer 'seek assistance': bystanders should seek assistance immediately.

confusables.difference: Both are correct. 'Go and get' is the everyday British spoken form; 'go to get' states the purpose slightly more formally.

She went to get help.

entry_json.avoid: 'Help' takes no article here: not 'go and get a help'.

entry_json.definition: used before another verb to mean go somewhere in order to do something: go and see, go and buy. Both verbs take the same tense, and in the imperative 'and' is often dropped in American English.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I might go and see that exhibition before it closes at the end of the month.
example_sentences: Go and ask at the desk; they will have a timetable.
We went and looked at three flats in one afternoon.

contexts.text: At the weekend I usually go and see my parents.
After a modal, 'go' stays in the base form: you should go and speak to your tutor.

contexts.text: In the past both verbs take the past form: we went and asked at reception.
contexts.note: Not 'went and ask'.

confusables.difference: 'Go and do' is informal and very common in British speech. 'Go to do' states purpose and is a shade more formal.
minimal_pair: I went and bought a ticket.
I went to buy a ticket.

entry_json.avoid: Do not mix the tenses: 'I went and buy a ticket' is wrong. Both verbs must agree.

entry_json.definition: to leave a place, to go somewhere for a holiday, or, of a problem or feeling, to disappear. It takes no object.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We try to go away for a few days in the spring, usually somewhere on the coast.
example_sentences: The headache went away as soon as I drank some water.
Are you going away this summer, or staying at home?
collocations: the problem will not go away

contexts.text: Do you often go away at the weekend? Not really, only two or three times a year.
contexts.note: The 'holiday' sense is extremely common in Part 1.

contexts.text: Ignoring the shortage will not make it go away.
contexts.note: The 'disappear' sense works well in an essay.

contexts.text: As a command it is rude: 'go away!' means leave me alone.
contexts.note: Tone warning.

confusables.difference: Leave usually names the place: leave the office. Go away has no object and often means going on a trip.
minimal_pair: I left the house at seven.
We went away for a week.

entry_json.avoid: It takes no object: not 'go away the city'. Use 'leave the city' instead.

entry_json.definition: to return to a place you have been before, or to a state or activity you had left. The destination takes 'to', but home, there and here take nothing.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I go back to my home town twice a year, usually at New Year and in the summer.
example_sentences: After the course finished I went back to full-time work.
The tradition goes back more than four hundred years.

contexts.text: Would you go back to that city on holiday? Definitely, there was far too much to see in three days.
Many mothers find it difficult to go back to work after a long break.
It also means date from: the building goes back to the twelfth century.
contexts.note: The 'origin' sense.

confusables.difference: Come back is towards where the speaker is. Go back is away from here, to somewhere else.
minimal_pair: Come back to London soon.
I am going back to Warsaw next week.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'go back to home'. And 'return back' is redundant: 'return' already contains the idea of back.

entry_json.definition: to return to a place, an activity or an earlier period. Before a noun it takes 'to'; before a verb the verb takes -ing: go back to studying.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: After ten years in industry she went back to studying and completed a master's degree part-time.
example_sentences: Let us go back to the point you made about funding.
Prices went back to their previous level within six months.

contexts.text: It took about a year for life to go back to normal.
contexts.note: Fixed collocation with no article.

contexts.text: The figure fell sharply in 2009 before going back to its earlier level in 2012.
contexts.note: Useful for describing recovery on a graph.

contexts.text: Before a verb use -ing: I would like to go back to living in a smaller town.
contexts.note: 'to' here is a preposition, not part of an infinitive.

confusables.difference: The same meaning, but 'return to' is more formal and is the better choice in Task 1 and Task 2.
minimal_pair: It went back to normal.
The figure returned to its 2005 level.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'go back to study' when you mean resuming study as an activity: it should be 'go back to studying'.

entry_json.definition: to become lower in number, level or price, or to move to a lower place. With figures it is the everyday equivalent of 'fall' or 'decrease'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The price of solar panels has gone down by around 80 per cent since 2010.
example_sentences: Unemployment went down slightly in the final quarter.
The temperature goes down very quickly once the sun sets.

contexts.text: My phone bill has gone down since I changed provider.
In Task 1 prefer 'fell' or 'declined': car use declined steadily between 2005 and 2015.
contexts.note: Register upgrade: 'went down' is correct but plain.

contexts.text: Use 'by' for the size of the change and 'to' for the final level: it went down by 5 per cent, to 20 per cent.
contexts.note: The preposition pair learners most often confuse.

confusables.difference: Direct opposite. Both take 'by' for the amount of change and 'to' for the level reached.
minimal_pair: Prices went up by 3 per cent.
Prices went down by 3 per cent.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'went down of 5 per cent'. It is 'by 5 per cent'.

entry_json.definition: to move along or descend something such as a street, a hill or a set of stairs. The place follows 'down' directly, with no extra preposition.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Go down this road as far as the traffic lights and the library is on your left.
example_sentences: We went down the stairs rather than waiting for the lift.
The path goes down the hill and then follows the river for a mile.

contexts.text: Go down the high street and take the second turning on the right.
contexts.note: Giving directions, imperative.

contexts.text: The route goes down the valley before climbing again towards the pass.
Note the difference from 'go down' with no object, which means decrease.
contexts.note: Same words, different structure and meaning.

confusables.difference: Go along a street stresses following its length. Go down suggests movement away from the speaker, and in British English is used for streets even when they are flat.
minimal_pair: Go along the corridor.
Go down the road.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add a second preposition: 'go down to the road' means something different, namely go as far as it.

entry_json.definition: to walk somewhere for pleasure or exercise rather than to get anywhere. The article 'a' is compulsory, and the same frame gives go for a run, a swim, a drink.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: When I need to think something through I go for a walk rather than sit at my desk.
example_sentences: We went for a long walk along the coast on Sunday morning.
Even a short walk after lunch improves concentration in the afternoon.
collocations: go for a walk in the park

chunk.pattern: go for a + walk / run / swim

contexts.text: At the weekend I usually go for a walk with my family in the park nearby.
contexts.note: Reliable Part 1 answer about free time or exercise.

contexts.text: Residents said they would use the new path to go for a walk after work.
The same frame builds other activities: go for a run, go for a swim, go for a coffee.
contexts.note: Productive pattern worth memorising.

confusables.difference: Go walking, like go swimming or go shopping, describes the activity in general and takes -ing with no article. Go for a walk is one particular occasion.
minimal_pair: We go walking in the hills every summer.
I went for a walk after dinner.

entry_json.avoid: The article cannot be dropped: 'go for walk' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: to choose something, or to leave in order to do or fetch something. In the 'choose' sense it is informal and slightly more casual than 'select'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In the end I went for the cheaper course, mainly because it was in the evening.
example_sentences: If I were you I would go for the one with the longer guarantee.
We went for a coffee after the lecture and talked for an hour.
collocations: which one would you go for?

contexts.text: Which would you go for, the flat in the centre or the house further out?
contexts.note: The 'choose' sense: natural in Speaking, too informal for Task 2.

contexts.text: In writing prefer 'opt for' or 'choose': most buyers opt for the smaller model.
contexts.note: Register upgrade.

contexts.text: It also means the rule applies to somebody too: that goes for everyone in the group.
contexts.note: Idiomatic third sense.

confusables.difference: Look for is searching. Go for is choosing, or setting off to fetch something.
minimal_pair: I am looking for a new phone.
I went for the cheaper phone in the end.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it in Task 2 to mean choose. Write 'opt for' or 'choose' instead.

entry_json.definition: to travel to the place where you live. 'Home' is an adverb here, so it takes no preposition and no article.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I usually go home straight after work, though on Fridays I meet friends first.
example_sentences: She felt unwell and went home early.
Many students go home for the summer rather than staying near the university.

contexts.text: What time do you go home from work? Usually about six.
Staff who are unwell should go home rather than risk infecting colleagues.
With a possessive the preposition returns: I went to my parents' home for the weekend.
contexts.note: Only bare 'home' drops 'to'.

confusables.difference: Go home is departing for home; get home is arriving there.
minimal_pair: I went home at six.
I got home at seven.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'go to home'. This is one of the most persistent beginner errors in English.

entry_json.definition: to enter a place, to start a career in a field, or to examine a subject in detail. The sense depends entirely on what follows 'into'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She went into teaching after five years in publishing, and has never regretted the change.
example_sentences: I do not want to go into the details here, but the project was cancelled.
A great deal of public money has gone into upgrading the rail network.

contexts.text: Fewer graduates are going into teaching, largely because of pay and workload.
contexts.note: The career sense: a strong Task 2 collocation.

contexts.text: I will not go into detail, but the trip did not go as planned.
contexts.note: Fixed phrase: 'go into detail', usually without an article.

contexts.text: Considerable investment has gone into flood defences along the estuary.
contexts.note: The 'be spent on' sense.

confusables.difference: Get into is often about becoming interested, or being admitted. Go into is about entering, or entering a profession.
minimal_pair: I got into photography last year.
She went into medicine after university.

entry_json.avoid: The fixed phrase is 'go into detail', not 'go into details' in most contexts, and never 'go in detail'.

entry_json.definition: to do something after finishing something else, often as the next stage of a career or life. The infinitive is compulsory; with -ing the meaning changes to continuing the same thing.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She studied engineering and went on to work on flood defences for the city council.
example_sentences: Most of the students on that course went on to do a master's degree.
He began as an apprentice and went on to run the company.

contexts.text: Around 40 per cent of school leavers go on to study at university.
contexts.note: A precise phrase for describing educational progression.

contexts.text: He finished the apprenticeship and went on to set up his own workshop.
Compare 'go on doing', which means continue: she went on talking for another hour.
contexts.note: The -ing form is a genuinely different meaning, not a variant.

confusables.difference: 'Go on to do' moves to a new activity. 'Go on doing' continues the same one. Getting this wrong reverses your meaning.
minimal_pair: He went on to speak about funding.
He went on speaking about funding.

entry_json.avoid: Do not swap the infinitive for -ing. 'He went on to talk' and 'he went on talking' say two different things.

entry_json.definition: to leave your home for a social activity, or, of a light or fire, to stop burning. It takes no object; add 'for' or 'to' for the purpose.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We do not go out much during the week, but we usually eat out once at the weekend.
example_sentences: Young people go out far less often than they did before everything moved online.
The lights went out across the whole street for about ten minutes.

contexts.text: Do you go out much in the evening? Not really, I am usually too tired after work.
contexts.note: Common Part 1 free-time question.

contexts.text: Rising prices mean families go out to eat far less than they used to.
The fire went out during the night and the room was freezing by morning.
contexts.note: The 'stop burning' sense.

confusables.difference: Go outside is simply leaving the building for the open air. Go out means going somewhere for entertainment.
minimal_pair: I went outside for some fresh air.
We went out for a meal.

entry_json.avoid: It takes no object: not 'go out the restaurant'. Say 'go out to a restaurant' or 'leave the restaurant'.

entry_json.definition: to experience a difficult period, or to examine or discuss something carefully from beginning to end. The object always follows 'through'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The whole industry went through a difficult period after the ban on single-use plastics.
example_sentences: Let us go through the figures once more before the meeting.
Anyone who has gone through a serious illness knows how slow recovery can be.

contexts.text: My tutor went through my essay line by line, which was painful but useful.
contexts.note: The 'examine carefully' sense.

contexts.text: The region has gone through rapid industrialisation in a single generation.
contexts.note: The 'experience' sense; 'undergone' is the formal alternative.

contexts.text: It also means be approved: the proposal finally went through in March.
contexts.note: Third sense, no object.

confusables.difference: Undergo is the formal one-word equivalent of the 'experience' sense and is common in academic writing. Go through is the everyday version.
minimal_pair: The city has gone through big changes.
The city has undergone significant change.

entry_json.avoid: Do not split it: 'go it through' is wrong. The object comes after 'through'.

entry_json.definition: to get into bed in order to sleep. There is no article, because the phrase names the purpose of the place rather than a particular piece of furniture.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I try to go to bed before eleven, though I do not always manage it.
example_sentences: Children who go to bed at a regular time sleep better and concentrate more at school.
He went to bed early because he had a six o'clock flight.
collocations: what time do you go to bed?

contexts.text: What time do you usually go to bed? About midnight, which is probably too late.
contexts.note: Standard Part 1 routine question.

contexts.text: Looking at a screen just before going to bed makes it harder to fall asleep.
With an article the meaning becomes physical: he sat on the bed to take off his shoes.
contexts.note: Article contrast.

confusables.difference: Go to bed is getting in. Go to sleep is losing consciousness. You can go to bed at ten and not go to sleep until midnight.
minimal_pair: I went to bed at ten.
I did not go to sleep until midnight.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'go to the bed'. The same rule covers go to school, go to work and go to hospital.

entry_json.definition: to attend school as a pupil. No article, because it names the activity of being educated rather than the building.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In my country children start going to school at six and stay until they are eighteen.
example_sentences: Almost all children in the region now go to school, compared with two thirds in 1990.
She goes to school by bus because the village has no secondary school of its own.

contexts.text: I went to school in a small town about an hour from the capital.
Girls in rural areas are still less likely to go to school beyond the age of twelve.
The article returns when you mean the building: I went to the school to collect my daughter.
contexts.note: Purpose versus place: the key distinction.

confusables.difference: Without 'the' you are a pupil. With 'the' you are visiting the building, perhaps as a parent or a visitor.
minimal_pair: My son goes to school.
I went to the school to meet his teacher.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add 'the' when you mean attending as a pupil, and do not say 'go to the university' in that sense either.

entry_json.definition: to travel to your place of employment. 'Work' is uncountable here and takes no article, in the same way as school and bed.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I go to work by bicycle in the summer and by train once the weather turns.
example_sentences: Fewer people go to work five days a week than before 2020.
He was too ill to go to work on Monday.

contexts.text: How do you go to work? On the underground, and it takes about half an hour.
If more people cycled to work, congestion would fall without any new roads.
contexts.note: Related pattern: verb of movement plus 'to work'.

contexts.text: I am writing to inform you that I will be unable to go to work this week.

confusables.difference: Go to work is the general activity. Go to the office names a particular building, which matters now that many people work from home.
minimal_pair: I go to work at eight.
I go to the office twice a week.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'go to the work'. And use 'by' with transport: by car, by bus, but 'on foot'.

entry_json.definition: to rise in number, level or price, or to move to a higher place. Use 'by' for the size of the increase and 'to' for the level reached.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rents in this area have gone up by nearly a third in three years.
example_sentences: Bus fares go up every January.
The proportion of households with broadband went up from 40 to 90 per cent over the period.

contexts.text: The cost of everything has gone up this year, especially food.
In Task 1 prefer 'rose' or 'increased': car ownership rose steadily throughout the period.
contexts.note: Register upgrade: 'went up' is correct but scores lower.

contexts.text: New flats are going up all along the waterfront.
contexts.note: The 'be built' sense.

confusables.difference: Go up has no object: prices go up. Raise needs one: the government raised taxes. Confusing them is a very common error.
minimal_pair: Prices went up.
They raised prices.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'the price was gone up' or 'they went up the price'. Go up cannot take an object and cannot be passive.

entry_json.definition: to stop working properly, or to develop badly. 'Wrong' is an adjective after 'go', which here means become, so it takes no object.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Almost everything that could go wrong on that journey did, and we arrived twelve hours late.
example_sentences: If anything goes wrong with the heating, the landlord is responsible for repairs.
The experiment went wrong because the samples had not been refrigerated.

contexts.text: Everything went wrong that morning: the alarm failed and then the train was cancelled.
contexts.note: A useful opening for a Part 2 'difficult day' card.

contexts.text: When something goes wrong with an online service, customers have almost no way of complaining.
contexts.note: The 'with' pattern names the faulty thing.

contexts.text: In formal writing prefer 'fail' or 'malfunction': the cooling system failed twice in a week.
contexts.note: Register upgrade.

confusables.difference: Be wrong means incorrect, about a fact or a person. Go wrong means a thing stopped working or a plan failed.
minimal_pair: The answer is wrong.
The printer has gone wrong.

entry_json.avoid: It takes no object: not 'I went wrong the machine'. Say 'the machine went wrong' or 'I broke the machine'.

entry_json.definition: able to do something well. The preposition is 'at', and a verb after it must be -ing: good at solving problems.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have never been good at remembering names, so I write them down as soon as I can.
example_sentences: She is extremely good at explaining difficult ideas simply.
Children are often better at picking up an accent than adults are.

contexts.text: Are you good at cooking? Not really, I can manage about five dishes.
contexts.note: Frequent Part 1 frame, and the answer needs -ing after 'at'.

contexts.text: Employers increasingly want people who are good at working in a team.
The comparative and superlative keep the preposition: better at languages, the best at maths in her year.

confusables.difference: 'Good in' is not used for ability. It appears only in phrases like 'good in bed' or 'good in a crisis', which mean something different.
minimal_pair: She is good at maths.
He is good in a crisis.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'good in English' when you mean skilled at it, and never 'good at speak'. Use 'good at speaking'.

entry_json.definition: beneficial to somebody or something. 'For' introduces who or what benefits, which is different from 'good at', which is about ability.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Walking to work is good for your health and good for the city's air quality at the same time.
example_sentences: Cutting corporation tax may be good for investors but not for public services.
Too much screen time before bed is not good for children.

contexts.text: Everyone knows vegetables are good for you, but that does not make people eat them.
Tourism is good for the local economy but damaging to the coastline.
contexts.note: A balanced Task 2 sentence built on one preposition.

contexts.text: It also means suitable: this bike is good for short journeys but uncomfortable on long ones.
contexts.note: The 'suitable for' sense.

confusables.difference: Good at is ability. Good for is benefit. 'She is good for maths' is meaningless; it must be 'good at maths'.
minimal_pair: She is good at sport.
Sport is good for her.

entry_json.avoid: Do not mix it up with 'good at'. The preposition changes the meaning completely.

entry_json.definition: used to wish somebody success before an important event. As a noun phrase it is uncountable and takes no article; with a person it takes 'with': good luck with the exam.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Good luck with the interview on Thursday, I am sure you will be fine.
example_sentences: Good luck in your new job, and do let us know how it goes.
It was pure good luck that we found a table without booking.

contexts.text: Good luck with your test tomorrow.
contexts.note: Everyday parting phrase.

contexts.text: I would like to wish you good luck in your new role.
contexts.note: Closing line of a semi-formal letter.

contexts.text: As a plain noun it means fortune: the harvest depended on good luck as much as hard work.
contexts.note: Uncountable noun sense.

confusables.difference: Good luck is fortune. A good chance is a strong probability. They are not interchangeable.
minimal_pair: Good luck with the exam.
There is a good chance you will pass.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'a good luck'. And the preposition is 'with' or 'in', never 'for'.

entry_json.definition: information that makes people pleased. 'News' is uncountable despite the s, so it takes a singular verb and never 'a' or a plural.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The good news is that the figures have started to fall; the bad news is that they are still twice the safe level.
example_sentences: I have some good news: the department has agreed to fund the trip.
Good news travels fast in a small office.

contexts.text: I got some good news last week: I have been offered a place.
contexts.note: 'Some', not 'a'.

contexts.text: The good news is that emissions have fallen; the difficulty is that they have not fallen fast enough.
contexts.note: A neat way to balance two findings in one sentence.

contexts.text: The verb is singular: the news was better than expected.
contexts.note: Agreement point.

confusables.difference: If you need to count, use 'a piece of news'. You cannot say 'a good news' or 'good newses'.
minimal_pair: I have some good news.
That is one piece of good news at least.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'a good news' and never 'the news are'. News is uncountable and singular.

entry_json.definition: something that is beneficial or fortunate. It is countable, so it needs an article: a good thing. 'It is a good thing that…' introduces a whole clause.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is a good thing that the deadline was extended, because half the class had not started.
example_sentences: Working from home has been a good thing for parents but harder for younger staff.
One good thing about living centrally is that you can walk almost everywhere.
collocations: it is a good thing that…

contexts.text: The good thing about my flat is that it is five minutes from the station.
contexts.note: A very natural way to give one advantage in Part 1.

contexts.text: In Task 2 prefer 'advantage' or 'benefit': the main advantage of this approach is its low cost.
contexts.note: Register upgrade: 'good thing' is a little vague for an essay.

contexts.text: It is a good thing that the service runs at night, otherwise shift workers could not use it.

confusables.difference: A good point is a valid argument in a discussion. A good thing is a benefit or a fortunate fact.
minimal_pair: That is a good point about the cost.
It is a good thing the cost has fallen.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the article: 'good thing about my flat is…' is missing 'the'.

entry_json.definition: to spend your childhood in a particular place or way, or to become an adult. It takes no object and is different from 'grow', which means increase in size.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I grew up in a small coastal town, which is probably why I still find big cities tiring.
example_sentences: Children who grow up near green space tend to be more physically active as adults.
What did you want to be when you were growing up?

contexts.text: Where did you grow up? In a village about thirty kilometres from the capital.
contexts.note: One of the most predictable Part 1 questions.

contexts.text: This generation grew up with smartphones, which makes their relationship with them quite different.
contexts.note: 'Grow up with' means it was normal throughout your childhood.

contexts.text: As a noun and adjective it is hyphenated: a grown-up daughter.

confusables.difference: Grow means get bigger and can take an object: farmers grow rice. Grow up is only about childhood and takes no object.
minimal_pair: The city has grown quickly.
I grew up in the city.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'I grew up my children'. To raise children say 'bring up' or 'raise'.

entry_json.definition: an increase in the size, amount or importance of something. 'In' introduces what is increasing; 'of' would introduce the size of the increase.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The chart shows a steady growth in online shopping between 2010 and 2020.
example_sentences: There has been rapid growth in demand for electric vehicles.
The growth in student numbers has put pressure on housing near the campus.

contexts.text: The graph shows a sharp growth in the use of renewable energy after 2015.
contexts.note: The noun form lets you avoid repeating 'increased' in Task 1.

contexts.text: Use 'of' for the size: a growth of 12 per cent, but a growth in car ownership.
contexts.note: The preposition pair that decides the meaning.

contexts.text: There has been a lot of growth in the tech sector where I live.

confusables.difference: Almost interchangeable. 'Growth' suggests natural, continuing expansion; 'increase' is neutral and works for any rise, including a one-off jump.
minimal_pair: growth in demand
an increase of 5 per cent

entry_json.avoid: Not 'growth of online shopping' when you mean what is growing: that needs 'growth in'.

entry_json.definition: used to give strong advice about the present or near future, with the sense that there will be a bad result otherwise. It is followed by the bare infinitive, and the negative is 'had better not'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: You had better leave now if you want to catch the last train.
example_sentences: We had better book the tickets today, because the price goes up at midnight.
You had better not tell her before the results are confirmed.

contexts.text: I had better go, or I will miss my bus.
contexts.note: In speech it is almost always contracted: I'd better go.

contexts.text: The negative keeps 'better' before 'not': you had better not be late again.
contexts.note: Not 'had not better'.

contexts.text: In formal writing use 'should' or 'ought to': applicants should submit the form by Friday.
contexts.note: Register warning: 'had better' is too direct for Task 2.

confusables.difference: Should is general advice. Had better is urgent advice about this situation, and hints at a bad consequence if it is ignored.
minimal_pair: You should exercise more.
You had better see a doctor about that.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'had better to go'. It takes the bare infinitive, and despite 'had' it refers to now, not the past.
entry_json.audio_hint: Usually contracted in speech: I'd better, you'd better.

entry_json.definition: thirty minutes. The article 'an' is compulsory because 'hour' begins with a vowel sound, and the whole phrase can act as a noun or an adverbial.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My commute takes about half an hour door to door, which I think is reasonable.
example_sentences: We waited half an hour for a table and then gave up.
Half an hour of moderate exercise a day is enough to make a measurable difference.

chunk.pattern: half an hour (+ later / of + noun)

contexts.text: How long does it take you to get to work? Roughly half an hour by tram.
Adults are advised to do at least half an hour of activity on most days.
As an adjective before a noun it is hyphenated: a half-hour journey.
contexts.note: Compound adjective form.

confusables.difference: 'A half hour' is American. British English says 'half an hour', and the article goes before 'hour', not before 'half'.
minimal_pair: half an hour
a half hour

entry_json.avoid: Never 'half hour' with no article, and not 'half of an hour' in ordinary use.
entry_json.audio_hint: 'Hour' begins with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an', not 'a'.

entry_json.definition: to wait for a short time. It is informal and mostly used as a command or on the phone. It also means hold something tightly: hang on to the rail.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Hang on a second, I will check the timetable on my phone.
example_sentences: Hang on, I think that is the wrong platform.
If you hang on until Friday, the price drops by twenty pounds.

chunk.pattern: hang on (a minute) / hang on to + sth

contexts.text: Hang on a minute, I have not finished writing that down.
contexts.note: Informal, spoken only.

contexts.text: It is worth hanging on to old photographs, even the bad ones.
contexts.note: The 'keep' sense, with 'to'.

contexts.text: In writing use 'wait' or 'please hold': please hold while I transfer your call.
contexts.note: Register upgrade.

confusables.difference: Almost identical in meaning and register. 'Hold on' is slightly more common on the telephone; 'hang on' is more common face to face.
minimal_pair: Hang on, I am nearly ready.
Hold on, I will put you through.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it in Writing. It is conversational, and in Task 1 letters 'please wait' is the correct choice.

entry_json.definition: to take place and affect a particular person or thing, usually by chance. 'Happen' is never passive and never takes a direct object: something happens to you, it does not happen you.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Nobody could explain what had happened to the missing luggage, and it turned up three days later.
example_sentences: The same thing happened to a colleague of mine last year.
What happens to all the plastic we put in the recycling bin?

contexts.text: What happened to your phone? I dropped it on the platform.
Very little is known about what happens to electronic waste once it leaves the country.
'Happen to do sth' means by chance: I happened to be in the area, so I called in.
contexts.note: A separate structure with its own meaning.

confusables.difference: Occur is the formal equivalent for events but is not used with a person in this way. 'The accident occurred' is fine; 'it occurred to him' means he suddenly thought of it.
minimal_pair: The accident happened at six.
It occurred to me that I had left the door open.

entry_json.avoid: Never make it passive: 'an accident was happened' is wrong. And do not drop 'to': not 'what happened you?'.

entry_json.definition: satisfied with something or somebody, or willing to accept it. 'With' is for satisfaction; 'about' is for feelings, and 'for' is for pleasure at somebody else's good news.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am reasonably happy with my current job, though the commute is longer than I would like.
example_sentences: Are you happy with the room, or would you prefer one facing the garden?
Most residents were not happy with the way the consultation was handled.

contexts.text: Are you happy with where you live? Very, apart from the noise at weekends.
I am not happy with the standard of the repair and would like it inspected again.
contexts.note: Understated complaint, which is the British register for a formal letter.

contexts.text: Use 'for' when somebody else has good news: I am very happy for you.
contexts.note: Different preposition, different meaning.

confusables.difference: 'Happy with' judges the quality of something you received. 'Happy about' describes your feelings towards an event.
minimal_pair: I am happy with the result.
I am happy about the news.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'happy from' or 'happy of'. English uses with, about or for depending on the meaning.

entry_json.definition: a great deal of effort, or an activity that requires it. 'Work' is uncountable here, so it takes no article and no plural.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Getting the grades I needed took two years of hard work and a lot of early mornings.
example_sentences: Success in any sport is the result of hard work rather than natural talent alone.
Looking after a small child on your own is hard work.

contexts.text: It was hard work, but I would do it again.
The company rewards hard work with promotion rather than with bonuses.
The adjective describing the person is hyphenated: she is very hard-working.
contexts.note: Do not confuse the noun phrase with the adjective.

confusables.difference: 'Hardly' means almost not at all, so 'he hardly works' is the opposite of 'he works hard'. The adverb from 'hard' is 'hard'.
minimal_pair: He works hard.
He hardly works.

entry_json.avoid: No article and no plural: not 'a hard work' and never 'hard works'.

entry_json.definition: to look at something for a short time. This is the delexical pattern have + a + noun, which British English prefers to the plain verb in conversation.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I will have a look this evening and let you know what I think.
example_sentences: Do you mind if I have a look before I decide?
We had a quick look round the town before the train left.

contexts.text: Come and have a look at the view from the top floor.
The pattern lets you add an adjective: have a quick look, have a proper look.
contexts.note: This is exactly why the delexical form is useful.

contexts.text: Americans say 'take a look'; both are correct, and British speakers use 'take' too.
contexts.note: Variety note.

confusables.difference: The plain verb is neutral. 'Have a look' suggests a brief, casual glance and lets you attach an adjective, which the verb alone cannot do easily.
minimal_pair: I looked at the report.
I had a quick look at the report.

entry_json.avoid: The article is compulsory: not 'have look'. The same family gives have a rest, have a try, have a go.

entry_json.definition: to examine or read something briefly. The thing being examined follows 'at', and an adjective can go before 'look': have a closer look at the figures.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Could you have a look at my personal statement before I submit it?
example_sentences: Let us have a look at the second graph, which tells a rather different story.
A mechanic had a look at the engine and said it was not worth repairing.
collocations: have a look at the figures
have a closer look at sth

contexts.text: Would you mind having a look at this form? I am not sure I have filled it in correctly.
contexts.note: After 'mind' the verb takes -ing.

contexts.text: If we have a closer look at the data, the pattern is less clear than it first appears.
contexts.note: Acceptable in a report, though 'examine' is more formal.

contexts.text: In an essay prefer 'examine' or 'consider': this paragraph examines the second argument.
contexts.note: Register upgrade.

confusables.difference: Look at is examining something in front of you. Look for is searching for something you cannot find.
minimal_pair: Have a look at this photo.
I am looking for my keys.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'at': 'have a look my essay' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: to enjoy yourself. 'Fun' is uncountable, so it takes no article, and a following verb takes -ing: have fun learning it.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We had a lot of fun on that trip, even though almost nothing went to plan.
example_sentences: The children had fun building a shelter out of branches.
Have fun at the weekend, and send me a photo.

contexts.text: I had a lot of fun learning to cook with my grandmother.
contexts.gap_span: had a lot of fun learning
contexts.note: The verb after 'fun' is -ing, with no preposition.

contexts.text: Children learn languages faster when they are having fun rather than being tested.
'Funny' means amusing or strange, and is not the adjective for 'enjoyable'.
contexts.note: The confusion that produces 'the party was very funny'.

confusables.difference: Fun as an adjective means enjoyable; funny means it makes you laugh, or that something is odd. Calling a trip 'funny' says it was strange.
minimal_pair: It was a fun evening.
It was a funny film.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'have a fun'. And do not say 'we had fun to swim'; it is 'fun swimming'.

entry_json.definition: to possess or hold something. It means the same as 'have' but is more common in British speech, and it is almost always contracted: I've got, she's got.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have got two older brothers, both of whom live abroad now.
example_sentences: Have you got a minute? I want to check something with you.
She has got more experience than anyone else on the team.

contexts.text: Have you got any brothers or sisters? Yes, one sister.
contexts.note: Note the question form: no 'do'.

contexts.text: In writing use plain 'have': the city has three universities.
contexts.note: Register warning: 'have got' is spoken British English.

contexts.text: The past is 'had', not 'had got': when I was a child we had a small garden.
contexts.note: 'Have got' has no past form in this sense.

confusables.difference: The meaning is identical. 'Have got' is informal and present-only; plain 'have' works in every tense and in writing.
minimal_pair: I have got a car.
I have a car.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'do' in questions or negatives: not 'do you have got'. And avoid it altogether in Task 2.
entry_json.audio_hint: Nearly always contracted in speech: I've got, he's got.

entry_json.definition: used to say that something is necessary. It means the same as 'have to' but is informal and present-only, and it takes the full infinitive with 'to'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have got to be at the station by seven, so I will have to leave early.
example_sentences: You have got to book in advance; they never take people at the door.
We have got to reduce emissions much faster than we are doing at the moment.
collocations: you have got to see sth
we have got to do sth

contexts.text: I have got to hand the essay in on Monday, so this weekend is already spoken for.
contexts.note: Usually contracted: I've got to, often heard as gotta.

contexts.text: In writing use 'must' or 'have to': governments must act before the deadline.
contexts.note: Register upgrade for Task 2.

contexts.text: There is no past form: yesterday I had to leave early, not 'had got to'.
contexts.note: Tense limitation.

confusables.difference: Same meaning. 'Have to' works in all tenses and in formal writing; 'have got to' is spoken, present-only British English.
minimal_pair: I have to work on Saturday.
I have got to work on Saturday.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'gotta' in the exam, and do not use 'have got to' in Writing at all.
entry_json.audio_hint: In fast speech it becomes gotta, but that spelling must never appear in writing.

entry_json.definition: to not know something at all. It is often followed by a wh-clause in statement word order: I have no idea where it is.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I had no idea how expensive the city would be until I started looking at rents.
example_sentences: Most consumers have no idea where their clothes are actually made.
I have no idea what the answer is, but I can find out for you.

contexts.text: To be honest I have no idea, I have never really thought about it.
contexts.note: A legitimate Part 3 stalling move, as long as you then attempt an answer.

contexts.text: The clause keeps statement order: I have no idea why it happened, not why did it happen.
contexts.note: Embedded question rule.

contexts.text: Many households have no idea how much energy their appliances use.

confusables.difference: The meaning is the same, but 'have no idea' is stronger and more emphatic. 'I do not know' is neutral.
minimal_pair: I do not know.
I have absolutely no idea.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add another negative: 'I have not no idea' is wrong. 'No' already makes the sentence negative.

vocab_new.lemma: have nothing to do with sb/sth

entry_json.headword: have nothing to do with sb/sth
entry_json.definition: to be completely unconnected with somebody or something, or to avoid all contact with them. The word order is fixed and cannot be rearranged.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The rise in prices has nothing to do with the new tax; it began two years earlier.
example_sentences: My job has nothing to do with what I studied at university.
She wanted nothing to do with the whole project after the first meeting.
collocations: have nothing to do with the decision
want nothing to do with sb
have little to do with sth

chunk.pattern: have nothing to do with + sb / sth

contexts.text: My degree was in history, so my current job has nothing to do with it.
The fall in crime has little to do with the new cameras and a great deal to do with employment.
contexts.note: The graded versions: nothing, little, something, a lot.

contexts.text: In the strong personal sense it means refuse contact: he wants nothing to do with them.

confusables.term: have something to do with sth
confusables.difference: The positive version means there is a connection, though you may not know exactly what: the delay had something to do with the weather.
minimal_pair: It has nothing to do with money.
It has something to do with money.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add another negative: 'it does not have nothing to do with it' is wrong. Use 'it has nothing to do with it'.

entry_json.definition: to be thinking of a particular person or thing as a possible choice. The object goes between 'have' and 'in mind', and 'mind' takes no article.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We need someone to lead the project, and I have a colleague in mind who has done it before.
example_sentences: What sort of budget did you have in mind?
The architect had older residents in mind when she designed the entrance.
collocations: have sb in mind for a job
what did you have in mind?

contexts.text: I would like to travel somewhere quieter next year, though I do not have anywhere particular in mind.
contexts.note: The object sits before 'in mind', however long it is.

contexts.text: The policy was designed with rural communities in mind.
contexts.note: The 'with X in mind' variant is very useful in Task 2.

contexts.text: What did you have in mind? Something around three hundred pounds.

confusables.difference: Have in mind is holding a specific candidate or plan now. Keep in mind is remembering a fact so that it influences a later decision.
minimal_pair: I have someone in mind for the role.
Keep in mind that the office closes at four.

entry_json.avoid: No article before 'mind': not 'in the mind'. And the object cannot follow 'mind': not 'have in mind a colleague'.

vocab_new.lemma: have sb/sth in mind for sth

entry_json.headword: have sb/sth in mind for sth
entry_json.definition: to be considering a particular person or thing for a specific role, job or purpose. 'For' names the position or use you are considering them for.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The manager already had two candidates in mind for the post before it was advertised.
example_sentences: We have the old library building in mind for the new community centre.
She had him in mind for the trip because he speaks the language.
collocations: have sb in mind for a role
have sth in mind for a purpose
who do you have in mind for sth?

chunk.pattern: have + sb/sth + in mind for + purpose

contexts.text: Do you have anyone in mind for the position? Yes, someone from the Leeds office.
The council has the riverside site in mind for affordable housing.
If the purpose is a verb, use 'for' plus -ing: they have the hall in mind for hosting exams.
contexts.note: Preposition plus gerund.

confusables.difference: Without 'for' you are simply thinking of someone. With 'for' you name the role you are considering them for.
minimal_pair: I have someone in mind.
I have someone in mind for the job.

entry_json.avoid: The order is fixed: person first, then 'in mind', then 'for'. Not 'have in mind him for the job'.

entry_json.definition: to share interests, features or experiences. The quantity goes between 'have' and 'in common': have a lot in common, have nothing in common.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We have a lot in common, which is probably why we became friends so quickly.
example_sentences: The two proposals have more in common than their supporters admit.
They have very little in common apart from a shared interest in football.

contexts.text: My brother and I have almost nothing in common, but we get on well.
The cities studied have one important feature in common: all grew faster than their transport networks.
contexts.note: A noun can also fill the slot: one feature in common.

contexts.text: The quantity always goes before 'in common': have a great deal in common, not have in common a great deal.
contexts.note: Word order rule.

confusables.difference: Be similar compares the things overall. Have in common names shared features and lets you count them: three things in common.
minimal_pair: The two systems are similar.
The two systems have three features in common.

entry_json.avoid: No article before 'common': not 'in the common'. And do not say 'have common' without the quantity word.

vocab_new.lemma: have sth in common with sb

entry_json.headword: have sth in common with sb
entry_json.definition: to share interests or characteristics with a particular person. 'With' names the other person, and is needed when they are not already the subject of the sentence.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have very little in common with most of my colleagues outside work, which is perfectly normal.
example_sentences: I found I had a lot in common with the other students on the course.
He has almost nothing in common with his older brother.
collocations: have a lot in common with sb
have nothing in common with sb
find you have sth in common with sb

chunk.pattern: have + quantity + in common with + sb

contexts.text: I had more in common with my flatmates than with the people on my course.
Without 'with', both people must be in the subject: my sister and I have a lot in common.
contexts.note: This is when you can drop 'with'.

contexts.text: Newcomers who have something in common with their neighbours settle in far more quickly.

confusables.difference: Use the plain form when the subject already covers both parties. Add 'with sb' when the second person appears later in the sentence.
minimal_pair: We have a lot in common.
I have a lot in common with her.

entry_json.avoid: The preposition is 'with', never 'to' or 'between': not 'in common to my sister'.

vocab_new.lemma: have sth in common with sth

entry_json.headword: have sth in common with sth
entry_json.definition: to share features with another thing, system or place. This is the comparison use, and it is a precise way of linking two items in an essay or a Task 1 report.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The new scheme has a great deal in common with the one introduced in Copenhagen ten years ago.
example_sentences: The two graphs have one striking feature in common: both peak in the same year.
Modern universities have little in common with the institutions of a century ago.
collocations: have much in common with sth
have one feature in common with sth
have little in common with sth

chunk.pattern: X has + quantity + in common with + Y

contexts.text: The Spanish system has a good deal in common with the French one.
contexts.note: Comparing two systems without repeating 'similar to'.

contexts.text: The three cities have one thing in common: all of them expanded outwards rather than upwards.
contexts.note: Useful for grouping data in Task 1.

contexts.text: Electric cars have more in common with laptops than with older vehicles.

confusables.difference: 'Similar to' is a general resemblance. 'Have in common with' points at shared features you can list, which is more precise and scores better in Writing.
minimal_pair: The systems are similar.
The systems have three features in common.

entry_json.avoid: Do not mix the structures: 'similar with' is wrong, and so is 'in common to'.

entry_json.definition: to have enough time available to do something. 'Time' is uncountable here, so it takes no article, and it is usually followed by 'to do sth' or 'for sth'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I do not have time to cook properly during the week, so I do most of it on Sunday.
example_sentences: If you have time, it is worth walking up to the castle for the view.
Parents working two jobs simply do not have time to help with homework.

chunk.pattern: have time (to do sth / for sth)

contexts.text: Do you have time to read for pleasure? Only on holiday, unfortunately.
Long working hours mean many employees do not have time to exercise.
With an article the meaning changes completely: we had a great time in Rome.
contexts.note: Countable 'a time' means an experience.

confusables.difference: 'Have time' is about availability. 'Have a good time' means enjoy yourself, and the article is compulsory there.
minimal_pair: I do not have time.
I had a good time.

entry_json.avoid: No article in the availability sense: not 'I do not have the time to' unless you mean a specific period.

entry_json.definition: to have enough time available for an activity, named as a noun. If you want a verb instead, use 'have time to do sth'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Between work and studying I hardly have time for anything else at the moment.
example_sentences: Do you have time for a coffee before your train?
Few people have time for long meals in the middle of the working day.

contexts.text: I do not really have time for hobbies during term, but I read a lot in the holidays.
Working parents rarely have time for the kind of preparation the school expects.
'Have no time for sb' can also mean dislike: he has no time for people who complain without acting.
contexts.note: Idiomatic second meaning.

confusables.difference: 'For' takes a noun; 'to' takes a verb. Mixing them is the usual mistake: not 'time for cook'.
minimal_pair: I have time for breakfast.
I have time to eat breakfast.

entry_json.avoid: Do not put a bare verb after 'for'. Either use a noun, or switch to 'have time to' plus the infinitive.

entry_json.definition: to have enough time available to carry out an action. This is the pattern that takes a verb; use 'have time for' when what follows is a noun.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I never have time to read the news properly in the morning, so I catch up in the evening.
example_sentences: Will you have time to look at the draft before Friday?
Doctors rarely have time to explain the alternatives in a ten-minute appointment.
collocations: not have time to do sth
have just enough time to do sth

contexts.text: I did not have time to eat breakfast, so I bought something at the station.
Teachers with thirty pupils do not have time to give individual feedback every week.
contexts.note: A strong Task 2 sentence about class sizes.

contexts.text: With a noun switch to 'for': I did not have time for breakfast.
contexts.note: Pattern contrast.

confusables.difference: A verb needs 'to'; a noun needs 'for'. The two patterns are not interchangeable.
minimal_pair: time to cook
time for cooking

entry_json.avoid: Not 'have time for cook' and not 'have time cooking'. The verb takes 'to'.

entry_json.definition: to be connected with somebody or something. It almost always carries a quantity word: a lot to do with, something to do with, nothing to do with.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The fall in road deaths has a lot to do with better car design and rather less to do with speed cameras.
example_sentences: The delay had something to do with a signalling fault further up the line.
What does that have to do with the point you were making?
collocations: have a lot to do with sth
have something to do with sth
have little to do with sth

chunk.pattern: have + quantity + to do with + sth

contexts.text: The improvement in air quality has a great deal to do with the switch away from coal.
contexts.gap_span: has a great deal to do with
contexts.note: A careful way of claiming a cause without overstating it.

contexts.text: I think it has something to do with the way the timetable is organised.
contexts.note: A natural hedge when you are not certain.

contexts.text: The negative is the strongest form: it has nothing to do with money.

confusables.difference: 'Be related to' is the formal, neutral way of stating a connection. 'Have to do with' is more conversational and lets you grade the strength with a quantity word.
minimal_pair: The two are closely related.
It has a lot to do with cost.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the quantity word: 'it has to do with money' is possible but weaker; native speakers normally say 'something to do with'.

entry_json.definition: used to refer to one person when you do not know whether they are male or female. It takes a singular verb, and 'they' is the common alternative in speech.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: If a student misses more than three classes, he or she must speak to the course tutor.
example_sentences: Every candidate should bring identification with him or her on the day.
Whoever takes the job will find that he or she has a great deal of freedom.
collocations: he or she must do sth

contexts.text: A patient should be told what he or she is being treated for.
contexts.note: Formal written English; the verb stays singular.

contexts.text: Singular 'they' is now widely accepted and avoids the repetition: a patient should be told what they are being treated for.
contexts.note: Often the smoother choice in an essay.

contexts.text: Using the plural throughout is simpler still: patients should be told what they are being treated for.
contexts.note: The cleanest fix: pluralise the noun.

confusables.difference: Singular 'they' does the same job in one word and is now standard. 'He or she' is more formal but becomes clumsy if repeated.
minimal_pair: Each student must bring his or her own laptop.
Each student must bring their own laptop.

entry_json.avoid: Do not follow it with a plural verb: 'he or she are' is wrong. And avoid repeating it three times in one paragraph; pluralise the noun instead.

entry_json.definition: illnesses or medical conditions affecting a person or a population. It is usually plural and general; for one specific condition say 'a health problem'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Long working hours are linked to a range of health problems, from poor sleep to heart disease.
example_sentences: Air pollution causes serious health problems in every large city in the region.
She had no health problems until she was well into her seventies.

contexts.text: A diet high in processed food leads to a range of health problems later in life.
contexts.note: Very high-frequency Task 2 collocation.

contexts.text: My grandfather has a few health problems now, but he still walks every day.
More precise alternatives score better: cardiovascular disease, respiratory illness, mental health conditions.
contexts.note: Upgrade: name the condition where you can.

confusables.difference: Practically interchangeable. 'Issues' is slightly softer and more common when talking about a person; 'problems' is more direct.
minimal_pair: He has health problems.
She has some health issues.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'health problem' with no article when you mean one condition: it should be 'a health problem'.

entry_json.definition: to be told the details of an event or a person, usually without looking for the information. 'About' introduces the subject you were told about.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I first heard about the scholarship from a friend who had applied the year before.
example_sentences: Did you hear about the flooding in the north last week?
Most applicants hear about the vacancy through the university careers service.

contexts.text: How did you hear about this course? Through an advertisement online.
contexts.note: Common interview and Part 1 question.

contexts.text: Most people now hear about breaking news on social media rather than television.
Use 'from' for the source: I heard about it from a colleague.
contexts.note: Two prepositions with different jobs.

confusables.difference: Hear of means you know the name exists. Hear about means you were told the details.
minimal_pair: I have heard of her, but I have never heard about her work.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse it with 'listen to'. Hearing happens to you; listening is deliberate.

entry_json.definition: to know that somebody or something exists, because you have come across the name before. It is used mostly in the present perfect and in negatives and questions.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I had never heard of the town before I was offered a job there.
example_sentences: Have you heard of this author? She won a major prize last year.
Nobody outside the industry had heard of the company until the scandal.
collocations: the first I have heard of it

contexts.text: I had never heard of that dish before I moved here, and now I cook it every week.
contexts.note: Past perfect, setting up a change.

contexts.text: The technology is so new that most consumers have not heard of it.
It is not usually used in the plain present: say 'I have heard of him', not 'I hear of him'.
contexts.note: Tense restriction.

confusables.difference: Hear of means you recognise the name only. Know means you have met them or are familiar with them.
minimal_pair: I have heard of her.
I know her quite well.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'I heard of him yesterday' when you mean you were told news about him; that needs 'heard about'.

entry_json.definition: any of the conditions that damage the heart and blood vessels. It is uncountable and takes no article, and 'heart' stays singular in the compound.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Heart disease remains the leading cause of death in most high-income countries.
example_sentences: Smoking, poor diet and inactivity together account for most cases of heart disease.
She was diagnosed with heart disease in her fifties and changed her diet completely.
collocations: reduce the risk of heart disease

contexts.text: Regular exercise reduces the risk of heart disease by around a third.
contexts.note: One of the most useful Task 2 health collocations.

contexts.text: There is heart disease in my family, so I have my blood pressure checked every year.
The formal term is cardiovascular disease, which covers strokes as well.
contexts.note: Upgrade for a science-focused essay.

confusables.difference: Heart disease is the long-term condition. A heart attack is a single event, and it is countable: he had a heart attack.
minimal_pair: He has heart disease.
He had a heart attack in March.

entry_json.avoid: No article and no plural: not 'a heart disease' and not 'heart diseases' in general statements. And 'hearts disease' is never correct.

entry_json.definition: a school for teenagers, roughly ages eleven to eighteen. It is the standard American term; in Britain the usual word is secondary school, though 'high school' appears in some school names.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was fifteen when I started thinking seriously about what to do after high school.
example_sentences: She teaches physics at a high school on the edge of the city.
Most of my friends from high school still live in the same town.

contexts.text: When I was at high school I was much more interested in sport than in studying.
contexts.note: British English says 'at school', not 'in school'.

contexts.text: In a British context write 'secondary school': pupils move to secondary school at eleven.
contexts.note: Variety note: the examiner voices are British.

contexts.text: High school students are increasingly choosing vocational courses over academic ones.

confusables.difference: The same stage of education. High school is American and international; secondary school is the British term and the safer choice in an IELTS essay about the UK.
minimal_pair: I went to high school in Ohio.
I went to secondary school in Manchester.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add 'the' when you mean attending: 'I went to the high school' names a building, not the stage of education.

entry_json.definition: the main shopping street of a British town, and by extension ordinary shops as a sector: high street banks, the decline of the high street. It normally takes 'the'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Half the shops on our high street are now either coffee places or charity shops.
example_sentences: Online shopping has done more damage to the high street than any recession.
There is a chemist on the high street, opposite the library.
collocations: the decline of the high street

contexts.text: The high street in my town has changed completely in ten years.
contexts.note: Good for the Part 2 card about how a place has changed.

contexts.text: Reviving the high street would require lower rents rather than more parking.
contexts.note: A distinctively British topic that examiners recognise.

contexts.text: The preposition is 'on', not 'in': there is a bakery on the high street.

confusables.difference: The town centre is the whole central area. The high street is one particular street, and stands for ordinary retail as a whole.
minimal_pair: I work in the town centre.
I work on the high street.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the high street' in modern British usage, and do not use it for a motorway or main road; it means a shopping street.

entry_json.definition: the finest work he has produced so far, leaving open that better may follow. The key element is 'to date', which means up to now and sits after the noun phrase.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Critics called the album his best work to date, though he was only twenty-six when he recorded it.
example_sentences: The exhibition brings together her best work to date, including three pieces never shown in public.
It is his best work to date, but he has said he is only beginning.
collocations: to date, no evidence has emerged

contexts.text: This is the largest survey of its kind to date, covering more than forty countries.
contexts.note: The productive pattern: superlative plus 'to date'.

contexts.text: To date, no government has met the target it set itself in 2015.
contexts.note: 'To date' can also open a sentence, with a comma.

contexts.text: In speech people simply say 'so far': it is the best thing he has done so far.
contexts.note: Register note: 'to date' is written English.

confusables.difference: The same meaning. 'So far' is the everyday spoken form; 'to date' is formal and belongs in reports and essays.
minimal_pair: his best work so far
his best work to date

entry_json.avoid: Not 'until date' or 'to the date'. And it pairs with the present perfect, not the past simple.

entry_json.definition: the possessive form used for one person of unknown gender. It comes before a singular noun, and modern writing often prefers singular 'their'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Each applicant must submit his or her portfolio by the end of the month.
example_sentences: A doctor should explain the risks to the patient in his or her own language.
Every member is responsible for his or her own equipment.

contexts.text: Each student is expected to manage his or her own time.
contexts.note: Formal, and correct after 'each' or 'every'.

contexts.text: Singular 'their' does the same job: each student is expected to manage their own time.
contexts.note: Now fully accepted in British writing.

contexts.text: Pluralising is often neatest: students are expected to manage their own time.
contexts.note: The cleanest of the three options.

confusables.difference: 'Their' with a singular subject is now standard and avoids the clumsy repetition of 'his or her' through a paragraph.
minimal_pair: Everyone should bring his or her ticket.
Everyone should bring their ticket.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'his/her' with a slash in an essay, and never mix the two systems in one sentence: not 'each student and their his or her book'.

entry_json.definition: a person, considered as a member of the human species. It is countable and usually plural in general statements: human beings need sleep.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Human beings are the only species that has changed the climate of the entire planet.
example_sentences: No human being can concentrate fully for eight hours without a break.
The disease can pass from animals to human beings.
collocations: the human being as a species

contexts.text: Human beings have always moved in search of better land and work.
contexts.note: Plural with no article for a general truth.

contexts.text: Machines can process data faster, but no machine understands context the way a human being does.
contexts.note: Singular with 'a' when contrasting with a machine.

contexts.text: In speech people simply say 'people': people need about eight hours of sleep.
contexts.note: Register note: 'human beings' sounds formal in conversation.

confusables.difference: 'Human' alone is normally an adjective: human behaviour. As a noun it is used mainly in scientific writing; 'human being' is the ordinary countable noun.
minimal_pair: human behaviour
a human being

entry_json.avoid: Not 'humans being' and not 'the human beings' in a general statement. Use the plural with no article.

entry_json.definition: the basic freedoms and protections every person is entitled to, such as freedom of speech and freedom from torture. It is always plural and takes a plural verb.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Access to clean water is increasingly treated as a human rights issue rather than a purely technical one.
example_sentences: Human rights are protected by international law as well as by national courts.
The organisation documents human rights abuses in conflict zones.

contexts.text: Human rights are frequently the first casualty of an economic crisis.
contexts.note: Plural verb: 'rights are', never 'rights is'.

contexts.text: Before a noun it acts as a modifier and stays plural: a human rights lawyer.
contexts.note: Unusually, the modifier keeps its plural s.

contexts.text: I think education should be treated as a basic human right.
contexts.note: The singular exists when you mean one specific entitlement.

confusables.difference: Human rights belong to everyone by virtue of being human. Civil rights are the rights a particular state grants its citizens, so they vary by country.
minimal_pair: Human rights apply everywhere.
Civil rights depend on national law.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'human rights is'. The noun is plural and takes a plural verb.

entry_json.definition: used to give advice by imagining yourself in the other person's position. The main clause takes 'would', and 'were' is the fixed subjunctive form even with 'I'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: If I were you, I would apply to both universities and decide once the offers come in.
example_sentences: I would not leave it until the last week if I were you.
If I were you I would speak to the landlord before you sign anything.
collocations: if I were you, I would…
I would not do sth if I were you
if I were in your position

chunk.pattern: If I were you, I would + bare infinitive

contexts.text: If I were you, I would take the job and see how it goes.
contexts.note: The most natural way to give advice in English conversation.

contexts.text: It can also come second: I would wait a few months if I were you.
contexts.note: No comma when it follows the main clause.

contexts.text: In writing use 'should' or a recommendation: the council should consult residents first.
contexts.note: Register warning: this phrase is spoken only.

confusables.difference: 'Was' is heard in casual speech but is not standard here. In the exam use 'were', which is the correct unreal past form.
minimal_pair: If I were you, I would go.
If I was you, I would go.

entry_json.avoid: The main clause must use 'would', not 'will': 'if I were you I will go' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: if the situation requires it. It is a reduced conditional clause with the subject and verb left out, and it can go at the start, middle or end of a sentence.
