entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am happy to provide further documents if necessary.
example_sentences: The deadline can be extended if necessary, but only by a week.
If necessary, the council will introduce a temporary ban on parking.

contexts.text: I would be glad to attend an interview in person if necessary.
contexts.note: Standard closing offer in a formal letter.

contexts.text: If necessary, additional staff can be brought in during the busiest months.
contexts.note: Fronted, with a comma.

contexts.text: The same reduction works elsewhere: if possible, if in doubt, if required.
contexts.note: A productive pattern worth copying.

confusables.difference: The same meaning. 'If necessary' is slightly more formal and more common in written English.
minimal_pair: if necessary
if needed

entry_json.avoid: Do not add a subject and verb: 'if it is necessary' is correct but longer, and 'if it necessary' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: used to express a strong wish or a regret. For the present it takes the past simple, and for regret about the past it takes the past perfect: if only I had known.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: If only I had started revising a month earlier, the exam would have felt far less rushed.
example_sentences: If only the trains were more reliable, far more people would leave their cars at home.
If only we had booked earlier, we would have paid half as much.
collocations: if only it were that simple
if only sb could do sth

chunk.pattern: If only + past simple / past perfect

contexts.text: If only I had taken the earlier train, I would not have missed the interview.
contexts.note: Past perfect for regret about a finished event.

contexts.text: If only it were that simple, the problem would have been solved decades ago.
contexts.note: 'Were' for all subjects in the unreal present.

contexts.text: It can stand alone as a reply: Do you think they will change it? If only.
contexts.note: Elliptical use, spoken only.

confusables.difference: Almost identical in meaning and grammar. 'If only' is more emphatic and more emotional than 'I wish'.
minimal_pair: I wish I had studied harder.
If only I had studied harder.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'would' straight after it: 'if only I would have known' is wrong. Use 'if only I had known'.

entry_json.definition: used to make an offer or suggestion sound optional. The verb after 'to' is left out because it has already been said, which is why the phrase ends on 'to'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: You can borrow my notes if you want to; I have finished with them now.
example_sentences: We could meet earlier if you want to.
If you want to, you can pay in instalments rather than all at once.

contexts.text: You can come with us if you want to, there is plenty of room.
contexts.note: The 'to' stands in for the whole repeated verb phrase.

contexts.text: In a letter prefer 'if you wish': please contact me if you wish to discuss this further.
contexts.note: Formal equivalent.

contexts.text: The same ellipsis appears elsewhere: I did not go, although I would have liked to.
contexts.note: Pattern worth noticing.

confusables.difference: Both are heard. Keeping 'to' points back to the verb you already said and is the more careful form.
minimal_pair: Come with us if you want.
Come with us if you want to.

entry_json.avoid: Do not repeat the whole verb: 'you can come if you want to come' is clumsy. The 'to' already does that work.

entry_json.definition: having a great effect on somebody or something, or necessary for them. 'For' names who is affected; 'to' names the person who cares about it.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Sleep is more important for academic performance than most students realise.
example_sentences: Reliable transport is important for anyone who works irregular hours.
It is important for children to spend part of the day outdoors.
collocations: it is important for sb to do sth

contexts.text: Tourism is important for the local economy, but it also drives up house prices.
It is important for governments to act before the damage is irreversible.
contexts.note: The 'it is important for sb to do sth' frame is a Task 2 workhorse.

contexts.text: Use 'to' for personal value: my family is very important to me.
contexts.note: The distinction learners most often blur.

confusables.difference: 'Important to me' means I value it. 'Important for me' means it has real effects on my situation.
minimal_pair: Music is important to me.
Exercise is important for me.

entry_json.avoid: In the 'it is important for X to do Y' frame the subject cannot be dropped: not 'it is important to governments act'.

entry_json.definition: during the month of April. Months take 'in', and the month always has a capital letter with no article.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The course starts in April, which gives me two months to save enough for the fees.
example_sentences: Rainfall peaks in April and falls away sharply during the summer.
We are hoping to move in April, once the lease ends.

contexts.text: My birthday is in April, so I usually take my holiday then.
Sales reached their highest point in April before falling steadily until September.
contexts.note: Naming a peak month in Task 1.

contexts.text: With a date the preposition changes to 'on': on 3 April, but in April.
contexts.note: Months take 'in', dates take 'on'.

confusables.difference: 'On' is only used with a specific date: on 12 April. A bare month always takes 'in'.
minimal_pair: in April
on 12 April

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the April' and never 'at April'. Months take 'in' with no article.

entry_json.definition: the pattern 'in + month', shown here with July and standing for all twelve months. Every month takes 'in', a capital letter and no article.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The figures always dip in July, when most families are away.
example_sentences: Temperatures are highest in July and August in this part of the country.
The new rules come into force in January, giving businesses six months to prepare.

contexts.text: Visitor numbers peak in July and drop sharply after the schools go back.
contexts.note: Task 1 seasonal description.

contexts.text: I usually take two weeks off in August because the office is quiet then.
The same preposition covers seasons and years: in summer, in 2019, in the 1990s.
contexts.note: 'In' for long periods, 'on' for days, 'at' for clock times.

confusables.difference: 'At' is used for clock times and a few fixed phrases such as 'at night' and 'at the weekend', never for months.
minimal_pair: in July
at six o'clock

entry_json.avoid: Never lower-case the month, and never write 'in the July'.

vocab_new.lemma: in a position to do sth

entry_json.headword: in a position to do sth
entry_json.definition: able to do something because your circumstances allow it. It is about opportunity or authority rather than skill, and it is very often used in the negative.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am not in a position to comment on the decision, since I was not at the meeting.
example_sentences: Few young people are in a position to buy a home without help from their parents.
Once the results are published we will be in a position to advise you properly.
collocations: not in a position to do sth
be in a better position to do sth
put sb in a position to do sth

chunk.pattern: be in a position + to + infinitive

contexts.text: Many graduates are simply not in a position to take an unpaid internship.
contexts.note: A precise way of saying it is not about willingness but about means.

contexts.text: I am afraid I am not in a position to help with that at the moment.
contexts.note: A polite refusal.

contexts.text: The comparative is common: wealthier countries are in a far better position to adapt.
contexts.gap_span: in a far better position to

confusables.difference: Be able to is about personal capability. In a position to is about circumstances, money or authority making it possible.
minimal_pair: I am able to drive.
I am not in a position to buy a car.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in position to' without the article, and the verb after it takes 'to', not -ing.

entry_json.definition: used to describe the manner or effect of an action, followed by a relative clause. It lets you add a whole clause where a single adverb would not be enough.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The report presents the data in a way that makes the fall look far steeper than it really is.
example_sentences: Cities should grow in a way that does not destroy the surrounding farmland.
She explained the process in a way that even a complete beginner could follow.
collocations: in a way that suggests sth
in a way that makes sth easier

chunk.pattern: verb + in a way that + clause

contexts.text: Technology has changed working life in a way that would have been unimaginable in 1990.
contexts.note: A useful complex structure for Task 2.

contexts.text: Tourism should be managed in a way that benefits local people as well as visitors.
The verb in the relative clause agrees with 'way', so it is singular: in a way that makes, not make.
contexts.note: Agreement point.

confusables.difference: 'In such a way that' usually introduces a deliberate result. 'In a way that' simply describes the manner.
minimal_pair: He spoke in a way that everyone understood.
The system is designed in such a way that errors are impossible.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'which' here without a preposition, and do not drop 'that' before a verb: 'in a way makes it easier' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: following the rules, instructions or wishes that have been set out. It is formal and belongs in official or legal writing.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: All personal data is stored in accordance with the university's privacy policy.
example_sentences: The building was constructed in accordance with the new fire regulations.
Payment will be made in accordance with the terms of the contract.

contexts.text: Waste must be disposed of in accordance with local environmental regulations.
contexts.note: Formal register: rules and regulations.

contexts.text: I have completed the form in accordance with the instructions you sent.
contexts.note: Formal letter.

contexts.text: In speech nobody says this; use 'according to the rules' or simply 'as the rules say'.
contexts.note: Register warning: it sounds absurd in conversation.

confusables.difference: 'According to' reports a source of information: according to the report. 'In accordance with' means following a rule.
minimal_pair: According to the report, numbers fell.
The work was carried out in accordance with the report's recommendations.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in accordance to'. The preposition is 'with', and 'according with' is wrong as well.

entry_json.definition: actually working or performing, rather than being described. It takes no article and is common after 'see' and 'watch'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: You only understand how the machine works once you have seen it in action.
example_sentences: The demonstration let visitors see the new equipment in action.
It is one thing to read about the policy and another to watch it in action.

contexts.text: We watched the printers in action, which made the whole process much clearer.
The exhibition shows traditional crafts in action rather than behind glass.
The related phrase is 'put sth into action', meaning start using a plan.
contexts.note: Note the change from 'in' to 'into'.

confusables.difference: In action means physically operating in front of you. In practice means in reality rather than in theory.
minimal_pair: We saw the robot in action.
In practice the rule is rarely enforced.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the action', which would mean in the middle of fighting.

entry_json.definition: used to add a further point. It stands alone at the start of a sentence with a comma, and does not take an object; for that you need 'in addition to'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The scheme reduces congestion. In addition, it raises money that can be spent on buses.
example_sentences: In addition, the college offers evening classes for people already in work.
The flat is small and expensive. In addition, it is a long way from the station.

contexts.text: In addition, cycling costs nothing to run once you have bought the bicycle.
contexts.note: Task 2 addition linker; a comma is required after it.

contexts.text: It must be followed by a full clause: not 'in addition the cost'.
contexts.note: The error that turns it into a fragment.

contexts.text: In speech people say 'and also' or 'on top of that'.
contexts.note: Spoken equivalents.

confusables.difference: 'In addition' stands alone before a clause. 'In addition to' takes a noun or -ing after it. Mixing them produces a broken sentence.
minimal_pair: In addition, the cost is high.
In addition to the cost, the journey is long.

entry_json.avoid: Do not put a noun straight after it: 'in addition the noise' is wrong; write 'in addition to the noise'.

entry_json.definition: as well as somebody or something already mentioned. Here 'to' is a preposition, so a verb after it must take -ing.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In addition to paying rent, students in this city have to find a large deposit up front.
example_sentences: In addition to the tuition fee, there is a charge for laboratory materials.
She works full-time in addition to studying for a qualification in the evenings.

contexts.text: In addition to reducing emissions, cycling improves public health.
contexts.note: The -ing form is compulsory after 'to' here.

contexts.text: In addition to the rent, I pay about ninety pounds a month for bills.
'Besides' does the same job in one word: besides the rent, there are bills.
contexts.note: Shorter alternative.

confusables.difference: The same meaning. 'As well as' is slightly less formal, and both take -ing after them.
minimal_pair: in addition to working
as well as working

entry_json.avoid: The 'to' here is a preposition, so never follow it with an infinitive: not 'in addition to reduce emissions'.

entry_json.definition: before an event, or before something is used or received. It takes no article and often follows a time expression: two weeks in advance.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Tickets are much cheaper if you book two months in advance.
example_sentences: Payment must be made in advance for all short courses.
It is worth checking the opening times in advance, as they change in winter.

contexts.text: I always book train tickets a few weeks in advance because the price doubles on the day.
Could you confirm whether the deposit must be paid in advance?
'Well in advance' means with plenty of time to spare: apply well in advance of the deadline.
contexts.note: The 'of' appears only when you name the event.

confusables.difference: In advance is about time. In front of is about physical position. Some learners confuse them because both translate the same way in their language.
minimal_pair: Book in advance.
I was standing in front of the door.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the advance'. And use 'of' only when the event follows: in advance of the meeting.

vocab_new.lemma: in an attempt to do sth

entry_json.headword: in an attempt to do sth
entry_json.definition: in order to try to achieve something, often with the implication that it may not have worked. It is followed by the infinitive with 'to'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In an attempt to reduce congestion, the city introduced a charge for driving into the centre.
example_sentences: The government cut fuel duty in an attempt to slow inflation.
Several schools have banned phones in an attempt to improve concentration.
collocations: in an attempt to reduce sth
in a further attempt to do sth
in an attempt to prevent sth

contexts.text: In an attempt to cut waste, the supermarket removed all plastic packaging from fruit.
contexts.note: A more analytical alternative to 'in order to' because it hints at uncertainty.

contexts.text: The measure was introduced in an attempt to protect small shops, with mixed results.
The article is compulsory: in an attempt to, not in attempt to.
contexts.note: Form note.

confusables.difference: 'In order to' states the purpose neutrally. 'In an attempt to' adds the suggestion that success was not guaranteed, which is useful when you go on to say it failed.
minimal_pair: The tax was raised in order to fund transport.
The tax was raised in an attempt to fund transport.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in an attempt of reducing' and not 'in attempt to'. The pattern is article plus 'to' plus infinitive.

entry_json.definition: used to add a point that settles the matter whatever else is true. It often introduces the stronger of two reasons.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The flight was expensive, and in any case I could not have taken the time off work.
example_sentences: The scheme may not work, and in any case there is no money to fund it.
In any case, the decision has already been made.

contexts.text: Building more roads is expensive, and in any case it tends to generate more traffic.
contexts.note: Adds a decisive second reason: strong Task 2 move.

contexts.text: I did not really want to go, and in any case it was raining.
'Anyway' is the informal spoken version: I did not want to go anyway.
contexts.note: Position differs: 'anyway' often ends the sentence.

confusables.difference: 'In case' introduces a precaution about the future. 'In any case' adds a point that holds whatever happens. They are not related in meaning despite looking similar.
minimal_pair: Take an umbrella in case it rains.
It is late, and in any case the shops are shut.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse it with 'in case'. Also, do not use it as a simple 'also'; it must add something conclusive.

entry_json.definition: lying or resting in your bed. No article, because the phrase describes the state rather than the object.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was still in bed when the delivery arrived, which was embarrassing.
example_sentences: He spent three days in bed with flu.
Reading in bed helps me fall asleep more easily than watching anything on a screen.

contexts.text: At the weekend I stay in bed until about nine, which feels like a luxury.
Patients recovering from surgery should not stay in bed longer than necessary.
With an article it becomes the physical object: the cat was sitting on the bed.
contexts.note: State versus object, and 'in' versus 'on'.

confusables.difference: In bed means under the covers, resting. On the bed means physically on top of it, usually still dressed.
minimal_pair: She is in bed with a cold.
The books are on the bed.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the bed' when you mean resting. That phrase describes position inside a particular bed, and sounds odd in everyday use.

entry_json.definition: working in commerce, or, of a company, still trading. 'Business' is uncountable here and takes no article.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The shop has been in business for over forty years, which is remarkable given how the high street has changed.
example_sentences: Both her parents are in business, which is probably why she studied economics.
Only about half of new restaurants are still in business after three years.

contexts.text: Small shops struggle to stay in business when rents rise faster than sales.
My uncle has been in business since he was twenty-five.
With an article the meaning narrows to one particular company: he works in the family business.
contexts.note: Countable use.

confusables.difference: 'On business' means travelling for work purposes. 'In business' means working in the commercial world or still trading.
minimal_pair: He is in business.
He is in Berlin on business.

entry_json.avoid: No article in this sense: not 'in the business' unless you mean one specific firm or industry.

entry_json.definition: because something might happen. It introduces a precaution, and the clause after it uses a present tense for the future: in case it rains, not in case it will rain.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I always take a spare charger in case the train is delayed.
example_sentences: Keep a copy of the receipt in case there is a problem with the delivery.
I set two alarms in case I sleep through the first one.

chunk.pattern: main clause + in case + present tense clause

contexts.text: I take an umbrella in case it rains, even in summer.
contexts.note: Present simple after 'in case', even though the meaning is future.

contexts.text: Households are advised to keep bottled water in case the supply is interrupted.
Before a noun the form is 'in case of': in case of fire, use the stairs.
contexts.note: The noun form takes 'of'.

confusables.difference: 'If' means the action happens only when the condition occurs. 'In case' means you act first, as a precaution, whether or not it occurs.
minimal_pair: I will take an umbrella if it rains.
I will take an umbrella in case it rains.

entry_json.avoid: Never use 'will' after it: 'in case it will rain' is wrong. And do not confuse it with 'in any case'.

entry_json.definition: having control of, or responsibility for, a person, group or activity. 'Charge' takes no article, and the thing controlled follows 'of'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was put in charge of a small team in my second year, which taught me a great deal.
example_sentences: Who is in charge of the department while the manager is away?
A single agency should be in charge of flood defences rather than three separate bodies.
collocations: be in charge of a team
put sb in charge of sth

chunk.pattern: be / put + in charge of + sb / sth

contexts.text: At home I am in charge of the cooking and my brother does everything else.
Local councils should be in charge of planning decisions rather than central government.
'The person in charge' can stand alone with no 'of': I would like to speak to the person in charge.

confusables.difference: Almost the same, but 'in charge of' stresses authority and control, while 'responsible for' stresses duty and blame.
minimal_pair: She is in charge of the team.
She is responsible for any mistakes.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the charge of', which means in somebody else's care and reverses the direction.

entry_json.definition: during a lesson. No article, because it names the activity of being taught rather than a particular room or group.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We do most of the speaking practice in class and the writing at home.
example_sentences: Students who ask questions in class tend to remember more of the material.
He was told off for using his phone in class.

contexts.text: I never used to speak in class, and that is exactly why my English took so long to improve.
Discussion in class is more effective than lecturing for developing critical thinking.
With an article it means a particular group: there are thirty students in the class.
contexts.note: Activity versus group.

confusables.difference: In class means during the lesson. In the classroom refers to the physical room, and is also used figuratively for teaching practice generally.
minimal_pair: She never speaks in class.
There is no projector in the classroom.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the class' when you mean during a lesson, and not 'at class'.

entry_json.definition: together with somebody or something, so that the two work as one. It is formal, and is used both for organisations working together and for measures used in combination.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Congestion charging works best in conjunction with a genuinely reliable bus network.
example_sentences: The research was carried out in conjunction with two European universities.
The drug should be used in conjunction with changes to diet and exercise.

contexts.text: Recycling schemes only reduce waste significantly when used in conjunction with limits on packaging.
contexts.note: A precise way of saying one measure alone is not enough.

contexts.text: The exhibition was organised in conjunction with the city museum.
In speech say 'together with' or 'alongside': it works alongside the bus service.
contexts.note: Register warning: this phrase is written English.

confusables.difference: In conjunction with means working together. In connection with means related to, or concerning. They are not interchangeable.
minimal_pair: The study was done in conjunction with the hospital.
He was questioned in connection with the theft.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in conjunction to'. The preposition is 'with', and the phrase is too formal for Speaking.

entry_json.definition: concerning, or related to. It is formal, and is especially common in news reports and official letters.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am writing in connection with the advertisement that appeared in Saturday's paper.
example_sentences: Two people have been arrested in connection with the fire.
The department has published new guidance in connection with data storage.

contexts.text: I am writing in connection with the room advertised on your website.
contexts.note: A formal opening line for a General Training letter.

contexts.text: Police are questioning a man in connection with the incident.
contexts.note: News style: it avoids saying the person is guilty.

contexts.text: In speech say 'about': I am calling about the advertisement.
contexts.note: Register warning.

confusables.difference: The meaning is the same. 'About' is normal in speech; 'in connection with' is formal written English and would sound strange in conversation.
minimal_pair: I am calling about the job.
I am writing in connection with the post advertised.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it in Speaking. It sounds like a police statement rather than a conversation.

entry_json.definition: used to introduce something that is strikingly different from what was just said. It stands alone before a clause and takes a comma; for a noun you need 'in contrast to'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rail use rose steadily over the period. In contrast, the number of bus journeys fell every single year.
example_sentences: Sales in the north grew by a fifth. In contrast, the southern region saw almost no change.
In contrast, older respondents said they preferred to shop in person.

contexts.text: Cycling increased by 40 per cent. In contrast, car use remained flat throughout the decade.
contexts.note: The standard Task 1 device for opposing two trends.

contexts.text: 'By contrast' means the same and is equally acceptable in academic writing.
The two things contrasted must be genuinely comparable, or the linker misleads the reader.
contexts.note: Logic warning.

confusables.difference: 'In contrast' stands alone before a clause. 'In contrast to' introduces a noun. Using the wrong one leaves a fragment or a double subject.
minimal_pair: In contrast, prices fell.
In contrast to prices, wages fell.

entry_json.avoid: Do not put a noun straight after it: 'in contrast the north' is wrong; write 'in contrast to the north'.
entry_json.audio_hint: The noun is stressed on the first syllable: CON-trast. The verb is con-TRAST.

entry_json.definition: very different from somebody or something named. It introduces a noun phrase, and the contrast that follows is usually the surprising one.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In contrast to the previous decade, growth in the 2010s was concentrated in a handful of cities.
example_sentences: In contrast to her sister, she has no interest in living abroad.
Wind generation rose sharply, in contrast to coal, which almost disappeared.

contexts.text: In contrast to the capital, rents in the north remained broadly stable.
contexts.note: Comparing two regions in Task 1.

contexts.text: 'In stark contrast to' is the emphatic version, used when the difference is dramatic.
After 'to' a verb takes -ing: in contrast to walking, cycling covers four times the distance.
contexts.note: 'To' is a preposition here.

confusables.difference: 'Compared to' notes any difference or similarity. 'In contrast to' insists the two are opposite, so it is stronger.
minimal_pair: Compared to last year, sales are slightly up.
In contrast to last year, sales collapsed.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in contrast with' in most academic writing, and never follow 'to' with a full clause.

entry_json.definition: likely to be harmed, or at risk of something bad happening. No article, and the risk itself follows 'of' plus a noun or -ing.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Several coastal villages are now in danger of being lost to erosion within twenty years.
example_sentences: The species is in danger of extinction across most of its former range.
Nobody was in danger, but the building had to be evacuated.

contexts.text: Without stronger protection, these forests are in danger of disappearing altogether.
contexts.note: -ing after 'of', not an infinitive.

contexts.text: Cyclists are in danger every time they share a narrow road with lorries.
The adjective is different: cycling on that road is dangerous.
contexts.note: Noun phrase versus adjective.

confusables.difference: Almost the same. 'At risk' is more common in formal and statistical writing; 'in danger' is stronger and more immediate.
minimal_pair: Children are at risk of obesity.
The building is in danger of collapse.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the danger'. And after 'in danger of' use -ing, not 'to': not 'in danger to disappear'.

entry_json.definition: used to say what the real result of something is, even if it is not officially described that way. It also means that a rule is currently operating.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Charging for the car park is, in effect, a tax on anyone who cannot walk to work.
example_sentences: The subsidy is in effect a payment to landlords rather than to tenants.
The new regulations have been in effect since January.

contexts.text: Free tuition funded by general taxation is, in effect, a transfer from non-graduates to graduates.
contexts.note: A sophisticated Task 2 move: restating what a policy really does.

contexts.text: The ban comes into effect at the end of the month.
contexts.note: The 'operating' sense uses 'come into effect' or 'be in effect'.

contexts.text: Do not confuse the noun 'effect' with the verb 'affect': the ban affected sales; the effect was immediate.
contexts.note: Spelling trap.

confusables.difference: 'In fact' corrects or strengthens a statement. 'In effect' restates something in terms of its real result, often differently from its official name.
minimal_pair: In fact, the tax was never introduced.
The charge is, in effect, a tax.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'in affect'. 'Affect' is the verb; the noun in this phrase is 'effect'.

entry_json.definition: used to correct what has just been said, or to add a stronger and often surprising detail. It usually sits at the start of the sentence or after the verb 'be'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: People assume the city is expensive. In fact, rents outside the centre are lower than in most of the region.
example_sentences: The journey looks long on the map. In fact, it takes less than an hour.
She is not just a colleague; in fact, we studied together.

contexts.text: Many people believe recycling solves the problem. In fact, reducing consumption matters far more.
contexts.note: Correcting a common assumption: a strong Task 2 move.

contexts.text: I thought it would be difficult, but in fact it was quite straightforward.
It can strengthen rather than correct: the course was good, in fact excellent.
contexts.note: Second function: intensifying.

confusables.difference: Very close in meaning. 'Actually' is more conversational and often softens a correction; 'in fact' is more emphatic and works in writing.
minimal_pair: Actually, it is quite cheap.
In fact, it is cheaper than the alternative.

entry_json.avoid: It needs something to correct or strengthen. Do not use it as a general opener when nothing has been claimed yet.

entry_json.definition: supporting a proposal or person, or choosing one option instead of another. British spelling keeps the u: favour.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am strongly in favour of making public transport free for under-eighteens.
example_sentences: Two thirds of residents voted in favour of the new cycle lanes.
The committee rejected the original design in favour of a cheaper alternative.

contexts.text: There are strong arguments in favour of raising the school leaving age.
contexts.note: The Task 2 discussion frame: arguments in favour of, arguments against.

contexts.text: Are you in favour of the new rules? On balance, yes.
The 'instead of' sense: the plan was dropped in favour of a smaller scheme.
contexts.note: Second meaning: replacing one thing with another.

confusables.difference: 'In favour with' means somebody approves of you, which is a completely different idea. Support takes 'of'.
minimal_pair: I am in favour of the plan.
The proposal found favour with the committee.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in favour to' and not 'in the favour of'. In British writing keep the u in favour.

entry_json.definition: in the position directly before something, on the side that faces forward. It also means in somebody's presence: do not say that in front of the children.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a small park in front of the station where people wait for their buses.
example_sentences: A tall building has gone up in front of our window and blocked most of the light.
He was too shy to speak in front of the whole class.
collocations: sit in front of a screen

contexts.text: The bus stop is right in front of my building, which is very convenient.
Adults now spend around six hours a day in front of a screen.
contexts.note: Fixed collocation with screens.

contexts.text: The presence sense: I did not want to say anything in front of her colleagues.

confusables.difference: In front of means on the forward-facing side, close by. Opposite means facing it from across a road or space.
minimal_pair: The car is parked in front of the house.
The bakery is opposite the house.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the front of' unless you mean inside, near the front of something, as in 'in the front of the car'.

entry_json.definition: completely, with nothing left out or unpaid. It goes after the verb or its object: pay the amount in full.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The deposit will be refunded in full provided the room is left in good condition.
example_sentences: Please write your name in full, including any middle names.
The loan must be repaid in full within five years.

contexts.text: I would be grateful if the amount could be refunded in full.
contexts.note: Letter of complaint: the standard way to request a complete refund.

contexts.text: The findings were published in full on the department's website.
It contrasts with 'in part': the costs were met in part by the council and in full by no one.

confusables.difference: 'Fully' modifies an adjective or participle: fully aware, fully funded. 'In full' follows a verb and is used mostly with payment, publication and writing things out.
minimal_pair: The project is fully funded.
The invoice was paid in full.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the full'. And do not use it where you need 'fully': 'in full aware' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: usually, or considering something as a whole rather than in detail. It can open a sentence with a comma or follow the noun it qualifies: people in general.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In general, students who attend every seminar do better, though there are always exceptions.
example_sentences: Public transport in this city is, in general, reliable and reasonably priced.
In general, the older the building, the more expensive it is to heat.

contexts.text: In general, wealthier countries produce more waste per person.
contexts.note: A hedge: it protects a general claim from obvious exceptions.

contexts.text: In general I prefer cooking at home, but I do eat out at the weekend.
After a noun it means 'as a whole': attitudes to work in general have changed.
contexts.note: Different position, slightly different job.

confusables.difference: The same meaning. 'Generally' is a single adverb and can sit before the verb; 'in general' is a phrase and usually opens the sentence.
minimal_pair: Generally, people work longer hours now.
In general, people work longer hours now.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the general' and not 'in generally'.

entry_json.definition: at any time in the recorded past. It takes no article and very often follows a superlative: the hottest year in history.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It was the largest peaceful demonstration in the country's history.
example_sentences: This was the wettest winter in recorded history for the region.
Few decisions in history have had such far-reaching consequences.

contexts.text: 2023 was the warmest year in recorded history.
contexts.note: Very common in environmental writing.

contexts.text: With a possessive the article stays away: the biggest change in the city's history.
As a school subject it also takes no article: I was never any good at history.

confusables.difference: 'In the past' means before now, at some unspecified time. 'In history' compares across the whole record and usually follows a superlative.
minimal_pair: In the past, people walked more.
It was the hottest summer in history.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the history' without a possessive. Say 'in history' or 'in the country's history'.

entry_json.definition: receiving treatment as a patient. British English drops the article when the meaning is the purpose of the place; American English says 'in the hospital'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My grandmother was in hospital for a fortnight after the operation.
example_sentences: He spent three nights in hospital and was discharged on the Friday.
The number of days patients spend in hospital has fallen steadily since 2000.

contexts.text: She was in hospital for a week, and the staff were excellent.
contexts.note: British usage, which the IELTS examiner voices use.

contexts.text: Average time spent in hospital fell from nine days to four over the period.
With an article you are visiting, not a patient: I was at the hospital to see a friend.
contexts.note: Patient versus visitor, exactly like 'at school'.

confusables.difference: Without 'the' you are a patient. With 'the' you are simply inside the building, perhaps working or visiting. American English uses 'the' for both.
minimal_pair: He is in hospital.
I met her in the hospital car park.

entry_json.avoid: In an IELTS answer about being ill, use the British form 'in hospital' with no article.

entry_json.definition: taking new information or events into account. It introduces the reason for reconsidering something, and is formal.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In light of the latest figures, the council has agreed to review the parking charges.
example_sentences: The policy was revised in light of the consultation responses.
In light of what we now know about air quality, the case for the ban is far stronger.

contexts.text: In light of the evidence linking pollution to asthma, stricter limits are justified.
contexts.note: A strong way to introduce evidence-based reasoning in Task 2.

contexts.text: The variant 'in the light of' is equally correct in British English.
contexts.note: Both forms are standard; British writing often keeps 'the'.

contexts.text: I would like to reconsider my application in light of my recent results.

confusables.difference: 'Because of' gives a plain cause. 'In light of' means new information has changed how something should be judged, which is a more analytical claim.
minimal_pair: The trip was cancelled because of the weather.
The plan was revised in light of the new forecast.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in light with' and not 'under the light of'. It takes 'of' plus a noun, never a clause.

entry_json.definition: matching or consistent with something else, such as a rule, a forecast or a trend. It is the standard phrase for saying a result was as expected.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Wages have not risen in line with the cost of living, which is why so many households feel poorer.
example_sentences: The results were broadly in line with what the model predicted.
Fees will increase in line with inflation each September.
collocations: bring sth into line with sth

contexts.text: The increase in car ownership was in line with the growth in average income.
contexts.note: Task 1: linking two trends that move together.

contexts.text: The policy brings this country into line with the rest of Europe.
contexts.note: The change-of-state version uses 'into'.

contexts.text: The negative is very common: pay has not kept in line with prices.

confusables.difference: 'In accordance with' means obeying a rule. 'In line with' means matching a pattern, forecast or level, and does not imply obedience.
minimal_pair: built in accordance with the regulations
rising in line with inflation

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in line to'. And do not use it for obeying rules; that needs 'in accordance with'.

entry_json.definition: feeling a strong romantic attachment. No article, and it follows a linking verb: be in love, fall in love.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: They met at university, fell in love and have been together ever since.
example_sentences: The film is about two people who fall in love in the middle of a war.
They were very much in love, but they lived on different continents.

contexts.text: My parents fell in love at a wedding and were married within a year.
The novel asks whether people who are in love make good decisions.
It is also used loosely about places: I fell in love with the city on the first day.
contexts.note: Extended, non-romantic use.

confusables.difference: 'Love' as a verb covers family and friends as well. 'In love' is specifically romantic, and 'fall in love' names the moment it began.
minimal_pair: I love my sister.
He is in love with her.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the love'. And 'fall in love' is the event, so do not say 'I am falling in love with my parents'.

entry_json.definition: romantically attached to a particular person. The person follows 'with', never 'to' or 'of'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She was clearly in love with him long before either of them admitted it.
example_sentences: He fell in love with a woman he met on an exchange programme.
Being in love with someone who lives abroad is harder than films suggest.

contexts.text: They fell in love with each other over a very long correspondence.
The preposition never changes: in love with her, not in love to her.
contexts.note: The error nearly every learner makes once.

contexts.text: It extends to things and places: he is in love with the idea of moving abroad.
contexts.note: Figurative use.

confusables.difference: 'In love' with no object describes the state; add 'with sb' when you name the person.
minimal_pair: They are in love.
He is in love with her.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'in love to' or 'in love of'. The preposition is 'with'.

entry_json.definition: used to signal that what follows is your personal view. It usually opens the sentence with a comma, and 'opinion' takes the possessive, never an article.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In my opinion, the money would achieve far more if it were spent on teacher training.
example_sentences: In my opinion, the advantages of remote working outweigh the drawbacks.
The design is, in my opinion, far better than the original.

contexts.text: In my opinion, schools should teach basic financial skills.
contexts.note: Fine in Task 2 when the question asks for your view, but use it once, not in every paragraph.

contexts.text: For variety try 'I would argue that' or 'to my mind'.
contexts.note: Repetition of one opinion phrase costs marks.

contexts.text: In my opinion the second option is better, though I can see the argument for the first.

confusables.difference: 'According to' is used for other sources, never for yourself. 'According to me' is a clear error that examiners notice immediately.
minimal_pair: In my opinion, it is too expensive.
According to the report, it is too expensive.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'according to me' or 'in my point of view'. The correct forms are 'in my opinion', 'in my view' and 'from my point of view'.

entry_json.definition: arranged according to a stated principle, such as size, importance or date. 'Order' takes no article in this phrase.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The candidates are listed in order of preference rather than alphabetically.
example_sentences: The countries are shown in order of population, from largest to smallest.
Please list your qualifications in order of date, starting with the most recent.

contexts.text: The table lists the five cities in order of average rainfall.
contexts.note: Useful when describing how a Task 1 table is organised.

contexts.text: I would rank the causes in order of importance, with cost first.
Some fixed versions drop 'of': in alphabetical order, in chronological order.
contexts.note: With an adjective, no 'of' is needed.

confusables.difference: Completely different. 'In order of' arranges things; 'in order to' states a purpose.
minimal_pair: listed in order of size
built in order to reduce traffic

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the order of' unless you mean approximately, as in 'in the order of 5,000', which is a different phrase.

entry_json.definition: with the purpose of doing something. It is the formal version of purpose 'to', and the negative is 'in order not to', which cannot be shortened.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In order to reduce congestion, several cities have made the centre car-free.
example_sentences: Many students take a part-time job in order to cover their living costs.
He left an hour early in order not to miss the connection.
collocations: in order not to do sth

contexts.text: In order to meet the target, emissions would have to fall by 7 per cent every year.
contexts.note: A clear Task 2 purpose clause; fronted, with a comma.

contexts.text: The negative is 'in order not to': she wrote it down in order not to forget.
contexts.note: You cannot say 'not in order to'.

contexts.text: 'So that' takes a full clause instead: they built the bypass so that lorries could avoid the village.
contexts.note: Alternative structure with a subject and verb.

confusables.difference: 'In order to' takes an infinitive and needs the same subject. 'So that' takes a full clause and allows a different subject.
minimal_pair: She left early in order to catch the train.
She left early so that the others could use the room.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in order for reduce' and not 'in order of reducing'. It is always 'in order to' plus the base verb.

entry_json.definition: used to restate something more simply or more directly. It signals that what follows means the same thing, not something new.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The scheme costs more per passenger than a taxi would. In other words, it is not a serious transport policy.
example_sentences: The proposal doubles the fee for everyone outside the zone. In other words, the poorest residents pay most.
Emissions must peak before 2030; in other words, action cannot wait for the next decade.

contexts.text: Only a fifth of applicants were successful. In other words, four out of five were turned away.
contexts.note: Restating a statistic in a way that makes its meaning land.

contexts.text: It is a long way from anywhere, or in other words, you need a car.
It must not introduce new information; if it does, use 'furthermore' instead.
contexts.note: The rule learners break most often with this linker.

confusables.difference: The same job. 'That is to say' is more formal and slightly more precise; 'in other words' is the everyday choice.
minimal_pair: In other words, it is too expensive.
That is to say, the cost exceeds the budget.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it to add a new point. It only reformulates what you have already said.

entry_json.definition: partly, but not completely. It is a careful way of naming one cause among several, and is common in academic writing.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The fall in high street sales can be explained in part by the rise of online shopping.
example_sentences: The delay was in part the result of a shortage of materials.
Her success is due in part to the support she received early on.

chunk.pattern: in part (+ because of / due to)

contexts.text: The improvement is due in part to cleaner vehicles and in part to the closure of the power station.
contexts.note: Splitting a cause between two factors, which is more honest than claiming one.

contexts.text: It is a hedge: it protects a claim you cannot fully prove.
contexts.note: Why it scores well in Task 2.

contexts.text: The everyday spoken version is 'partly': it was partly my fault.

confusables.difference: Identical in meaning. 'Partly' is a single adverb and is more common in speech; 'in part' is the formal written variant.
minimal_pair: It was partly due to the weather.
It was due in part to the weather.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the part'. And do not use it where you mean 'in some places', which is 'in parts'.

entry_json.definition: especially, or more than the others. It normally comes straight after the noun it singles out, or at the start of a sentence with a comma.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Young families in particular have been priced out of the areas near the centre.
example_sentences: Older residents, in particular, rely on the bus service.
In particular, the report criticises the lack of consultation.

contexts.text: Coastal cities in particular will have to invest heavily in flood defences.
contexts.note: Placed after the noun it picks out: precise and unmistakable.

contexts.text: Were you looking for anything in particular? Just browsing, thank you.
contexts.note: Fixed question form.

contexts.text: 'Particularly' is the adverb and goes before the word it modifies: particularly expensive.
contexts.note: Different position, same idea.

confusables.difference: Almost interchangeable, but 'especially' goes before the item and 'in particular' after it. Both single one thing out of a group.
minimal_pair: especially older residents
older residents in particular

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in particularly' and not 'in the particular'.

entry_json.definition: existing and ready to operate, of a system, rule or arrangement. It also means in the correct position. No article.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Flood defences are now in place along the whole of the eastern bank.
example_sentences: The new safety procedures have been in place since April.
Once the funding is in place, work can begin on the second phase.

contexts.text: Strict recycling targets are already in place in several European countries.
contexts.note: A compact way of saying a policy exists and is operating.

contexts.text: The council should put proper cycle lanes in place before encouraging people to cycle.
contexts.note: 'Put sth in place' is the active version.

contexts.text: 'In place of' is a different phrase meaning instead of: tea in place of coffee.
contexts.note: Adding 'of' changes the meaning completely.

confusables.difference: 'In place' means operating. 'In place of' means instead of. One word changes the sense entirely.
minimal_pair: The system is in place.
They used gas in place of coal.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the place' when you mean operating. That would mean physically inside a location.

entry_json.definition: in the real situation, as opposed to what was intended or expected. It almost always sets up a contrast with theory or with an official rule.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In theory anyone can appeal the decision; in practice the process is so slow that almost nobody does.
example_sentences: The law bans it, but in practice it is rarely enforced.
In practice, most people take the shortest route regardless of the signs.

contexts.text: In theory the scheme is open to everyone; in practice, only those with a car can reach it.
contexts.note: The theory-versus-practice pairing is a strong Task 2 structure.

contexts.text: It sounds sensible, but in practice it would be very hard to enforce.
The British spelling of the verb is 'practise' with an s; the noun keeps the c.
contexts.note: Spelling trap in British English.

confusables.difference: 'In fact' corrects a statement. 'In practice' contrasts what actually happens with what was supposed to happen.
minimal_pair: In fact, the law was repealed.
In practice, the law is ignored.

entry_json.avoid: In British English the noun is spelled 'practice' with a c. 'In practise' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: serving a sentence as a prisoner. No article, because the phrase names the purpose of the institution rather than the building.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: He spent four years in prison and has found it almost impossible to get work since.
example_sentences: The number of people in prison has risen sharply over the past twenty years.
Keeping non-violent offenders in prison is expensive and achieves very little.

contexts.text: Education programmes reduce the chance that people who have been in prison will offend again.
contexts.note: Central Task 2 crime-and-punishment vocabulary.

contexts.text: The related forms are 'go to prison' and 'be sent to prison', both without an article.
With an article it becomes the building: she works at the prison as a teacher.
contexts.note: Prisoner versus staff, exactly as with school and hospital.

confusables.difference: The same meaning. 'Prison' is the standard British term in formal writing; 'jail' is more common in journalism and American English.
minimal_pair: He is in prison.
He is in jail.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the prison' when you mean serving a sentence, and never 'in a prison' in a general statement.

entry_json.definition: where other people can see or hear you. No article, and it contrasts with 'in private'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I still find it difficult to speak in public, even after years of teaching.
example_sentences: Smoking in public places was banned here more than fifteen years ago.
She rarely discusses her work in public.

contexts.text: Speaking in public is one of the skills schools ought to teach and mostly do not.
I get nervous speaking in public, so I practise in front of a mirror.
Before a noun 'public' is an adjective: public transport, a public place.

confusables.difference: 'The public' is a noun meaning ordinary people. 'In public' means where others can see. 'In the public' is not idiomatic.
minimal_pair: He never sings in public.
The public were not consulted.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the public'. And 'publicly' is the adverb, spelled without an a.

entry_json.definition: during the last few years, up to now. It pairs naturally with the present perfect, because the period is unfinished.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In recent years the city has invested heavily in cycling, and the results are now visible.
example_sentences: Rents have risen sharply in recent years, particularly near the university.
In recent years there has been a marked increase in remote working.

contexts.text: In recent years, more and more people have chosen to work from home.
contexts.note: The classic Task 2 opening move, and it requires the present perfect.

contexts.text: Do not pair it with the past simple: not 'in recent years the number rose'.
contexts.note: Tense rule: the period includes now.

contexts.text: Things have changed a lot in recent years, especially since the pandemic.

confusables.difference: The same meaning and the same tense requirement. 'In recent years' is slightly more formal and is the better choice in writing.
minimal_pair: in recent years
in the last few years

entry_json.avoid: It cannot take a finished past tense. 'In recent years the government introduced' should be 'has introduced'.

entry_json.definition: concerning something, or compared with it. It is formal, and is used both to introduce a topic and to make a proportional comparison.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Housing costs are extremely high in relation to average earnings in this part of the country.
example_sentences: The report makes several recommendations in relation to staff training.
The country's emissions are small in relation to its population.

contexts.text: Spending on health is low in relation to the size of the population.
contexts.note: The comparison sense: it makes a claim proportional rather than absolute.

contexts.text: I would like to raise a concern in relation to the timetable change.
contexts.note: The topic sense, in a formal letter.

contexts.text: In speech simply say 'about' or 'compared with'.
contexts.note: Register note.

confusables.difference: 'In terms of' names the measure you are using. 'In relation to' compares one thing against another or introduces a topic.
minimal_pair: expensive in terms of fuel
expensive in relation to income

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in relation with'. The preposition is 'to'.

entry_json.definition: concerning a particular matter. It is formal and largely legal or administrative, and is rare outside official documents.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The council has no liability in respect of items left in the car park.
example_sentences: A refund will be issued in respect of the two nights you did not stay.
The regulations set out the employer's duties in respect of health and safety.
collocations: a claim in respect of sth

contexts.text: I am writing in respect of the invoice dated 14 March.
contexts.note: Very formal letter opening; 'regarding' is usually better.

contexts.text: 'With respect to' means the same and is a little more common in academic writing.
In an essay prefer 'regarding' or simply 'on': the report comments on staffing levels.
contexts.note: Simpler is usually better in Task 2.

confusables.difference: 'With respect' before a disagreement is a politeness formula, as in 'with respect, I disagree'. 'In respect of' simply means concerning.
minimal_pair: With respect, that is not what the data show.
A claim in respect of damaged goods.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it in Speaking; it sounds like a contract. And not 'in respect to' in British usage.

entry_json.definition: as a reaction to something that happened or was said. It names the trigger, and is common in reports and formal letters.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In response to repeated complaints, the company extended its opening hours.
example_sentences: The measure was introduced in response to a sharp rise in air pollution.
I am writing in response to your letter of 12 May.

contexts.text: In response to growing demand, several universities now offer the course online.
contexts.note: Names the cause of a policy without using 'because'.

contexts.text: I am writing in response to your advertisement in Friday's paper.
contexts.note: Standard formal letter opening.

contexts.text: The verb form takes the same preposition: the council responded to the complaints.

confusables.difference: 'As a result of' states a cause and effect. 'In response to' implies a deliberate reaction by someone who chose to act.
minimal_pair: Prices rose as a result of the shortage.
The government acted in response to the shortage.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in response of'. The preposition is 'to', matching the verb 'respond to'.

entry_json.definition: attending school as a pupil, or enrolled in education. British English usually prefers 'at school' for this; 'in school' is the American norm and is also used in statistics about enrolment.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Around 90 per cent of children in that age group are now in school, compared with half in 1990.
example_sentences: Keeping girls in school for longer has a measurable effect on family income.
He is still in school and will not finish until next summer.

contexts.text: The number of children in school rose steadily across the whole period.
contexts.note: The enrolment sense, standard in reports of both varieties.

contexts.text: British speakers normally say 'at school': I was at school with her.
contexts.note: Use 'at school' in Speaking, since the exam is British.

contexts.text: With an article it means inside the building: the meeting is in the school hall.

confusables.difference: British English uses 'at school' for attending; American English uses 'in school'. Both appear in writing about enrolment figures.
minimal_pair: I was at school in Leeds.
Sixty per cent of children are in school.

entry_json.avoid: In Speaking prefer 'at school'. And never add 'the' when you mean attending as a pupil.

entry_json.definition: for part of the group being discussed, but not all of it. It is a hedge that stops a general claim from sounding absolute.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Working from home saves time and money, though in some cases it makes people feel isolated.
example_sentences: In some cases the treatment has to be repeated after a year.
Fees have doubled, and in some cases tripled, since 2010.

contexts.text: Longer sentences deter some offenders and, in some cases, make reoffending more likely.
contexts.note: A hedge that shows you know the picture is mixed: valuable in Task 2.

contexts.text: The same family gives 'in many cases' and 'in most cases', which are stronger.
contexts.note: A scale of certainty you can choose from.

contexts.text: It depends really; in some cases it works well, in others it does not.

confusables.difference: 'Sometimes' is about frequency in time. 'In some cases' is about a proportion of the examples, which is what an essay usually needs.
minimal_pair: Sometimes the train is late.
In some cases the treatment fails.

entry_json.avoid: Keep 'cases' plural: not 'in some case'.

entry_json.definition: beyond the earth's atmosphere. In this sense 'space' is uncountable and takes no article; with an article it means an area or gap.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There are now more satellites in space than at any point in history, and most of them are commercial.
example_sentences: Astronauts spend months in space, which weakens their bones.
The money spent on exploring space would fund a great deal of research on earth.

contexts.text: Whether governments should spend money in space rather than on earth is a standard essay question.
contexts.note: A recurring Task 2 topic.

contexts.text: With an article it means a gap or an area: there is a space between the two buildings.
contexts.note: Countable sense.

contexts.text: 'Green space' is a fixed collocation about parks and is often uncountable too.

confusables.difference: Without an article you mean outer space. With one you mean a particular gap or room.
minimal_pair: Satellites orbit in space.
Put it in the space under the stairs.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in the space' when you mean beyond the atmosphere, and never 'in a space' in that sense.

entry_json.definition: although something is true. It is followed by a noun or -ing, never by a full clause, and it means the same as 'despite', which takes no 'of'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In spite of the rain, the whole event went ahead as planned.
example_sentences: In spite of the cost, most families still take at least one holiday a year.
She passed in spite of missing almost a month of lessons.
collocations: in spite of the fact that…

contexts.text: In spite of heavy investment, journey times have barely improved.
contexts.note: Concession, fronted with a comma: a strong Task 2 structure.

contexts.text: To use a clause you must add 'the fact that': in spite of the fact that it was raining.
contexts.gap_span: in spite of the fact that
contexts.note: The bridge from noun to clause.

contexts.text: 'Despite' means exactly the same but takes no 'of': despite the rain.
contexts.note: The most common mix-up in the whole area.

confusables.difference: 'Although' takes a full clause with a subject and verb. 'In spite of' takes a noun or -ing. Mixing them is the classic error.
minimal_pair: Although it rained, we went.
In spite of the rain, we went.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'in spite of it was raining' and never 'despite of'. One takes a clause, the other a noun.

entry_json.definition: in a manner that produces a particular result, usually deliberately. The result follows 'that' as a full clause; 'as to' plus an infinitive is the more formal variant.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The building is designed in such a way that it needs almost no heating in winter.
example_sentences: The questions were worded in such a way that only one answer seemed reasonable.
Resources should be allocated in such a way that the poorest regions benefit most.
collocations: designed in such a way that…
arranged in such a way that…
in such a way as to do sth

chunk.pattern: in such a way that + clause

contexts.text: Cities should be planned in such a way that most daily journeys can be made on foot.
contexts.note: A complex structure that shows deliberate design, ideal for a Task 2 solution paragraph.

contexts.text: The formal variant uses 'as to': arranged in such a way as to minimise waste.
contexts.gap_span: in such a way as to
contexts.note: Takes an infinitive, not a clause.

contexts.text: Without 'such' the meaning weakens to plain manner: in a way that everyone understood.

confusables.difference: 'So that' introduces a purpose in plain language. 'In such a way that' emphasises the manner of doing it as well as the result.
minimal_pair: It was built so that it would need no heating.
It was built in such a way that it needs no heating.

entry_json.avoid: Do not mix the two versions: 'in such a way as that' is wrong. Use 'that' plus a clause, or 'as to' plus an infinitive.

entry_json.definition: during the summer season, in general. With no article it means summers as a rule; 'in the summer' can mean either the general season or one particular summer.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In summer the whole town fills up with visitors and the traffic becomes impossible.
example_sentences: Electricity demand peaks in winter here, unlike in countries where air conditioning is used in summer.
We usually go back in summer, when the schools are closed.

contexts.text: It gets very humid here in summer, which is why nobody works in the afternoon.
contexts.note: General habit: no article.

contexts.text: Rainfall is lowest in summer and highest between November and January.
contexts.note: Describing a climate chart.

contexts.text: 'In the summer' is equally correct in British English and slightly more common in speech.
contexts.note: Both are acceptable; neither is an error.

confusables.difference: Seasons take 'in', never 'at'. 'At' is reserved for clock times and a few fixed phrases such as 'at night'.
minimal_pair: in summer
at night

entry_json.avoid: Never 'at summer' and never 'on summer'.

entry_json.definition: measured by a particular aspect, or as far as that aspect is concerned. It names the yardstick you are using and is followed by a noun or -ing.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In terms of cost, cycling is far cheaper than any other way of crossing the city.
example_sentences: The two courses are similar in terms of content but very different in terms of assessment.
In terms of energy use, the newer building is a third more efficient.
collocations: both in terms of sth and sth

contexts.text: In terms of population, the city has doubled in size since 1980.
contexts.note: Naming the measure explicitly, which Task 1 rewards.

contexts.text: It is very useful for structuring a comparison: cheaper in terms of fuel, dearer in terms of maintenance.
It is overused. If the sentence works without it, delete it: 'in terms of my opinion' says nothing.
contexts.note: Warning: examiners notice empty uses.

confusables.difference: 'Regarding' introduces a topic. 'In terms of' introduces the measure you are judging by, so it must be followed by something measurable.
minimal_pair: Regarding the cost, I have a question.
It is expensive in terms of fuel.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it as a general filler before any noun. It must name a genuine measure or aspect.

entry_json.definition: when something or somebody is not there or not available. It is formal, and in academic writing it usually introduces the lack of evidence or regulation.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In the absence of reliable data, any estimate of the true figure is guesswork.
example_sentences: In the absence of a national policy, each city has developed its own approach.
In the absence of the chairperson, the deputy took the meeting.
collocations: in the absence of any alternative

contexts.text: In the absence of strong evidence, governments have been reluctant to legislate.
contexts.note: A precise formal way of saying 'because there is no...'.

contexts.text: In the absence of public transport, car ownership in rural areas is a necessity rather than a choice.
In speech say 'without' or 'since there is no': without any evidence, nobody will act.
contexts.note: Register note.

confusables.difference: The same meaning, but 'without' is neutral and works everywhere. 'In the absence of' is formal and stresses that the thing ought to have been there.
minimal_pair: without evidence
in the absence of evidence

entry_json.avoid: The article is compulsory: not 'in absence of'.

entry_json.definition: during the hours between midday and evening. Parts of the day take 'in the', except night, which takes 'at'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I concentrate much better in the morning, so I leave routine work for the afternoon.
example_sentences: The library is quietest in the afternoon, between two and four.
Deliveries are made in the afternoon on weekdays.

contexts.text: I usually study in the afternoon because the mornings are taken up with classes.
With a day name the preposition changes to 'on': on Monday afternoon, not in Monday afternoon.
contexts.note: The rule learners forget most often.

contexts.text: Usage peaks in the afternoon and falls away sharply after seven.

confusables.difference: Morning, afternoon and evening take 'in the'. Night is the exception and takes 'at'.
minimal_pair: in the evening
at night

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in afternoon' and not 'at the afternoon'. And with a named day switch to 'on'.

entry_json.definition: carried by the atmosphere, or flying rather than on the ground. Figuratively it means that a feeling or possibility is noticeable but not yet settled.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The amount of particulate matter in the air near the ring road exceeds the legal limit on most winter days.
example_sentences: You can smell the salt in the air long before you see the sea.
There was a real sense of change in the air after the election.

contexts.text: Levels of nitrogen dioxide in the air have fallen since the low-emission zone was introduced.
contexts.note: The literal, measurable sense.

contexts.text: Everything is still up in the air; we will not know until the results come out.
contexts.note: The idiom 'up in the air' means undecided.

contexts.text: The plane was in the air for eleven hours.

confusables.difference: 'On air' means broadcasting live on radio or television, and has no article. 'In the air' is about the atmosphere.
minimal_pair: Pollen in the air causes hay fever.
The programme goes on air at six.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the article: 'in air' is only used in technical writing about the substance itself.

entry_json.definition: as far as this particular example is concerned. It singles out one member of a group you are discussing, and is not a conditional.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most of the sites recovered within a year; in the case of the largest lake, it took almost a decade.
example_sentences: In the case of older buildings, insulation is far more expensive to fit.
The rule applies to everyone, except in the case of medical students, who follow a separate timetable.
collocations: as in the case of sth
except in the case of sth

contexts.text: In the case of Germany, the figure rose steadily throughout the period.
contexts.note: Task 1: picking one country out of several without repeating 'as for'.

contexts.text: It is not a conditional. 'In case of fire' is a different phrase meaning if there is a fire.
contexts.note: The article is what separates the two.

contexts.text: In the case of very young children, screen time seems to matter more.

confusables.difference: 'In case of fire' is a precaution: if a fire happens. 'In the case of X' picks out one example from a set. The article changes the meaning entirely.
minimal_pair: In case of fire, use the stairs.
In the case of fire damage, a separate form is required.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'the' when you mean 'as for this example', and do not add it when you mean a precaution.

entry_json.definition: in the middle part of a place, especially the central area of a town or city. British spelling is centre; American is center.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Almost nobody can afford to live in the centre now, so people commute in from thirty kilometres away.
example_sentences: Parking in the centre costs more than the train fare from the suburbs.
There is a small market in the centre every Saturday morning.

contexts.text: I work in the centre but live about twenty minutes out by bus.
Restricting traffic in the centre has improved air quality in several European cities.
The map shows the station in the centre, with residential areas to the north and south.
contexts.note: Describing a map in Task 1.

confusables.difference: 'In the middle' is about physical position anywhere. 'In the centre' is the standard term for the central district of a town, and for the exact midpoint.
minimal_pair: a table in the middle of the room
an office in the centre of town

entry_json.avoid: In British writing spell it 'centre'. And do not drop the article: not 'in centre'.

entry_json.definition: in the middle of a named place or object. 'Of' introduces the whole that the centre belongs to.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The cathedral stands in the centre of the old town, and every street seems to lead back to it.
example_sentences: There is a large roundabout in the centre of the diagram.
She lives in the centre of Madrid, five minutes from her office.
collocations: in the centre of the city
in the centre of the map
right in the centre of sth

contexts.text: The park is in the centre of the site, with car parking to the east.
contexts.note: Standard Task 1 map language.

contexts.text: We stayed in a small hotel in the centre of the old quarter.
The 'r' is pronounced when 'of' follows: centre-of.
contexts.note: Linking r in British English.

confusables.difference: 'At the centre of' is usually figurative: at the centre of the debate. 'In the centre of' is physical position.
minimal_pair: in the centre of the town
at the centre of the argument

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'of' before a place name: 'in the centre Madrid' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: in the central district of a city, where the main shops and offices are. It is the standard British term; Americans say downtown.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rents in the city centre have risen so fast that most of my colleagues now live outside it.
example_sentences: Cars have been banned from much of the city centre since 2019.
There are far more restaurants in the city centre than in the suburbs.

contexts.text: Do you live in the city centre? No, about half an hour out.
contexts.note: One of the most common Part 1 exchanges of all.

contexts.text: Pedestrianising the city centre would reduce pollution but might harm small shops.
contexts.note: A standard Task 2 argument.

contexts.text: Americans say 'downtown' with no article: I work downtown.
contexts.note: Variety note; use the British form in this exam.

confusables.difference: The same idea at a smaller scale. Use 'town centre' for a town and 'city centre' for a city; British English is consistent about this.
minimal_pair: in the city centre
in the town centre

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in city centre' and not 'in the centre city'. The article is required and the word order is fixed.

entry_json.definition: in the countryside, away from towns and cities. With this meaning 'country' is uncountable and always takes 'the'; it can also mean within the nation.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I grew up in the country and still find the constant noise of the city difficult.
example_sentences: Houses in the country are cheaper, but you need a car for everything.
Life in the country moves at a slower pace, for better and for worse.
collocations: a day out in the country

contexts.text: Would you rather live in the city or in the country? The country, if I could still get to work easily.
contexts.note: A very common Part 3 comparison question.

contexts.text: Young people continue to leave the country for the cities in search of work.
The other meaning is national: unemployment in the country as a whole has fallen.
contexts.note: Context tells you which sense is meant.

confusables.difference: 'Countryside' is unambiguous and always rural, so it is the safer word in writing where 'the country' could mean the nation.
minimal_pair: a cottage in the country
walking in the countryside

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in country' and not 'in a country' when you mean rural areas. The article is compulsory.

entry_json.definition: during a period or process. It is formal, and it emphasises that something happened while something else was going on.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In the course of the last decade, the proportion of people cycling to work has more than doubled.
example_sentences: Several errors came to light in the course of the investigation.
In the course of a normal week I speak three languages without thinking about it.
collocations: in the course of the year
in the course of a conversation
in the course of doing sth

contexts.text: In the course of the twentieth century the population of the city grew tenfold.
contexts.note: A formal alternative to 'during' or 'over'.

contexts.text: After 'of' a verb takes -ing: in the course of preparing the report, several gaps emerged.
'Of course' is a completely different phrase meaning naturally or certainly.
contexts.note: Do not confuse the two.

confusables.difference: The same meaning. 'During' is short and works everywhere; 'in the course of' is formal and slightly emphasises the passage of time.
minimal_pair: during the meeting
in the course of the meeting

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse it with 'of course'. And the article is compulsory: not 'in course of'.

entry_json.definition: in the eastern part of a country or area. Compass points take 'the' after 'in', and the whole area follows 'of': in the east of the country.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rainfall is much lower in the east of the country than on the western coast.
example_sentences: Most of the heavy industry was concentrated in the east.
The map shows a forest in the east and farmland in the south.
collocations: in the east of the country

contexts.text: The new housing is in the east of the site, next to the railway line.
contexts.note: Task 1 map description.

contexts.text: 'In the east of' means inside it; 'to the east of' means outside and beyond it.
contexts.note: The distinction that decides whether your map description is accurate.

contexts.text: The adjective form is 'eastern': the eastern half of the country.

confusables.difference: In the east means within the area. To the east means outside it, in that direction.
