minimal_pair: The mountains are in the east of the country.
The sea lies to the east of the country.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in east' and not 'on the east' when describing location within an area.

entry_json.definition: finally, after a period of uncertainty or several changes of plan. It reports what actually happened, and is not a way of concluding an essay.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We looked at half a dozen flats and in the end took the first one we had seen.
example_sentences: The meeting was postponed twice, but in the end it went ahead in March.
In the end I decided the extra money was not worth the longer commute.
collocations: in the end it worked out

contexts.text: In the end we cancelled the trip because the flights kept being delayed.
contexts.note: Closing a Part 2 narrative.

contexts.text: To close an essay use 'in conclusion' or 'to conclude', not 'in the end'.
contexts.note: The error that costs marks in Task 2.

contexts.text: 'At the end' needs 'of' and names a point in time or space: at the end of the road.

confusables.difference: 'At the end of' names a position: at the end of the film. 'In the end' means eventually, after uncertainty, and takes no 'of'.
minimal_pair: At the end of the film, she leaves.
In the end, she decided to leave.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it to introduce your conclusion in Task 2. It means 'eventually', not 'finally, to sum up'.

entry_json.definition: during the hours between the end of the afternoon and bedtime. Like morning and afternoon it takes 'in the'; only night takes 'at'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I do most of my studying in the evening, once the house is quiet.
example_sentences: The library stays open until ten in the evening during exam periods.
We usually eat at about seven in the evening.

contexts.text: What do you usually do in the evening? Cook, and then watch something with my flatmates.
contexts.note: Standard Part 1 routine question.

contexts.text: Energy use peaks in the evening, when everyone is at home.
With a named day use 'on': the class is on Wednesday evening.

confusables.difference: Evening is roughly six until bedtime and takes 'in the'. Night takes 'at' and has no article.
minimal_pair: in the evening
at night

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in evening' and not 'at the evening'.

entry_json.definition: if something happens. It is a formal conditional used in notices, contracts and official instructions, and it is followed by a noun, never a clause.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In the event of a fire, staff should assemble in the car park behind the building.
example_sentences: In the event of cancellation, a full refund will be issued.
The deposit is not returnable in the event of a late withdrawal.
collocations: in the event of an emergency
in the unlikely event of sth

contexts.text: In the event of severe flooding, residents will be moved to the community centre.
contexts.note: Formal notices and letters.

contexts.text: For a clause you must add 'that': in the event that the flight is cancelled.

contexts.text: In speech simply say 'if': if there is a fire, use the stairs.
contexts.note: Register warning.

confusables.difference: Very close. 'In case of' is shorter and appears on signs; 'in the event of' is the fuller, more formal version used in documents.
minimal_pair: In case of fire, break glass.
In the event of fire, the alarm will sound.

entry_json.avoid: Do not follow it with a clause: 'in the event of the flight is cancelled' is wrong. Use a noun, or 'in the event that'.

entry_json.definition: despite having to deal with a difficulty, or when confronted by it. It is formal and usually introduces opposition, danger or hardship.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The community kept the library open in the face of repeated attempts to close it.

Coastal towns are being forced to adapt in the face of rising sea levels.

contexts.text: In the face of falling revenues, several councils have cut library opening hours.

contexts.text: The word after 'of' must be a difficulty; 'in the face of good weather' does not work.

contexts.text: In speech say 'even though there was' or 'despite'.

confusables.difference: 'Despite' works with anything. 'In the face of' requires an obstacle or threat, and adds the sense of standing firm against it.
minimal_pair: despite the cost
in the face of fierce opposition

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it for a neutral circumstance. It needs something being resisted or endured.

entry_json.definition: at the very beginning, before everything that followed. It usually appears at the end of a sentence and questions why something was started at all. It can also mean firstly, when listing points.

should not have done sth in the first place

confusables.difference: 'Firstly' only lists points. 'In the first place' can also mean 'at the outset, before any of this happened', which 'firstly' cannot.
minimal_pair: Firstly, the cost is high.
It should never have been built in the first place.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in first place', which means winning a competition, and not 'at the first place'.

entry_json.definition: having the particular shape, type or appearance named. It is used to specify how something is delivered, and often introduces a concrete example of an abstract idea.

The information is presented in the form of a bar chart.

in the form of a chart

entry_json.avoid: Not 'in form of' and not 'under the form of'. The article is required.

entry_json.definition: at some time after now. It takes 'the', and it goes with will, may, is likely to and other future forms.

contexts.text: Cities will need far more green space in the future than they have today.

confusables.difference: 'In the future' means at some later time. 'In future' means from now on, and often carries a note of complaint.
minimal_pair: I may study abroad in the future.
In future, please arrive on time.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'the' when you mean at some later time. And do not follow it with a past tense.

fall into the hands of sb

minimal_pair: in the hands of the committee

entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am in town this afternoon anyway, so I can pick it up for you.
example_sentences: Is there anywhere in town that repairs shoes?
She is in town for a conference and leaves again on Thursday.

contexts.text: I usually go into town on Saturday morning, before it gets busy.
contexts.note: Movement takes 'into', position takes 'in'.

contexts.text: It is the cheapest place in town for fruit and vegetables.
For a town that is not yours, use the name or an article: I was in the town where she grew up.
contexts.note: Article rule.

confusables.difference: 'In town' means your own town, treated as familiar. 'In the town' identifies a specific town you have named or described.
minimal_pair: I will be in town later.
We stopped in the town where my mother was born.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'go in town' for movement; use 'go into town'.

entry_json.definition: as a result of what has just been described, in a chain of effects. It also means one after another, each taking a turn.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Higher rents push workers further out, which in turn lengthens journeys and increases congestion.
example_sentences: Warmer seas produce stronger storms, which in turn cause more coastal erosion.
Each member of the group spoke in turn.

contexts.text: Deforestation reduces rainfall, which in turn makes farming harder in the surrounding area.
contexts.note: The cleanest way to show a chain of consequences in Task 2.

contexts.text: The candidates were interviewed in turn, in alphabetical order.
contexts.note: The 'one after another' sense.

contexts.text: It usually sits between the subject and the verb: this in turn reduces costs.
contexts.note: Position note.

confusables.difference: 'As a result' starts a new sentence about one effect. 'In turn' continues a chain, showing that an effect became a cause in its turn.
minimal_pair: As a result, prices rose.
Prices rose, which in turn reduced demand.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'in the turn'. And keep it for chains of two or more linked effects.

entry_json.definition: during the winter season, as a general rule. With no article it makes a statement about winters in general rather than one particular winter.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In winter the roads over the pass are often closed for days at a time.
example_sentences: Demand for electricity is highest in winter in this part of Europe.
Many of the coastal hotels close completely in winter.

contexts.text: It rarely snows here, but it rains almost every day in winter.
Gas consumption is roughly three times higher in winter than in summer.
contexts.note: Comparing seasons in Task 1.

contexts.text: 'In the winter' is equally correct, and is needed when you name a particular year.

confusables.difference: Seasons take 'in'. 'At' is used for clock times and a small set of fixed phrases such as 'at night' and 'at Christmas'.
minimal_pair: in winter
at Christmas

entry_json.avoid: Never 'at winter' or 'on winter'.

entry_json.definition: in the place of something else. It is followed by a noun, a pronoun or an -ing form, never by a plain infinitive.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I now cycle to work instead of driving, which saves about eighty pounds a month.
example_sentences: Instead of building a new road, the money could be spent on buses.
She had tea instead of coffee because it was late.

contexts.text: Instead of banning cars altogether, cities could simply make them expensive to park.
contexts.note: -ing after 'of' is compulsory.

contexts.text: Without 'of', 'instead' stands alone at the end of a clause: I did not drive; I cycled instead.
contexts.note: The single word needs no object.

contexts.text: In an essay 'rather than' is often smoother: rather than banning cars, cities could tax them.

confusables.difference: 'Instead of' takes an object; 'instead' alone does not and usually ends the sentence. Mixing them produces 'I went instead of' with nothing after it.
minimal_pair: I had tea instead of coffee.
I did not want coffee, so I had tea instead.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'instead of to drive'. After 'of' use -ing or a noun.

entry_json.definition: money put into something in order to improve it or make a profit. The thing invested in follows 'in'; the amount follows 'of'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Sustained investment in public transport would do more for air quality than any single ban.
example_sentences: Investment in renewable energy has risen sharply since 2015.
The region has suffered from decades of under-investment in housing.

contexts.text: Greater investment in education tends to pay for itself within a generation.
contexts.note: A high-value Task 2 noun phrase; it lets you avoid repeating 'the government should spend'.

contexts.text: Use 'of' for the sum: an investment of two million pounds in new equipment.
contexts.note: Two prepositions, two jobs.

contexts.text: The verb takes the same preposition: the council invested in cycle lanes.

confusables.difference: 'On' is not used with investment. The fixed preposition is 'in', matching the verb 'invest in'.
minimal_pair: investment in housing
spending on housing

entry_json.avoid: Not 'investment on' and not 'investment to'. Note that 'spending' takes 'on' while 'investment' takes 'in'.

entry_json.definition: the fact of taking part in an activity or being connected with it. The activity follows 'in', and the word is often used about crime, politics or community life.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Parental involvement in schooling has a measurable effect on how well children do.
example_sentences: He denied any involvement in the decision.
Community involvement in planning decisions is often limited to a single consultation.

contexts.text: Greater involvement in local decision-making tends to increase trust in institutions.
The company denied any involvement in the pollution of the river.
'Involvement with' is used for people and organisations: her involvement with the charity.
contexts.note: Preposition depends on what follows.

confusables.difference: 'In' introduces an activity or event; 'with' introduces a person or organisation.
minimal_pair: involvement in the project
involvement with the union

entry_json.avoid: Not 'involvement to'. And the adjective takes a different preposition again: involved in a project.

entry_json.definition: used to say that the answer varies according to the circumstances. It is more emphatic than 'it depends', and is normally followed by 'on' or a wh-clause.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It all depends on how much time you have; if you only have a day, stay in the centre.
example_sentences: Whether it is worth buying depends on how long you plan to stay. It all depends.
It all depends what you mean by success.

contexts.text: Is studying abroad worth it? It all depends on what you want from it.
contexts.note: A legitimate Part 3 opener, provided you then give a real answer.

contexts.text: The wh-clause keeps statement order: it all depends how much it costs.
In writing use 'depends largely on' or 'varies according to'.
contexts.note: Register upgrade.

confusables.difference: The same meaning; 'all' adds emphasis and suggests the answer changes completely with the circumstances.
minimal_pair: It depends.
It all depends.

entry_json.avoid: Do not stop there. An examiner will hear 'it all depends' alone as an evasion, so follow it with what it depends on.

entry_json.definition: used to say the answer is not fixed but changes with the situation. The factor follows 'on', and in speech 'on' is often dropped before a wh-word.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Do I prefer working from home? It depends on the week, honestly.
example_sentences: It depends on the weather; if it is dry we will walk.
How long does it take? It depends whether you go by bus or by train.

contexts.text: Do you watch a lot of television? It depends on how busy I am that week.
contexts.note: A natural Part 1 answer that then needs a detail.

contexts.text: The preposition is compulsory before a noun: it depends on the cost, not it depends the cost.
contexts.note: The commonest error with this verb.

contexts.text: In writing prefer 'this depends largely on' or 'the outcome depends on'.

confusables.difference: 'Depending on' is a participle phrase inside a sentence: the price varies depending on the season. 'It depends' is a complete reply.
minimal_pair: It depends on the season.
Prices vary depending on the season.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'it depends of'. The preposition is 'on', and it cannot be dropped before a noun.

vocab_new.lemma: it is difficult for sb to do sth

entry_json.headword: it is difficult for sb to do sth
entry_json.definition: used to say that a particular group finds something hard. 'It' is a dummy subject standing for the to-infinitive, and 'for' introduces the person affected.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is difficult for young people to save for a deposit while paying market rents.
example_sentences: It is difficult for parents to monitor everything their children see online.
It was difficult for me to concentrate with building work going on next door.
collocations: it is difficult for sb to do sth
it is easy for sb to do sth
it is impossible for sb to do sth

chunk.pattern: It is + adjective + for + sb + to + infinitive

contexts.text: It is difficult for rural residents to reach a hospital without a car.
contexts.note: A clean Task 2 way of stating a problem for a specific group.

contexts.text: The same frame works with other adjectives: it is essential for governments to act.
contexts.note: Highly productive pattern.

contexts.text: Compare 'find it difficult to', which reports personal experience.

confusables.term: find it difficult to do sth
confusables.difference: 'It is difficult for X' states a general fact about a group. 'X finds it difficult' reports their experience of it.
minimal_pair: It is difficult for students to find housing.
Students find it difficult to find housing.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'it': 'is difficult for students to find housing' has no subject. And do not use 'to' before the person: not 'difficult to young people'.

vocab_new.lemma: it is important to do sth

entry_json.headword: it is important to do sth
entry_json.definition: used to state that an action matters. The dummy subject 'it' stands for the infinitive that follows, and a person can be added with 'for'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is important to distinguish between the cost of building the line and the cost of running it.
example_sentences: It is important to read the terms before signing anything.
It is important for children to learn how to handle failure.
collocations: it is important to remember that…
it is important to note that…
it is important for sb to do sth

contexts.text: It is important to note that the figures cover only urban areas.
contexts.gap_span: It is important to note that
contexts.note: A useful way of adding a qualification in Task 1 or Task 2.

contexts.text: It is important to me that the work is useful, not just well paid.
contexts.note: 'To me' for personal value, 'for me' for effect.

contexts.text: Do not overuse it. Two of these frames in one paragraph reads as padding.
contexts.note: Style warning.

confusables.difference: The that-clause version needs a subject and often a subjunctive or 'should': it is important that everyone should attend.
minimal_pair: It is important to attend.
It is important that everyone attends.

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop the 'it', and do not follow it with -ing: 'it is important reading the terms' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: as a precaution, because something might possibly happen. It can end a sentence on its own, or introduce a clause in the present tense.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I always keep a printed copy of the ticket just in case my phone runs out of battery.
example_sentences: Take some cash just in case the card machine is not working.
I set off half an hour early, just in case.

chunk.pattern: main clause + just in case (+ present tense clause)

contexts.text: I take an umbrella every day in October, just in case.
contexts.note: It can stand alone at the end, unlike most conditionals.

contexts.text: Save a copy on a memory stick just in case the file becomes corrupted.
Use a present tense after it even for the future: just in case it rains, not just in case it will rain.
contexts.note: Tense rule.

confusables.difference: 'If' means you act only when the thing happens. 'Just in case' means you act now, in advance, whether or not it happens.
minimal_pair: I will take a coat if it rains.
I will take a coat just in case it rains.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'just in case it will rain'. And do not confuse it with 'in any case', which is a different phrase.

entry_json.definition: used to ask somebody to remember an important fact when they judge or decide something. It is followed by a full clause, and 'mind' takes no article.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Keep in mind that these figures cover only the people who actually completed the survey.
example_sentences: It is worth keeping in mind that the sample was very small.
Keep in mind that the office closes at four on Fridays.

contexts.text: It should be kept in mind that the two countries measure unemployment differently.
contexts.note: Passive version, common in careful academic writing.

contexts.text: 'Bear in mind that' means exactly the same and is slightly more British.
With a short object it becomes 'keep sth in mind': keep the deadline in mind.
contexts.note: Object version, with different word order.

confusables.difference: 'Have in mind' means you are considering a specific option now. 'Keep in mind' means remember a fact so that it affects a later judgement.
minimal_pair: I have a candidate in mind.
Keep in mind that the budget is fixed.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'keep in the mind'. And with a that-clause the object cannot also appear: not 'keep it in mind that'.

entry_json.definition: to continue contacting somebody from time to time, so that the relationship does not fade. The person follows 'with'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We promised to keep in touch when the course ended, and to my surprise we actually have.
example_sentences: Do keep in touch and let me know how the new job goes.
It is much easier to keep in touch with people abroad than it was twenty years ago.

contexts.text: Do you keep in touch with friends from school? Only two or three of them.
contexts.note: Very common Part 1 question about friendship.

contexts.text: Thank you again for your help. I hope we can keep in touch.
contexts.note: Standard friendly letter ending.

contexts.text: Social media has changed what keeping in touch actually means.

confusables.difference: Get in touch is making contact once, often for a purpose. Keep in touch is maintaining contact over time.
minimal_pair: Get in touch if you need anything.
We have kept in touch for ten years.

entry_json.avoid: No article, and the preposition is 'with': not 'keep in touch to my friends'.

entry_json.definition: to remember somebody or something so that they can be considered later. The object sits between 'keep' and 'in mind', and 'mind' takes no article.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Thank you for the application; we will keep your details in mind if something suitable comes up.
example_sentences: Keep the deadline in mind when you plan your reading.
We kept her suggestion in mind throughout the redesign.
collocations: keep sb in mind for a job
keep sth in mind when doing sth

contexts.text: Keep the cost of maintenance in mind, not just the purchase price.
contexts.note: The object goes before 'in mind', however long it is.

contexts.text: I will keep you in mind if a vacancy comes up.
contexts.note: Pronoun object, always in the middle.

contexts.text: With a whole fact use 'keep in mind that': keep in mind that prices change seasonally.
contexts.note: The clause version has different word order.

confusables.difference: Interchangeable. 'Bear in mind' is slightly more formal and very common in British English.
minimal_pair: Keep that in mind.
Bear that in mind.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'keep in mind it'. A pronoun object must come between the verb and 'in mind'.

entry_json.definition: the unit for measuring speed in the metric system, abbreviated km/h. 'Per' means 'for each', and the noun after it is singular.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The speed limit in most residential streets here is thirty kilometres per hour.
example_sentences: The train travels at up to 300 kilometres per hour on the new line.
Wind speeds reached 120 kilometres per hour during the storm.
collocations: a speed of x kilometres per hour

contexts.text: Reducing urban speed limits to thirty kilometres per hour cuts serious injuries substantially.
The unit after 'per' stays singular: per hour, not per hours.
contexts.note: Grammar of 'per'.

contexts.text: In speech people usually say 'kilometres an hour'.
contexts.note: 'An' replaces 'per' in conversation.

confusables.difference: The UK still uses miles per hour for road speeds, while most of the world uses kilometres per hour. One mile is about 1.6 kilometres.
minimal_pair: 30 miles per hour
50 kilometres per hour

entry_json.avoid: Not 'kilometres per hours' and not 'kilometre per hour' after a number greater than one.
entry_json.audio_hint: British English also allows KIL-o-mee-ters; both stress patterns are heard.

entry_json.definition: a type or class of person or thing. After 'this kind of' the noun is usually singular; after 'these kinds of' it is plural.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: This kind of job did not exist twenty years ago, and half of it is still being invented.
example_sentences: What kind of music do you listen to?
These kinds of problems are best solved locally rather than nationally.

contexts.text: What kind of films do you enjoy? Mostly documentaries, actually.
contexts.note: One of the most frequent Part 1 question frames.

contexts.text: This kind of scheme works only where public transport is already good.
contexts.note: Singular 'kind' takes a singular noun.

contexts.text: As a hedge in speech it means 'somewhat': it was kind of expensive.
contexts.note: Informal adverbial use; avoid it in Writing.

confusables.difference: Interchangeable in most contexts. 'Type of' is slightly more formal and is preferred in technical or academic writing.
minimal_pair: this kind of problem
this type of soil

entry_json.avoid: Not 'these kind of problems'. Match the demonstrative to 'kind': this kind, these kinds. And avoid the hedging use in Writing.

entry_json.definition: the fixed sequence used before a to-infinitive to talk about practical ability: know how to swim. Written with a hyphen as a noun, know-how means practical expertise.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Plenty of people know how in theory, but very few have actually done it.
example_sentences: He has the technical know-how but very little patience with beginners.
Nobody in the office knew how, so we had to call someone in.

contexts.text: The country has the money but lacks the technical know-how to build the plants itself.
contexts.note: The noun is hyphenated and uncountable.

contexts.text: As a verb sequence it needs 'to': I know how to fix it, not I know how fix it.
contexts.note: The infinitive is compulsory.

contexts.text: Transferring know-how matters more than transferring equipment.

confusables.difference: Knowledge is what you know; know-how is knowing how to do something in practice. A textbook gives knowledge, experience gives know-how.
minimal_pair: He has a deep knowledge of history.
She has the know-how to run the machine.

entry_json.avoid: As a noun it needs the hyphen. As a verb sequence it needs 'to' before the next verb.

entry_json.definition: to have the skill or knowledge needed to do something. The infinitive with 'to' is compulsory after 'how'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Every school leaver should know how to read a contract and manage a bank account.
example_sentences: Do you know how to get to the station from here?
Fewer young people know how to cook a meal from raw ingredients.
collocations: not know how to do sth

contexts.text: I did not know how to use a spreadsheet until I started this job.
Schools should teach pupils how to manage money as well as how to pass examinations.
contexts.note: The same 'how to' pattern after 'teach'.

contexts.text: The wh-word is followed directly by 'to', with no subject: not 'know how I to do it'.
contexts.note: Structure note.

confusables.difference: 'Know that' introduces a fact. 'Know how to' introduces a skill. They are not interchangeable.
minimal_pair: I know that it is difficult.
I know how to do it.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'know how do it' or 'know how doing it'. The pattern is how plus the to-infinitive.

entry_json.definition: in the month before this one. It is a finished past time, so it takes the past simple and never the present perfect, and it takes no preposition or article.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I moved into the flat last month and I am still unpacking.
example_sentences: Sales fell by 4 per cent last month.
We had a meeting about it last month and nothing has changed since.

contexts.text: I started the course last month, so it is all still quite new.
contexts.note: Past simple: the month is over.

contexts.text: Unemployment rose slightly last month, according to the latest figures.
With 'since' the tense changes: I have not seen her since last month.
contexts.note: 'Since' makes the period reach the present.

confusables.difference: 'Last month' is the previous calendar month. 'The last month' means the most recent thirty days, and takes the present perfect: I have been ill for the last month.
minimal_pair: I went there last month.
I have been ill for the last month.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'in last month' or 'the last month' when you mean the previous calendar month. And do not use the present perfect with it.

entry_json.definition: during the summer before this one. Like other 'last' time phrases it takes no preposition and requires the past simple.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Last summer we spent two weeks walking in the mountains, and I have wanted to go back ever since.
example_sentences: Last summer was the driest on record in this region.
I worked in a hotel last summer to save money for the course.

contexts.text: Where did you go on holiday last summer? To the coast, as usual.
contexts.note: Past simple, because the summer is finished.

contexts.text: Visitor numbers last summer were the highest since 2019.
The same pattern gives last winter, last week, last year, all with no preposition.

confusables.difference: 'In the summer' is general or refers to a named year. 'Last summer' points to the single most recent one, with no preposition.
minimal_pair: In the summer it is very hot.
Last summer was unusually hot.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'in last summer' or 'the last summer'.

entry_json.definition: on the most recent occasion. As an adverbial it takes no article; with 'the' it becomes a noun phrase followed by a clause: the last time I saw her.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Last time I visited, the whole area was still under construction.
example_sentences: The last time I flew was three years ago.
It was much quieter last time, probably because it was midweek.
collocations: the last time I did sth

contexts.text: The last time I went to the cinema was probably a year ago.
contexts.note: With 'the' plus a clause, the verb is past simple.

contexts.text: As a bare adverbial it drops the article: last time it rained all week.
'For the last time' means finally, never again: the factory closed for the last time in 1998.
contexts.note: Different meaning with 'for'.

confusables.difference: 'At last' means finally, after a long wait. 'Last time' identifies the most recent occasion.
minimal_pair: At last the train arrived.
Last time the train was late too.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use the present perfect after 'the last time I': it must be 'the last time I saw her', not 'have seen'.

entry_json.definition: during the week before this one. It is finished past time, so it takes the past simple and no preposition or article.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I had three interviews last week and heard back from none of them.
example_sentences: The results came out last week and were better than I expected.
Last week the temperature reached 34 degrees.

contexts.text: What did you do last week? Mostly revision, unfortunately.
I am writing about an item I purchased in your shop last week.
contexts.note: Complaint letter opening.

contexts.text: 'In the last week' means during the past seven days and takes the present perfect: I have had three interviews in the last week.
contexts.note: Different phrase, different tense.

confusables.difference: 'Last week' is the previous calendar week and takes the past simple. 'In the last week' is the past seven days and takes the present perfect.
minimal_pair: I saw her last week.
I have seen her twice in the last week.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'in last week'. And do not pair it with the present perfect.

entry_json.definition: during the weekend before this one. It takes no preposition and requires the past simple, like all 'last' time phrases.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Last weekend I finally cleared out the spare room, which had been on my list for a year.
example_sentences: We went to a food festival last weekend and ate far too much.
The roads were closed last weekend for the marathon.

contexts.text: What did you do last weekend? Not much, I was catching up on sleep.
contexts.note: Almost guaranteed to come up in Part 1.

contexts.text: British English says 'at the weekend' for the general habit; Americans say 'on the weekend'.
contexts.note: Use the British form in this exam.

contexts.text: 'The weekend before last' means two weekends ago.

confusables.difference: 'Last weekend' names one finished weekend. 'At the weekend' describes what you usually do, and takes the present simple.
minimal_pair: Last weekend I went walking.
At the weekend I usually go walking.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'in last weekend' or 'on last weekend'.

entry_json.definition: during the year before this one. It is finished past time, so it takes the past simple and no preposition or article.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Last year the company opened two new sites and closed three older ones.
example_sentences: Visitor numbers were 12 per cent higher last year than in 2019.
I took the test last year and just missed the score I needed.

contexts.text: Did you travel much last year? Only once, and that was for work.
Emissions fell by 3 per cent last year, the first fall since 2015.
'In the last year' means the past twelve months and takes the present perfect.
contexts.note: One article changes both the meaning and the tense.

confusables.difference: 'Last year' is the previous calendar year, with the past simple. 'In the last year' is the past twelve months, with the present perfect.
minimal_pair: I changed job last year.
I have changed job twice in the last year.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'in last year'. And avoid the present perfect with it: 'I have moved last year' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: to have something as a result. Here 'to' is a preposition, so a verb after it must be -ing, and the subject is the cause.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cutting bus services in rural areas leads directly to greater car dependence.
example_sentences: A poor diet can lead to a range of long-term health problems.
The decision led to protests in several cities.
collocations: lead to a rise in sth

contexts.text: Rising temperatures lead to more frequent and more intense storms.
contexts.note: The core Task 2 cause-and-effect verb.

contexts.text: After 'to' a verb takes -ing: this can lead to spending more than you earn.
contexts.note: 'To' is a preposition here, not part of an infinitive.

contexts.text: Hedge it when the link is not certain: this may lead to higher costs.
contexts.note: Modal hedging protects an unproven claim.

confusables.difference: Nearly identical. 'Result in' is slightly more formal; 'lead to' can suggest a longer chain rather than an immediate effect.
minimal_pair: The strike led to long delays.
The strike resulted in long delays.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'lead to increase' when you mean the process: write 'lead to an increase' or 'lead to increasing'.

entry_json.definition: to acquire the skill needed to do something. 'How' can be left out with no change of meaning: learn to drive, learn how to drive.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I learned how to cook properly only after I moved out of my parents' house.
example_sentences: Children should learn how to manage money before they leave school.
It took me a year to learn how to use the software confidently.

contexts.text: I would like to learn how to swim properly, not just stay afloat.
contexts.note: A reliable Part 2 answer for 'a skill you want to learn'.

contexts.text: Schools should teach pupils how to evaluate what they read online.
contexts.note: The same structure after 'teach'.

contexts.text: 'How' is optional here: I learned to drive at eighteen.
contexts.note: Both versions are correct.

confusables.difference: You study a subject; you learn a skill or a fact. 'I am studying English' is the course; 'I am learning how to write essays' is the skill.
minimal_pair: I study economics.
I am learning how to use the software.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'learn how doing sth' and not 'learn how I do it'. The pattern is how plus the to-infinitive.

entry_json.definition: to not include somebody or something. It is separable: leave out the details, leave them out. With a pronoun it must split.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The summary leaves out the one figure that would have made the trend clear.
example_sentences: You have left out your date of birth on the form.
It is easy to feel left out when everyone else already knows each other.

contexts.text: I left out the middle section because I ran out of time.
New arrivals often feel left out until they can speak the language.
contexts.note: The passive adjective sense: excluded socially.

contexts.text: With a pronoun the phrase must split: I left it out by mistake.
contexts.note: Never 'left out it'.

confusables.difference: 'Omit' is the formal one-word equivalent and is better in academic writing. 'Leave out' is the everyday phrasal verb.
minimal_pair: The report omits the 2019 figures.
They left out the 2019 figures.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'leave out it'. A pronoun object goes between 'leave' and 'out'.

entry_json.definition: below a stated amount. It goes with uncountable nouns and with numbers and measurements; countable nouns normally take 'fewer than'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Less than a third of the people surveyed could name their local representative.
example_sentences: The journey takes less than an hour on the fast train.
Less than 5 per cent of plastic is genuinely recycled.

contexts.text: Less than a quarter of households owned a car in 1970, compared with four fifths today.
contexts.note: Essential Task 1 language for proportions.

contexts.text: With countable nouns careful writers use 'fewer': fewer than ten students applied.
contexts.note: The distinction examiners notice.

contexts.text: Numbers and measurements take 'less than' even when countable: less than 20 kilometres.
contexts.note: The exception to the fewer rule.

confusables.difference: 'Fewer' is for things you can count individually: fewer cars. 'Less' is for amounts and quantities: less traffic, less than an hour.
minimal_pair: fewer cars
less traffic

entry_json.avoid: Not 'less cars' or 'less people' in careful writing. Use 'fewer' with countable nouns.

entry_json.definition: used to ask somebody to tell you something later. 'Let' takes a bare infinitive, so it is 'let me know', never 'let me to know'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Let me know if the time does not suit you and I will rearrange it.
example_sentences: Please let me know whether you will be attending.
Let me know how you get on at the interview.
collocations: let me know as soon as possible

contexts.text: Please let me know if you require any further information.
contexts.note: A standard closing line for a semi-formal letter or email.

contexts.text: Just let me know what time suits you.
'Let' never takes 'to': not 'let me to know'.
contexts.note: Verb pattern note.

confusables.difference: 'Inform me' is much more formal and slightly cold. 'Let me know' is polite and neutral, and works in almost any letter.
minimal_pair: Please let me know.
Please inform me in writing.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'let me to know'. And in a formal complaint 'I would be grateful if you could let me know' is safer than the bare imperative.

entry_json.definition: the 'like' that ends questions asking for a description: What is it like? What does she look like? The word cannot be moved to the front, so the question ends on it.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: What is the weather like in your country in December?
example_sentences: What was the course like? Harder than I expected, but worth it.
What does the new building look like?
collocations: what was it like doing sth?

contexts.text: What is your home town like? Quite small, but there is always something happening.
contexts.note: One of the most common Part 1 questions of all, and it always ends on 'like'.

contexts.text: 'What is she like?' asks about character; 'what does she look like?' asks about appearance.
contexts.note: Two questions that learners regularly confuse.

contexts.text: 'How is she?' asks about health or mood, not description.
contexts.note: A third question that is easy to mix in.

confusables.difference: 'What is it like?' asks for a description. 'How is it?' asks how it is going or how someone feels. They are not interchangeable.
minimal_pair: What is your job like?
How is your job going?

entry_json.avoid: Never 'How is your city like?'. If the question ends in 'like', it must begin with 'what'.

entry_json.definition: probably going to do something. It is an adjective, not an adverb, so it follows 'be' and takes the to-infinitive.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Younger workers are far more likely to change career at least once than their parents were.
example_sentences: Prices are likely to rise again before the end of the year.
People who cycle to work are less likely to be overweight.

contexts.text: Graduates are three times more likely to be employed in professional roles.
contexts.note: The standard way of expressing comparative probability in Writing.

contexts.text: It is a hedge: 'is likely to fall' claims far less than 'will fall'.
contexts.note: Why it scores well: it avoids overclaiming.

contexts.text: 'Likely' can also start a dummy-subject clause: it is likely that prices will rise.
contexts.note: Alternative structure.

confusables.difference: 'Probably' is an adverb and goes with a verb: it will probably rise. 'Likely' is an adjective and needs 'be' plus 'to'.
minimal_pair: It will probably rise.
It is likely to rise.

entry_json.avoid: In British English 'likely' is not an adverb: 'it will likely rise' is American. Write 'it is likely to rise'.

entry_json.definition: to pay attention to a sound, a person or a piece of music deliberately. The preposition 'to' is compulsory whenever there is an object.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I listen to podcasts on the way to work, which is how I get through about three a week.
example_sentences: What kind of music do you listen to?
Nobody listened to the residents until the plan was almost final.

contexts.text: Do you listen to the radio? Only in the car, and mostly for the news.
contexts.note: Frequent Part 1 media question.

contexts.text: Planners who listen to local residents tend to produce schemes that actually get used.
contexts.note: The 'take advice from' sense.

contexts.text: Without an object 'to' disappears: just listen for a moment.
contexts.note: The only case where 'to' is dropped.

confusables.difference: Hearing happens without effort; listening is deliberate. You can hear traffic without listening to it.
minimal_pair: I heard a noise outside.
I listened to the whole programme.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'listen music' or 'listen the radio'. With an object, 'to' is compulsory.
entry_json.audio_hint: The t in 'listen' is silent: LISS-en.

entry_json.definition: only, and no more than that. It dismisses something as insufficient or unimpressive, and is a critical judgement rather than a neutral measurement.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The consultation was little more than a formality; the decision had already been taken.
example_sentences: The scheme is little more than a way of moving the problem somewhere else.
The building was little more than a shell when they bought it.

contexts.text: Recycling targets without enforcement are little more than a statement of intent.
contexts.note: A sharp, economical criticism: exactly the kind of phrasing Task 2 rewards.

contexts.text: With a number it means barely: little more than half the seats were filled.
contexts.note: Quantifying use.

contexts.text: In speech people say 'basically just': it was basically just a formality.
contexts.note: Register note.

confusables.difference: 'A little more than' means slightly above: a little more than half. 'Little more than' with no article means barely anything beyond, and is dismissive.
minimal_pair: a little more than half
little more than a gesture

entry_json.avoid: Do not add 'a'. 'A little more than' reverses the meaning from criticism to simple measurement.

entry_json.definition: to have a particular amount of money to survive on, or to eat a particular food as your main diet. The amount or the food follows 'on'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is almost impossible to live on the minimum wage in a city like this.
example_sentences: Students often live on very little during term time.
For three months I lived on rice, eggs and whatever was on offer.

contexts.text: Around a tenth of the population lives on less than the official poverty line.
contexts.note: Standard phrasing in writing about poverty and income.

contexts.text: When I was a student I lived on pasta and not much else.
contexts.note: The food sense.

contexts.text: 'Live on your own' means alone, which is a separate meaning of 'on'.

confusables.difference: 'Live in' names the place: live in Manchester. 'Live on' names what supports you: live on a small pension.
minimal_pair: I live in a flat.
I live on a very small income.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse it with 'live with', which means share a home with somebody.

entry_json.definition: to share a home with somebody. With a thing rather than a person it means to accept a difficult situation: you have to live with the noise.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I live with two other students, which keeps the rent manageable.
example_sentences: More young adults are living with their parents than at any time since the 1970s.
The village has had to live with the noise from the airport for decades.

contexts.text: Do you live with your family or on your own? With my family, for now.
contexts.note: Very common Part 1 question.

contexts.text: In many countries it is normal for several generations to live with one another.
The figurative sense means tolerate: we will have to live with the decision.

confusables.difference: 'Live with' takes a person; 'live in' takes a place. Saying 'I live with London' is a clear error.
minimal_pair: I live with my brother.
I live in Bristol.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'live together with' in the simple sense; 'live with my parents' or 'we live together' are the natural forms.

entry_json.definition: the main room in a house where people sit and relax. It is countable and takes an article, and British English also says sitting room or lounge.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The flat has one bedroom and a living room with a small balcony off it.
example_sentences: We knocked the kitchen and living room into one large space.
The living room faces south, so it gets sun most of the day.

contexts.text: My favourite room is the living room, mainly because of the light.
contexts.note: Direct answer to the Part 2 'describe a room' card.

contexts.text: The plan shows a kitchen at the rear and a living room at the front of the house.
contexts.note: Task 1 floor plan.

contexts.text: British alternatives are 'sitting room' and 'lounge', which mean the same thing.

confusables.difference: 'Living space' is uncountable and means the total area available to live in. 'Living room' is one particular room.
minimal_pair: a small living room
not enough living space

entry_json.avoid: Two words, no hyphen: not 'livingroom'. And it is countable, so it needs an article.

entry_json.definition: a lot of. It is informal and spoken, and works with both countable and uncountable nouns: loads of people, loads of time.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There are loads of places to eat around the station, most of them open late.
example_sentences: I have got loads of work this week, so I cannot really go out.
Loads of people applied, which is why the interviews took three days.

contexts.text: There is loads to do in the summer, but it goes very quiet in winter.
contexts.note: Natural in Speaking; it shows genuine informal fluency.

contexts.text: In Writing use 'a great deal of' or 'a large number of' instead.
contexts.note: Register warning: 'loads of' in Task 2 lowers your lexical score.

contexts.text: The verb agrees with the noun after 'of': loads of people are, loads of time is.
contexts.note: Agreement rule.

confusables.difference: Same meaning; 'a lot of' is neutral and acceptable in semi-formal writing, while 'loads of' is strictly conversational.
minimal_pair: a lot of people
loads of people

entry_json.avoid: Never use it in Task 1 or Task 2. In Speaking it is fine and even natural.

entry_json.definition: to be responsible for somebody or something and keep them safe or in good condition. It never splits: look after the children, look after them.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My grandmother looked after us every afternoon while our parents were at work.
example_sentences: Who looks after the garden when you are away?
You need to look after yourself as well as everybody else.

contexts.text: Who looked after you when you were small? My grandparents, mostly.
As people live longer, more adults find themselves looking after both children and parents.
contexts.note: A key Task 2 point about ageing populations.

contexts.text: It cannot split, even with a pronoun: look after them, never look them after.
contexts.note: Contrast with separable phrasal verbs like 'fill in'.

confusables.difference: The same meaning. 'Take care of' is a shade more formal and is also used for tasks: I will take care of the booking.
minimal_pair: She looks after her mother.
He takes care of the finances.

entry_json.avoid: Never split it: 'look them after' is wrong. And do not confuse it with 'look for', which means search.

entry_json.definition: to turn your eyes towards something deliberately, or to examine and consider it. The preposition 'at' is compulsory when there is an object.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: If you look at the second graph, the pattern is completely different.
example_sentences: We looked at four flats before choosing this one.
This essay looks at the effects of tourism on small coastal towns.

contexts.text: Looking at the chart, it is clear that consumption peaked in 2008.
contexts.note: Participle opening for a Task 1 sentence.

contexts.text: In an essay 'examine' or 'consider' is more formal: this paragraph considers the cost.
contexts.note: Register upgrade.

contexts.text: The three 'look' phrases are quite different: look at, look for, look after.
contexts.note: Worth learning as a set.

confusables.difference: Seeing is passive and happens automatically; looking is deliberate and takes 'at'. You see a building; you look at a photograph.
minimal_pair: I saw her in the street.
I looked at the photograph for a long time.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'look the chart'. With an object, 'at' is compulsory.

entry_json.definition: to think about something that happened in the past, usually to assess it. 'On' is equally common: look back on your schooldays.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Looking back at that year, I can see it was the right decision, though it did not feel like it at the time.
example_sentences: When I look back at my time abroad, the language was the least difficult part.
Historians looking back at this decade will focus on the shift to remote working.

chunk.pattern: look back at / on + past period

contexts.text: Looking back, I wish I had taken more time before deciding.
contexts.note: A strong Part 2 reflective opening; it pairs naturally with 'I wish I had'.

contexts.text: 'Look back on' is more common in British English for a whole period of life.
contexts.note: Both prepositions are correct.

contexts.text: It also means turn round physically: she looked back at the house one last time.
contexts.note: Literal sense.

confusables.difference: Remember is simply retrieving a memory. Look back at adds the sense of evaluating a period from a distance.
minimal_pair: I remember my first day.
Looking back at that year, I learned a lot.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'look back to' for reflection; 'to' suggests physical direction. Use 'at' or 'on'.

entry_json.definition: to try to find somebody or something. It describes the process of searching, not the result, so 'I looked for it' does not mean you found it.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I spent three months looking for a flat before I found anything I could afford.
example_sentences: Employers are looking for people who can work in a team.
I am looking for a book on urban planning; do you have anything?

contexts.text: What do employers look for in a graduate? Communication skills, mostly.
Governments are still looking for a solution that does not involve raising taxes.
Finding is the result: I looked for it all morning and finally found it.
contexts.note: Process versus result.

confusables.difference: Look for is the search; find is the success. You can look for something for hours without finding it.
minimal_pair: I looked for my keys.
I found my keys.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'look for' when you mean 'look after'. And do not drop 'for': 'I am looking a job' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: to feel pleased about something that is going to happen. 'To' is a preposition here, so a verb after it must be -ing, not the infinitive.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am really looking forward to starting the course in September.
example_sentences: I look forward to hearing from you.
We are all looking forward to the weekend after a week like this.
collocations: look forward to hearing from you

contexts.text: I look forward to hearing from you at your earliest convenience.
contexts.note: The standard formal letter closing, and the -ing is compulsory.

contexts.text: I am looking forward to the summer, mostly because of the light evenings.
contexts.note: Continuous form is more common in speech.

contexts.text: The present simple is more formal in letters: I look forward to meeting you.
contexts.note: Simple for letters, continuous for speech.

confusables.difference: Expect is neutral about whether you want it. Look forward to always means you want it to happen.
minimal_pair: I expect a reply next week.
I look forward to your reply.

entry_json.avoid: The single most common error in formal English: 'I look forward to hear from you' must be 'to hearing'.

entry_json.definition: to have a similar appearance to somebody or something. Before an adjective 'like' disappears: it looks expensive, but it looks like an expensive shop.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The new development looks like a business park rather than the housing it was meant to be.
example_sentences: She looks like her mother, especially around the eyes.
It looks like rain, so take a coat.

contexts.text: What does your home town look like? Mostly low buildings and a lot of green space.
Before an adjective drop 'like': the room looks bigger with the door open.
contexts.note: The rule learners break most often.

contexts.text: 'It looks like it will rain' introduces a prediction, and here 'like' can take a clause.
contexts.note: Informal clause use.

confusables.difference: 'Look like' is appearance only. 'Be like' is character: she is like her mother means their personalities match.
minimal_pair: She looks like her mother.
She is like her mother.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'it looks like expensive'. Before an adjective use 'looks expensive'; before a noun use 'looks like a bargain'.

entry_json.definition: used as a warning to tell somebody to be careful of immediate danger. With 'for' it means watch carefully in order to notice something.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Look out for the step; it is much higher than it looks.
example_sentences: Look out! There is a cyclist coming.
Look out for a blue door on the left; it is easy to miss.
collocations: be on the lookout for sth

chunk.pattern: Look out! / look out for + sth

contexts.text: Look out for the sign; it comes up very quickly after the bridge.
contexts.note: The 'watch for' sense, with 'for'.

contexts.text: As a bare warning it is urgent and needs no object: Look out!
contexts.note: Immediate danger only.

contexts.text: In writing use 'watch for' or 'be alert to': drivers should be alert to cyclists at junctions.
contexts.note: Register upgrade.

confusables.difference: Look out (for) is watching for danger or noticing something. Look after is taking care of somebody.
minimal_pair: Look out for the ice.
Look after your sister.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use the bare warning in an essay. And with an object you need 'for': not 'look out the sign'.

entry_json.definition: to find a piece of information in a reference source such as a dictionary, a timetable or online. It is separable: look up a word, look a word up, look it up.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: If I meet a word I do not know, I try to guess it first and only look it up afterwards.
example_sentences: I looked up the opening times before we set off.
Rather than looking every word up, read the whole paragraph first.

contexts.text: Do you look up new words when you read? Sometimes, but not every one.
contexts.note: A common Part 1 question about learning languages.

contexts.text: With a pronoun the phrase must split: I did not know the word, so I looked it up.
contexts.note: Never 'looked up it'.

contexts.text: Compare 'look after', which never splits at all.
contexts.note: Separable versus inseparable.

confusables.difference: Search for is looking through a whole space or database. Look up is finding one specific item you know exists, in an organised source.
minimal_pair: I searched for information about the course.
I looked up the phone number.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'look up it'. A pronoun object always goes in the middle.

entry_json.definition: a large amount or number of. It works with both countable and uncountable nouns, and the verb agrees with the noun after 'of'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There are lots of small parks in this part of the city, which is one reason I moved here.
example_sentences: Lots of people cycle to work now that the lanes are separated from the traffic.
There is lots of information online, but not much of it is reliable.

contexts.text: There are lots of things to do at the weekend if you know where to look.
In Writing use 'many', 'a great deal of' or 'a large number of'.
contexts.note: Register upgrade: 'lots of' is too casual for Task 2.

contexts.text: The verb follows the noun, not 'lots': lots of people are, lots of work is.
contexts.note: Agreement rule.

confusables.difference: Practically identical; 'a lot of' is very slightly more acceptable in semi-formal writing, but neither belongs in Task 2.
minimal_pair: lots of people
a lot of people

entry_json.avoid: Do not drop 'of' before a noun: 'lots people' is wrong. And avoid the phrase entirely in Writing.

entry_json.definition: to have a noticeable effect. The person or thing affected follows 'to' in British English: it makes a difference to the cost.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Even half an hour of exercise a day makes a real difference to how well I sleep.
example_sentences: Small changes at home make very little difference compared with industrial emissions.
Having a good teacher in the first year makes an enormous difference.

contexts.text: Insulating older homes would make a substantial difference to national energy use.
contexts.note: The adjective slot lets you grade the claim precisely.

contexts.text: It made a huge difference to me having someone to practise speaking with.
British English uses 'to'; American English often uses 'in'.
contexts.note: Use 'to' in this exam.

confusables.difference: 'Be different' compares two things. 'Make a difference' means having an effect on a situation.
minimal_pair: The two systems are different.
The new system made a real difference.

entry_json.avoid: The article is compulsory: not 'make difference'. And in British English the preposition is 'to', not 'for'.

entry_json.definition: to do something wrong or incorrectly. The verb is always 'make', never 'do', and the noun is countable so it needs an article.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I made a mistake on the form and had to submit the whole application again.
example_sentences: Everyone makes mistakes when they are learning a language; the point is to notice them.
The council made a serious mistake in approving the development so close to the river.

contexts.text: I am not afraid of making mistakes when I speak; that is how you improve.
contexts.note: Plural with no article for the general habit.

contexts.text: It would be a mistake to assume that all young people are comfortable with technology.
contexts.note: A neat way to challenge an assumption in Task 2.

contexts.text: The verb is fixed: never 'do a mistake'.
contexts.note: The most persistent make-or-do error.

confusables.difference: A mistake is something done wrongly. A fault is a defect in a thing, or responsibility for a problem: it was my fault.
minimal_pair: I made a mistake in the calculation.
There is a fault in the heating system.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'do a mistake'. Mistakes are always made.

entry_json.definition: to earn money, especially through business or investment. 'Money' is uncountable, so it takes no article and no plural.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The airline makes most of its money from baggage charges rather than from the fares themselves.
example_sentences: It is very hard to make money from music unless you tour constantly.
The company made money in its first year, which is unusual for a start-up.

contexts.text: Streaming platforms make money from subscriptions rather than from individual sales.
I did not do it to make money; I did it because I enjoyed it.
For wages the verb is 'earn': she earns about thirty thousand a year.
contexts.note: Business profit versus salary.

confusables.difference: 'Earn' is what you receive for work, usually a wage. 'Make money' suggests profit from a business or activity.
minimal_pair: She earns a good salary.
The shop is finally making money.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'moneys' and never 'a money'. And do not say 'win money' unless it was a prize or a bet.

entry_json.definition: to decide in advance what you are going to do. The event follows 'for'; use 'plan to do sth' when you want a verb.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We have already made plans for the summer, so I cannot change the dates now.
example_sentences: The council is making plans for a new footbridge across the railway.
Have you made any plans for the weekend?

contexts.text: Have you made any plans for the summer? Nothing definite yet.
contexts.note: Common Part 1 exchange.

contexts.text: Cities that make plans for population growth avoid the worst housing shortages.
For a verb, use 'plan to' or 'make plans to': we are making plans to move next year.
contexts.note: Pattern contrast.

confusables.difference: 'Plan' as a verb is shorter and often better: we planned the trip. 'Make plans for' emphasises the process of arranging.
minimal_pair: We planned the trip carefully.
We made plans for the trip.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'do plans' and not 'make plans of'. The verb is 'make' and the preposition is 'for' or 'to'.

entry_json.definition: to be clear and understandable, or to be a sensible course of action. 'Sense' takes no article, and 'make sense of sth' means succeed in understanding it.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It makes sense to insulate the building before installing a new heating system.
example_sentences: The instructions did not make sense, so we rang the helpline.
Financially, renting makes more sense than buying at these prices.
collocations: it makes sense to do sth

contexts.text: It makes sense to invest in prevention rather than paying for treatment later.
contexts.note: A confident but not arrogant way of recommending something in Task 2.

contexts.text: I could not make sense of the timetable at first.
contexts.note: With 'of' the meaning changes to understanding.

contexts.text: The negative is very common: that does not make any sense to me.

confusables.difference: Without 'of' the subject is the thing being understood: the instructions make sense. With 'of' the subject is the person doing the understanding: I made sense of the instructions.
minimal_pair: The map makes sense.
I could not make sense of the map.

entry_json.avoid: No article: not 'make a sense'. And do not say 'it has sense'; the verb is 'make'.

entry_json.definition: to invent something, especially a story or an excuse that is not true. It also means to form the whole of something: women make up 60 per cent of the workforce.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: He made up an excuse about the traffic rather than admitting he had overslept.
example_sentences: The children made up a story about how the window broke.
Renewables now make up almost half of the country's electricity.
collocations: make up a percentage of sth

contexts.text: Students under 25 make up more than half of the town's population.
contexts.note: The 'constitute' sense: extremely useful for describing pie charts.

contexts.text: I think he made the whole thing up, honestly.
contexts.note: The 'invent' sense; separable.

contexts.text: In academic writing 'account for' or 'constitute' is more formal.
contexts.note: Register upgrade for Task 1.

confusables.difference: 'Make up for' means compensate: the view makes up for the climb. Adding 'for' changes the meaning entirely.
minimal_pair: He made up an excuse.
The pay makes up for the long hours.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'make up it'. And in the percentage sense the verb agrees with the group: students make up, not makes up.

entry_json.definition: to check or take action so that something definitely happens. It is followed by a that-clause, by 'of' plus a noun, or by 'to do sth'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Make sure you keep a copy of everything you send.
example_sentences: I always make sure I leave early enough to walk from the station.
Governments must make sure the money reaches the schools that need it most.

contexts.text: Make sure you take a photograph of the meter before you move out.
contexts.note: 'That' is normally dropped in speech.

contexts.text: Use a present tense for the future after it: make sure you arrive by nine, not will arrive.
contexts.note: Tense rule.

contexts.text: In formal writing prefer 'ensure': the policy must ensure that funding reaches rural schools.
contexts.note: Register upgrade.

confusables.difference: The same meaning; 'ensure' is one word and more formal, and is the better choice in Task 2.
minimal_pair: Make sure the door is locked.
The system ensures that data is protected.

entry_json.avoid: Never use 'will' in the clause after it. And 'make sure to do sth' is acceptable but slightly American; the that-clause is safer.

entry_json.definition: to check that something is true or in place, or to do what is needed to secure it. 'Of' takes a noun or an -ing form.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Make sure of the closing date before you start writing the application.
example_sentences: I wanted to make sure of my facts before I raised it at the meeting.
Booking early makes sure of a seat, though not necessarily a cheap one.

contexts.text: Make sure of the price before you agree to anything.
contexts.note: With a noun, 'of' is required.

contexts.text: With a clause, drop 'of': make sure that the price includes delivery.
contexts.note: The two patterns cannot be combined.

contexts.text: It can also mean secure something: an early goal made sure of the win.
contexts.note: Second sense.

confusables.difference: 'Of' takes a noun; 'that' takes a clause. Not 'make sure of that the price is right'.
minimal_pair: make sure of the price
make sure that the price is right

entry_json.avoid: Do not combine the two patterns. Choose either 'of' plus a noun or 'that' plus a clause.

entry_json.definition: to take whatever action is needed so that something happens. The clause after 'that' uses a present tense even when it refers to the future, and 'that' is often dropped in speech.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The council must make sure that new housing comes with the schools and buses to support it.
example_sentences: Make sure that everyone knows where the meeting is.
We need to make sure that the data is stored securely.
collocations: make sure that sb does sth

contexts.text: Schools should make sure that every pupil can swim before they leave primary education.
contexts.note: A clear recommendation structure for Task 2, though 'ensure' scores higher.

contexts.text: Make sure the windows are closed before you leave.
contexts.note: 'That' is optional and usually dropped in speech.

contexts.text: The clause takes a present tense for future meaning: make sure you are there by eight.
contexts.note: Never 'will be there'.

confusables.difference: Identical in meaning. 'Ensure' is the formal single-word version and is the better choice in academic writing.
minimal_pair: Make sure that everyone is informed.
Ensure that all staff are informed.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'make sure that it will happen'. Use a present tense in the clause.

entry_json.definition: to succeed in doing something difficult. It always implies effort or obstacles, and it takes the to-infinitive.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Somehow I managed to finish the essay before the deadline, though I did not sleep much.
example_sentences: We managed to get tickets, even though they had sold out weeks earlier.
Very few countries have managed to reduce emissions while growing their economies.

contexts.text: I managed to get a seat, but only because I left twenty minutes early.
contexts.note: The difficulty is implied, which is why it is more expressive than 'I got'.

contexts.text: Sweden has managed to cut emissions without reducing growth.
'Could' does not work for a single past success: not 'I could get a seat' when you mean you succeeded.
contexts.note: The classic modal trap.

confusables.difference: 'Could' describes general past ability. For one particular occasion where you succeeded despite difficulty, English uses 'managed to' or 'was able to'.
minimal_pair: I could swim when I was five.
I managed to swim across despite the current.

entry_json.avoid: Not 'manage doing sth' in this sense, and do not use it when there was no difficulty at all.

entry_json.definition: used to say that something is quite likely. 'Well' strengthens 'may', so it claims more probability than 'may' alone but less than 'will'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The scheme may well work in a compact city, but it is hard to see it succeeding in a rural county.
example_sentences: Prices may well fall again once the new supply arrives.
She may well be the best candidate they have interviewed.
collocations: may well turn out to be sth

contexts.text: Automation may well eliminate more jobs than it creates in the next two decades.
contexts.note: A confident hedge: it makes a real claim without overstating it.

contexts.text: It is often used to concede a point before disagreeing: that may well be true, but it misses the wider issue.
contexts.note: A very effective Task 2 concession move.

contexts.text: 'Might well' means the same with slightly less confidence.

confusables.difference: 'May' alone is a bare possibility. 'May well' says the possibility is a strong one, which is a genuinely different claim.
minimal_pair: It may rain.
It may well rain, so take a coat.

entry_json.avoid: The word order is fixed: 'may well be', not 'may be well'. And it takes the bare infinitive, never 'to'.

entry_json.definition: to intend to do something. With the -ing form the meaning changes completely: mean doing sth means involve or result in it.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I meant to reply to your message last week and it went completely out of my head.
example_sentences: I did not mean to interrupt; please carry on.
She had meant to apply, but the deadline passed before she finished the form.
collocations: did not mean to do sth
have been meaning to do sth

contexts.text: I have been meaning to take up cycling again for about two years.
contexts.note: 'Have been meaning to' is a very natural way of admitting an unfulfilled intention.

contexts.text: With -ing the meaning changes: moving abroad would mean leaving my family.
contexts.note: Two structures, two entirely different meanings.

contexts.text: I did not mean to cause any trouble.
contexts.note: Apologising for an unintended effect.

confusables.difference: 'Mean to do' is intention. 'Mean doing' is consequence: taking the job would mean moving. Choosing the wrong form reverses your meaning.
minimal_pair: I meant to call her.
Calling her would mean admitting I was wrong.

entry_json.avoid: Do not mix the two patterns. 'I meant calling you' says something quite different from 'I meant to call you'.

entry_json.definition: a person's psychological and emotional wellbeing. It is uncountable and takes no article, and it works as a modifier in phrases like mental health services.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Long working hours have a measurable effect on mental health, particularly among younger employees.
example_sentences: Waiting times for mental health services have doubled in five years.
Regular exercise is good for physical and mental health alike.

contexts.text: Social media has been linked to poorer mental health among teenagers, though the evidence is contested.
contexts.note: A very frequent Task 2 topic; note the hedge at the end.

contexts.text: People talk about mental health far more openly than they did twenty years ago.
As a modifier it stays singular: a mental health service, mental health support.

confusables.difference: Mental health is the whole spectrum, including good health. Mental illness names a diagnosed condition. Using them interchangeably is inaccurate.
minimal_pair: Exercise improves mental health.
Depression is a common mental illness.

entry_json.avoid: No article and no plural: not 'a mental health' or 'mental healths'.

entry_json.definition: the pattern used to say that an event is possible but not certain: anything might happen, it might happen again. 'Might' takes the bare infinitive, and 'happen' is never passive.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Nobody knows what might happen to the housing market once interest rates change.
example_sentences: If the barriers are not repaired, the same flooding might happen again next winter.
It is worth thinking about what might happen if the funding is withdrawn.

contexts.text: It is impossible to say what might happen to employment if automation accelerates.
contexts.note: Speculating about the future without overclaiming, which Task 2 rewards.

contexts.text: I did not go, because I was worried about what might happen on the way back.
'Happen' is never passive: not 'an accident might be happened'.
contexts.note: The error this pattern most often attracts.

confusables.difference: 'Will happen' is a prediction you are confident about. 'Might happen' is one possibility among several, and is much safer in an essay.
minimal_pair: Prices will rise.
Prices might rise.

entry_json.avoid: Never make 'happen' passive, and never write 'might to happen'. After 'might' the verb is bare.

entry_json.definition: the unit used for road speeds in the United Kingdom and the United States, abbreviated mph. One mile is roughly 1.6 kilometres, and the noun after 'per' stays singular.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The limit on most British motorways is seventy miles per hour, which is about 113 kilometres per hour.
example_sentences: Winds of up to 80 miles per hour were recorded on the coast.
In built-up areas the limit is normally 30 miles per hour.
collocations: a speed limit of x miles per hour

contexts.text: Lowering the urban limit from 30 to 20 miles per hour sharply reduces pedestrian deaths.
contexts.note: Relevant if your essay refers to the UK, where road signs are in miles.

contexts.text: In speech people say 'miles an hour' or just 'mph'.
'Per' is always followed by a singular noun: per hour, per person, per year.
contexts.note: Grammar of 'per'.

confusables.difference: The UK measures road speed in miles per hour; most other countries use kilometres per hour. Seventy miles per hour is roughly 113 kilometres per hour.
minimal_pair: 70 miles per hour
113 kilometres per hour

entry_json.avoid: Not 'miles per hours' and not 'mile per hour' after a number greater than one.

entry_json.definition: a very large but unspecified number. In this vague sense 'million' takes an s and 'of'; after an exact number it does neither: two million people.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Millions of people around the world still have no reliable access to clean water.
example_sentences: Millions of tonnes of plastic enter the oceans every year.
The campaign reached millions of viewers within a week.

contexts.text: Millions of people are expected to move to cities over the next twenty years.
contexts.note: Vague large number: the s and 'of' are both required.

contexts.text: After an exact figure there is no s and no 'of': the city has three million residents.
contexts.note: The rule learners break most often with big numbers.

contexts.text: The same pattern covers hundreds, thousands and billions.

confusables.difference: With a specific number, 'million' is singular and takes no 'of': two million people. Without one, it is 'millions of people'.
minimal_pair: two million people
millions of people

entry_json.avoid: Never 'two millions of people' and never 'million of people'.

entry_json.definition: a telephone that works over a wireless network and can be carried anywhere. It is the British term; Americans say cell phone, and in speech British people usually just say 'mobile'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I use my mobile phone for almost everything now, including tickets and banking.
example_sentences: Mobile phone ownership has reached nearly 100 per cent in most European countries.
Schools in several countries have banned mobile phones during lessons.

chunk.pattern: a mobile phone / on your mobile

contexts.text: Do you use your mobile phone a lot? Probably more than I should.
contexts.note: One of the most predictable Part 1 topics.

contexts.text: Banning mobile phones in classrooms improves concentration, according to several studies.
contexts.note: A recurring Task 2 question.

contexts.text: In British speech the noun is usually shortened: I left my mobile at home.

confusables.difference: 'Cell phone' is American; 'mobile phone' is British. Since the examiner voices are British, 'mobile' is the safer choice.
minimal_pair: mobile phone
cell phone

entry_json.avoid: Not 'handy' or 'portable' for a phone, and remember it is countable: 'a mobile phone', not 'mobile phone'.

entry_json.definition: increasing steadily over time. Before a noun it means a growing number; before an adjective it means increasingly: more and more expensive.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: More and more people are choosing to rent rather than buy, and not always by choice.
example_sentences: Housing in the centre is becoming more and more expensive.
More and more of the work is done by machines rather than people.

contexts.text: More and more employers now allow staff to work from home at least part of the week.
contexts.note: A common Task 2 opener; use it once, not in every paragraph.

contexts.text: With long adjectives the pattern is 'more and more': more and more complicated, not complicateder.
Short adjectives double instead: bigger and bigger, worse and worse.
contexts.note: The parallel pattern for one-syllable adjectives.

confusables.difference: 'Increasingly' is a single adverb and is more formal: increasingly expensive. 'More and more' is the everyday equivalent and also works before nouns.
minimal_pair: more and more expensive
increasingly expensive

entry_json.avoid: Do not use it with a short adjective: 'more and more big' should be 'bigger and bigger'.
