entry_json.definition: approximately, or almost completely. It softens a statement, and can go before an adjective, before a verb, or after a number.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The work is more or less finished; there are only a few small things left.
example_sentences: The two figures are more or less the same.
It takes an hour, more or less, depending on the traffic.

contexts.text: The figures for the two years are more or less identical.
contexts.note: Acceptable in Task 1, though 'broadly similar' is more formal.

contexts.text: I have more or less decided to apply, but I want to see the fees first.
In writing prefer 'approximately' or 'broadly': the two totals are broadly equal.
contexts.note: Register upgrade.

confusables.difference: 'Roughly' is used mainly with numbers: roughly 200 people. 'More or less' also works with adjectives and verbs: more or less finished.
minimal_pair: roughly 200 people
more or less finished

entry_json.avoid: The order is fixed: never 'less or more'.

entry_json.definition: above a stated amount, or, before an adjective, very: more than happy to help. With a number the noun stays plural.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: More than half of the city's residents live within ten minutes of a park.
example_sentences: More than 200 people applied for the three places.
I would be more than happy to send you the details.

contexts.text: More than three quarters of journeys under two kilometres are still made by car.
contexts.note: Core Task 1 proportion language.

contexts.text: Before an adjective it means 'very': I would be more than willing to help.
contexts.note: A polite formula in letters.

contexts.text: The verb agrees with the noun: more than half of the students are, more than half of the money is.
contexts.note: Agreement rule.

confusables.difference: With numbers they are interchangeable: more than 200, over 200. 'More than' is slightly more formal and is safer in academic writing.
minimal_pair: more than 200 people
over 200 people

entry_json.avoid: Not 'more than of half'. And keep the noun plural after a number: more than three years, not year.

entry_json.definition: to leave one place, job or subject and go to the next, or to stop dwelling on something that has ended. Without 'to' it takes no object.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: After four years in the same role I felt it was time to move on.
example_sentences: Let us move on; we have three more points to cover.
It took her a year to move on after the business closed.

contexts.text: I stayed two years and then moved on to a larger company.
Communities affected by the closure found it hard to move on economically.
With an object you need 'to': let us move on to the second question.
contexts.note: Pattern note.

confusables.difference: Move out means leave the place where you were living. Move on means progress to the next stage of life, work or discussion.
minimal_pair: I moved out of my parents' house.
I moved on to a better job.

entry_json.avoid: Do not add an object without 'to': 'move on the next point' is wrong.

entry_json.definition: to go from one topic, stage or activity to the next. In a talk or an essay it signals a change of subject, and the new topic follows 'to'.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Having looked at the causes, I will now move on to the possible solutions.
example_sentences: Let us move on to the question of cost.
After a year in the basic class I moved on to the intermediate one.
collocations: move on to the next point
move on to a new topic

contexts.text: Having considered the environmental case, this essay moves on to the economic one.
contexts.note: A clear signpost between paragraphs in Task 2.

contexts.text: Shall we move on to the next question? Yes, I think we have covered that one.
After 'to' a verb takes -ing: we moved on to discussing the budget.
contexts.note: 'To' is a preposition here.

confusables.difference: 'Go on to do' describes what somebody did next in their life or career and takes an infinitive. 'Move on to' changes topic or stage and takes a noun or -ing.
minimal_pair: She went on to study medicine.
Let us move on to the next section.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'move on to discuss' when you mean the activity: it should be 'move on to discussing'.

entry_json.definition: considerably better. 'Much' is one of the few intensifiers that works with a comparative, alongside far, a lot and rather.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The new bus service is much better than the one it replaced, though it is still not frequent enough.
example_sentences: I sleep much better since I stopped looking at my phone in bed.
The results were much better than anyone had predicted.

contexts.text: The rail network in Japan is much better integrated than most European systems.
I feel much better than I did last week, thank you.
'Very' cannot be used here: 'very better' is impossible in English.
contexts.note: The rule this phrase teaches.

confusables.difference: 'Very' modifies a plain adjective: very good. Comparatives take 'much', 'far' or 'a lot': much better.
minimal_pair: very good
much better

entry_json.avoid: Never 'very better' and never 'much gooder'. The comparative of good is 'better', intensified with 'much' or 'far'.

entry_json.definition: in the month after this one. Like 'last month' it takes no preposition and no article, and it goes with future forms or the present continuous for arrangements.
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I start the new job next month, so this is my last week here.
example_sentences: The new timetable comes into force next month.
We are moving next month, which is why the flat is full of boxes.
collocations: by the end of next month

contexts.text: What are you doing next month? I am taking the exam, finally.
contexts.note: Present continuous for a fixed arrangement.

contexts.text: I would be grateful if the work could be completed before the end of next month.
'The next month' means the coming thirty days: over the next month, prices are expected to fall.
contexts.note: The article changes the meaning.

confusables.difference: 'Next month' is the following calendar month. 'The next month' is the coming period of thirty days, usually with 'over' or 'for'.
minimal_pair: I start next month.
Over the next month I have three deadlines.

entry_json.avoid: Never 'in next month' or 'on next month'. And do not use the past simple with it.
